title: The Environmental Macroeconomics of the Circular Economy
text:
The pages
This appendix gives a reader of the paper three things more: the complete proofs of the results the paper proves only in sketch, numbered O.1, O.2 and so on in the order the paper cites them; the robustness checks it names, one family to a page; and figures to move, each with a table view and its data. Each page stands alone. It opens with what the paper states and where, uses the paper’s notation, which the notation page collects, and needs nothing beyond the paper and the pages it links.
The data behind the figures: century.json, taxonomy.json, surface.json, leakage.json, corners.json, gatefee.json, phases.json, cn.json, experiments.json, instruments.json and sensitivity.json.

title: Notation
text:
Rules
This page collects the paper’s symbols, with their meanings and units, and the rules by which they are formed. It is to be consulted, not read: each symbol is defined in the paper where it is introduced, and the pages of this appendix use it with that meaning.

title: Notation
text:
A superscript names a use or a process; a subscript names time. \(K^Y\) is capital in production, \(K^R\) capital in recycling, \(C^N\) the cost of extraction, \(W^Y\) the waste from production. The period subscript is suppressed wherever timing carries no content and written wherever it does, which in practice means the transition equations. The exogenous time argument of a primitive (\(F\), \(a\), \(C^N\), \(C^D\), \(c^c\), \(c^T\)) is suppressed on the same terms.
A stock is dated at the beginning of its period; a flow occurs during it. A transition equation therefore states what the period-\(t\) flows leave behind for \(t+1\). This is capital-style dating and it fixes, once, which period a costate attaches to: the period in which the transition it prices is chosen.
A calligraphic capital is a function, a base or an aggregate, never a quantity of the same kind as its Roman counterpart. \(\mathcal F\) is the technology whose value is \(Y\); \(\mathcal R\) is the recycling technology whose value is \(R^R\); \(\mathcal W\) is the waste stock whose per-period outflow is \(H\); \(\mathcal D\) is the base of the intensity condition and \(\mathcal N\) the displaced mass; \(\mathcal G^{\varpi}\) and \(\mathcal G^{K}\) are the two recycling margins.
\(\lambda\) is the multiplier on the goods constraint, in utils per final good, and every shadow price is stated net of it. Dividing by \(\lambda\) is what puts \(p^S\), \(p^X\), \(p^P\), \(p^{\mathcal W}\), \(p^M\), \(p^W\), \(\zeta\) and \(\Psi\) into final goods per tonne. Sign conventions are carried in the definitions, not in the symbols.
\(\Omega\) is the material intensity of the final good and \(\omega^j\) the relative intensity of use \(j\), so that \(\Omega^j=\Omega\omega^j\) carries units and \(\omega^j\) is a pure number. The same split applies to the durables coefficient: \(\Phi^I=\Omega\phi^I\). The nature-attributable intensities \(\Omega^{N,S}\) and \(\Omega^{D,S}\) convert tonnage to tonnage and are pure numbers despite the capital letter, because the mass they carry never passes through \(Y\). The two families are not comparable.
A bar is a bound, and it is the same kind of object in every case. \(\bar R\) the material floor, \(\bar a\) the yield ceiling, \(\bar X_{\max}\) the exhaustion point of discovery.
A per-period rate lies in \((0,1)\): \(\delta\), \(\theta\), \(d^W\) and the handling share \(\mu\), whose limit \(\mu=1\) is the one-period buffer \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=W_t\). An elasticity and a discount rate do not, and never take those letters.
Growth is stated through positive gross factors. A variable grows at rate \(g\) when \(Z_{t+1}/Z_t\to1+g\) with \(1+g>0\), and decays at rate \(\nu\in(0,1)\) when \(Z_{t+1}/Z_t\to1-\nu\), so a decay rate is a share lost per period, like \(\delta\) and \(\mu\), and a growth factor of a product is the product of the factors. A variable whose ratio \(Z_{t+1}/Z_t\) tends to zero falls faster than at every geometric rate and has no rate. Where growth factors must be solved for, the equations are linear in their logarithms, and the solution is reported back as a factor.
One symbol, one meaning. A symbol on this page has the meaning given here wherever the paper and this appendix use it; a symbol the paper needs and this page does not carry is defined where the paper introduces it.

title: O.1 Which long-run states each cell makes available
text:
The statement
Proposition 4 of the paper (availability) states which of the three long-run states each cell of the taxonomy makes available, and what a candidate in state B or C must look like. This page proves it in full. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page; a symbol a proof needs beyond them is defined where it is first used. Lemma A, the collected ledger (L) and the first-order conditions (C), (G), (KR), (T) and (PP) are proved on the page of lemmas shared by the long-run proofs, and the workhorse clause of item (iii) rests on Lemmas W1 and W2 of the page on the workhorse’s balanced paths.
Proposition 4 (availability). Under Assumption 1, along paths that converge in the sense of its part (ii):
(i) With a floor. State A is available, and state B is not. Under the hard ceiling every feasible path is in state A, whatever \(g_A\) and \(g_B\). Under the soft ceiling a path that operates infinitely often closes the loop and has \(\mathcal M_\infty\ge\bar R\,\mathcal T\), and it operates from some date on if \(R_\infty>\bar R\). Hence state C is available only if some feasible path closes the loop with \(\mathcal M_\infty>\bar R\,\mathcal T\), which requires \(\mu\mathcal B>\bar R\); a path with \(\mathcal M_\infty<\bar R\,\mathcal T\) collapses, and so does every path if \(\mu\mathcal B<\bar R\).
(ii) Without a floor. State A is not available, and under the hard ceiling state C is not available. Where state B is available its margins obey the bound of Lemma B.1.
(iii) Candidates. In either soft-ceiling cell a candidate state-C path exists only if the closure criterion of Proposition 7 holds, and with a floor a candidate whose yield fails it collapses. In the Cobb-Douglas workhorse of Section 3.6 the circular balanced growth path is a candidate configuration under these conditions, subject to two inequalities on its wedges (Appendix B.6), and a candidate state-B path with converging recycling margins has the rates of Appendix B.6, which exist exactly when \(\left(\mu_N-1\right)\left(1-\beta_K\right)+\gamma>0\).
We take the simplest route for the paper’s assumptions. Items (i) and (ii) and the first sentence of item (iii) hold for general primitives and follow from the constraints of Problem 1 and the accounting; a first-order condition enters only through the definition of a candidate. The second sentence of item (iii) is a statement about the workhorse, proved from the first-order conditions of Appendix A with the two inequalities on the wedges taken as given; we prove nothing about whether they hold.

title: O.1 Which long-run states each cell makes available
text:
What the proofs use
The shared page restates a feasible path with the mass restrictions, the displaced mass \(\mathcal N\) and the emission flow \(\Xi=\Xi^h+\mathcal N\), the material budget \(\mathcal B=\bar N+M^K_0+\mathcal W_0\) with the virgin budget \(\bar N=S_0+\bar X_{\max}-X_0\), the loop closing, the operating set \(\mathcal O\), states A and C of Definition 1, availability and candidates, and Assumption 1(i) and (ii). We use in addition:

State B (Definition 1): “balanced dematerialization if \(C_t>0\) at every date and, asymptotically, \(C\), \(Y\) and \(K^Y\) grow at a common rate \(g\) with \(Y/C\) bounded above and away from zero, while \(R\) and \(\mathcal W\) decay at a common rate \(\nu\in\left(0,1\right)\)”.
Assumption 1(iii): “\(\theta\left(P\right)\ge\theta_{\min}>0\) for all \(P\), and \(\rho+\theta\left(P\right)+\theta'\left(P\right)P>0\) on the relevant range”. We use its first half.
The storage share and the residence time. Appendix A writes \(\sigma\equiv\Phi^IG/R\) for the storage share, and Proposition 3 writes \(\mathcal T\equiv1/\mu+\sigma_\infty/\delta\) for the mean residence time of a tonne per pass, with \(\sigma_\infty\) the limit of \(\sigma_t\) along the path; the retained material endowment is \(\mathcal M_\infty\equiv\lim_t\left(M^K_t+\mathcal W_t\right)\).
The closure criterion (Proposition 7). At a date with \(\varpi_tH_t>0\), \(x_t=K^R_t/\left(\varpi_tH_t\right)\) and the leakage rate of a treated tonne is \(L_t\equiv1-a_t\). Along a candidate whose recycling-capital margin (KR) is interior with \(\mathcal G^K_t\ne0\) from a date \(T_0\) on, the closure criterion is \(\sum_{t\ge T_0}L_t<\infty\); the candidate’s yield fails it when such a \(T_0\) exists and \(\sum_{t\ge T_0}L_t=\infty\).
The loss rate of the waste stock, \(\ell_t\equiv\mu\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)\), the share of the stock at the start of period \(t\) that is handled and not recovered. With \(H_t=\mu\mathcal W_t\), the collected ledger of Section 2, \(\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)H_t=N_t-\Delta M^K_{t+1}-\Delta\mathcal W_{t+1}\), reads \(\mathcal W_{t+1}-\mathcal W_t=N_t-\left(M^K_{t+1}-M^K_t\right)-\ell_t\mathcal W_t\).

Two short lemmas complete the list.
Lemma L (the flow identity of Little’s law). On a feasible path along which \(N_t\to0\), \(a_t\varpi_t\to1\), and \(R_t\), \(M^K_t\) and \(\mathcal W_t\) converge, with \(R_\infty\equiv\lim_tR_t>0\): \(\sigma_t\) converges, to \(\sigma_\infty=\delta M^K_\infty/R_\infty\ge0\), and \(\mathcal M_\infty=R_\infty\mathcal T\) with \(\mathcal T\ge1/\mu\).

Proof. Since \(R_t=N_t+a_t\varpi_t\mu\mathcal W_t\), \(R_\infty=\mu\mathcal W_\infty\). The transition of embodied material gives \(\Phi^I_tG_t=M^K_{t+1}-\left(1-\delta\right)M^K_t\to\delta M^K_\infty\), so \(\sigma_t=\Phi^I_tG_t/R_t\to\delta M^K_\infty/R_\infty\), which is nonnegative because \(M^K_t\ge0\). Adding the two stocks, \(\mathcal M_\infty=R_\infty/\mu+\sigma_\infty R_\infty/\delta=R_\infty\mathcal T\), and \(\sigma_\infty\ge0\) gives \(\mathcal T\ge1/\mu\).

Lemma B (the bound of the paper’s Lemma B.1). Along a feasible path in state B with decay rate \(\nu\) on which \(M^K\) is eventually nonincreasing, \(\liminf_t\ell_t\ge\nu\), that is \(\limsup_ta_t\varpi_t\le1-\nu/\mu\); so \(\nu\le\mu\), with equality only if \(a\varpi\to0\), and under the hard ceiling a path with \(a_t\to\bar a\) and \(\varpi_t\to1\) has \(\nu\le\mu\left(1-\bar a\right)\).

Proof. Since \(\mathcal W\) decays at rate \(\nu\), \(\mathcal W_t>0\) from some date on, and there the ledger divided by \(\mathcal W_t\) gives \[
\ell_t=\frac{N_t-\left(M^K_{t+1}-M^K_t\right)}{\mathcal W_t}+1-\frac{\mathcal W_{t+1}}{\mathcal W_t} .
\] Once \(M^K\) is nonincreasing the first term is nonnegative, as \(N_t\ge0\), and the second tends to \(\nu\); so \(\liminf_t\ell_t\ge\nu\), which is \(\limsup_ta_t\varpi_t\le1-\nu/\mu\). Since \(a_t\varpi_t\ge0\), \(\ell_t\le\mu\) at every date, so \(\nu\le\mu\), and \(\nu=\mu\) forces \(\limsup_ta_t\varpi_t\le0\), that is \(a\varpi\to0\). If \(a_t\to\bar a\) and \(\varpi_t\to1\), then \(a_t\varpi_t\to\bar a\le1-\nu/\mu\).

title: O.1 Which long-run states each cell makes available
text:
Proof of item (i)
Let \(\bar R>0\).

Proof. State A is available. Fix \(\varkappa\in\left(0,1-\delta\right)\) and set, at every date, \(N_t=D_t=0\), \(\varpi_t=0\), \(K^R_t=0\), \(\Omega_t=0\), \(K_{t+1}=\varkappa K_t\), \(C_t=\left(1-\delta-\varkappa\right)K_t\) and \(W_t=\delta M^K_t\), the states following the transitions of Problem 1. Nothing is treated, so \(R^R_t=0\) and \(R_t=0<\bar R\): no date operates, and \(Y_t=0\). The cost flows are zero, by \(C^N\left(0,S,t\right)=C^D\left(0,X,t\right)=0\) and \(C^W_t=\left[c^c\cdot0+c^T\left(0\right)\right]H_t=0\), and \(C_t+I_t+\delta K_t=\left[\left(1-\delta-\varkappa\right)+\left(\varkappa-1\right)+\delta\right]K_t=0=Y_t\): the goods constraint holds. The intensity condition holds as \(0=0\). With \(\Phi^I_t=\Omega_t\phi^I=0\), \(M^K_{t+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)M^K_t\), and the ledger \(W_t=R_t-\left(M^K_{t+1}-M^K_t\right)=\delta M^K_t\) holds. The domains hold: \(C_t,K_{t+1}\ge0\) from \(K_0\ge0\), \(W_t\ge0\), and the mass restrictions \(S_t=S_0\ge0\), \(X_t=X_0\le\bar X_{\max}\), \(M^K_t=\left(1-\delta\right)^tM^K_0\ge0\). So the path is feasible, \(\mathcal O\) is empty and finite, and the path is in state A. It converges in the sense of Assumption 1(ii): \(K\) and \(C\) have the constant ratio \(\varkappa\), or are zero; \(Y\) and the flows \(N\), \(D\), \(R\) are zero; \(S\) and \(X\) are constant; \(M^K_t\to0\), and \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W_t+\delta M^K_t\to0\). Pollution converges too: \(\mathcal N_t=0\), so \(\Xi_t=\Xi^h_t=\mu\mathcal W_t\to0\), and \(P_{t+1}\le\left(1-\theta_{\min}\right)P_t+\Xi_t\) by Assumption 1(iii); for any \(b>0\), once \(\Xi_s\le b\,\theta_{\min}\) for all \(s\ge t\), \(P_{t+n}\le\left(1-\theta_{\min}\right)^nP_t+b\), so \(P_t\to0\).
State B is not available. On a path in state B, \(R\) decays at a rate \(\nu\in\left(0,1\right)\), so \(R_t\to0\), and \(R_t<\bar R\) from some date on; there \(Y_t=0\) while \(C_t>0\), so \(Y_t/C_t=0\) is not bounded away from zero. No feasible path is in state B.
The hard ceiling. At a date with a treated flow, \(a_t\varpi_t\le a\left(x_t,t\right)<\bar a\), the yield staying below its ceiling at every finite intensity; at a date without one, \(a_t\varpi_t=0\). So \(\left(1-\bar a\right)H_t\le\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)H_t\), and Lemma A(b) gives \(\sum_tH_t\le\mathcal B/\left(1-\bar a\right)\). With \(R_t=N_t+a_t\varpi_tH_t\le N_t+\bar aH_t\) and Lemma A(a), \[
\sum_{t\ge0}R_t\;\le\;\bar N+\frac{\bar a\,\mathcal B}{1-\bar a}\;\equiv\;\bar{\mathcal R}.
\] Every operating date has \(R_t\ge\bar R\), so \(\bar R\cdot\#\mathcal O\le\bar{\mathcal R}\): \(\mathcal O\) is finite, and the path is in state A by the gloss of Definition 1(A) on the shared page. No property of \(F\) was used, so this holds whatever \(g_A\) and \(g_B\), and on every feasible path.
The soft ceiling: a path that operates infinitely often. Let a path converge in the sense of Assumption 1(ii), with \(\mathcal O\) infinite. \(R\) is a material flow, so it decays at a constant rate or converges, and it is bounded, \(R_t\le N_t+\mu\mathcal B\le\bar N+\mu\mathcal B\) by Lemma A; either way \(R_t\to R_\infty\) for a finite \(R_\infty\ge0\). Since \(R_t\ge\bar R\) at infinitely many dates, \(R_\infty\ge\bar R>0\). Lemma A(c) closes the loop, so \(a_t\varpi_t\to1\); \(N_t\to0\) by Lemma A(a); and \(M^K\) and \(\mathcal W\), material stocks, decay at constant rates or converge, and converge either way. Lemma L gives \(\mathcal M_\infty=R_\infty\mathcal T\ge\bar R\,\mathcal T\). If \(R_\infty>\bar R\), then \(R_t>\bar R\) from some date on, and the path operates from that date on.
State C is available only if some feasible path closes the loop with \(\mathcal M_\infty>\bar R\,\mathcal T\). A feasible path in state C has \(R_t\to R_\infty>\bar R>0\), \(N_t\to0\), \(a_t\varpi_t\to1\) and both stocks convergent, by Definition 1(C). Lemma A(c) closes its loop, and Lemma L gives \(\mathcal M_\infty=R_\infty\mathcal T>\bar R\,\mathcal T\). As \(\mathcal M_\infty\le\mathcal B\) by Lemma A(b) and \(\mathcal T\ge1/\mu\), \[
\frac{\bar R}{\mu}\;\le\;\bar R\,\mathcal T\;<\;\mathcal M_\infty\;\le\;\mathcal B,
\] so \(\mu\mathcal B>\bar R\).
A path with \(\mathcal M_\infty<\bar R\,\mathcal T\) collapses. Let a path that converges in the sense of Assumption 1(ii) have \(\mathcal M_\infty<\bar R\,\mathcal T\), with \(\mathcal T\) formed from the limit \(\sigma_\infty\) of its storage shares. If \(\mathcal O\) were infinite, the argument for a path that operates infinitely often would give \(\mathcal M_\infty=R_\infty\mathcal T\ge\bar R\,\mathcal T\) with the same \(\sigma_\infty\). So \(\mathcal O\) is finite, and the path is in state A.
Every path collapses if \(\mu\mathcal B<\bar R\). On every feasible path \(R_t\le N_t+\mu\mathcal B\) by Lemma A(b), and \(N_t\to0\) by Lemma A(a). If \(\mu\mathcal B<\bar R\), then \(R_t<\bar R\) from some date on, \(\mathcal O\) is finite, and the path is in state A, under either ceiling and whether or not it converges.

Proof of item (ii)
Let \(\bar R=0\).

Proof. State A is not available. \(R_t=N_t+R^R_t\ge0=\bar R\) at every date, so on every feasible path \(\mathcal O\) is the set of all dates, which is infinite.
Under the hard ceiling state C is not available. State C requires \(a_t\varpi_t\to1\), while under the hard ceiling \(a_t\varpi_t<\bar a<1\) at every date, as in the proof of item (i).
The margins of state B. Wherever a state-B path exists, Lemma B bounds its margins where \(M^K\) is eventually nonincreasing: this is the bound of the paper’s Lemma B.1.

title: O.1 Which long-run states each cell makes available
text:
Proof of item (iii), first sentence

Proof. A candidate in state C meets the criterion. Let a candidate be in state C, in either soft-ceiling cell. Then \(R_t\to R_\infty>\bar R\ge0\), so the loop closes by Lemma A(c), as Definition 1(C) also states. Let \(T_0\) be a date from which (KR) is interior with \(\mathcal G^K_t\ne0\); then \(K^R_t>0\) and \(\varpi_tH_t>0\), so \(x_t\) and \(L_t\) are defined, for \(t\ge T_0\). Since \(0\le a_t\le1\) and \(\varpi_t\le1\), \(L_t=1-a_t\le1-a_t\varpi_t\), and \[
\sum_{t\ge T_0}L_t\;\le\;\sum_{t\ge T_0}\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)\;<\;\infty :
\] the closure criterion holds.
With a floor, a candidate whose yield fails the criterion collapses. Let \(\bar R>0\), and let a candidate that converges in the sense of Assumption 1(ii) fail the criterion: (KR) is interior with \(\mathcal G^K_t\ne0\) from some \(T_0\) on, and \(\sum_{t\ge T_0}L_t=\infty\). As in the proof of item (i), \(R_t\to R_\infty\) for a finite \(R_\infty\ge0\). If \(\mathcal O\) were infinite, \(R_\infty\ge\bar R>0\), Lemma A(c) would close the loop, and the inequality \(L_t\le1-a_t\varpi_t\) would make \(\sum_{t\ge T_0}L_t\) finite. So \(\mathcal O\) is finite: the candidate collapses.

title: O.1 Which long-run states each cell makes available
text:
Proof of item (iii), second sentence
Lemmas W1 and W2 of the workhorse page prove it. In the workhorse under the soft ceiling, Lemma W1 shows that along the circular balanced growth path the deflated prices of Appendix A are the closed-form block (B); that, if the extraction and discovery costs vanish against output, \(\left(C^N_t+C^D_t\right)/Y_t\to0\), the limit system has a solution at a capital-output ratio in the admissible range, and is admissible exactly under the two inequalities (WI) on its wedges; and that along the path the recycling-capital margin has a root at every late date with a summable leakage rate, and, if the marginal handling charge at full treatment, \(c^c\left(t\right)+c^{T\prime}\left(1,t\right)\), is bounded over time, treatment is full. So the closure criterion, the condition the first sentence places on a candidate in state C, holds along the margin: the path is a candidate configuration under these conditions, subject to the two inequalities. Lemma W2 derives the rates of the state-B candidates that Appendix B.6 describes, and shows that they exist exactly when \(\left(\mu_N-1\right)\left(1-\beta_K\right)+\gamma>0\).

title: O.1, continued: the workhorse’s balanced paths
text:
What the lemmas use
The second sentence of item (iii) of Proposition 4 of the paper (availability) makes two claims about the Cobb-Douglas workhorse of Section 3.6: its circular balanced growth path is a candidate configuration, subject to two inequalities on its wedges, and a candidate state-B path with converging recycling margins has the rates of Appendix B.6, which exist exactly when \(\left(\mu_N-1\right)\left(1-\beta_K\right)+\gamma>0\). This page proves both, as Lemmas W1 and W2. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page; Lemma A, Lemma P and the conditions (C), (G), (KR), (T) and (PP) are on the page of lemmas shared by the long-run proofs. We take the simplest route for the paper’s assumptions: the workhorse’s exponential yield makes the recycling-capital margin explicit, and we take the two inequalities on the wedges as given, proving nothing about whether they hold.
From the paper’s long-run section, besides what the shared page restates, the material budget \(\mathcal B\) among it:
The workhorse (Section 3.6 and Appendix B.6). For \(R\ge\bar R\), \(F=A_te^{-\kappa P}\left(K^Y\right)^{\beta_K}\left(B_tR^e\right)^{\gamma}\) with \(\kappa\ge0\), \(\beta_K,\gamma>0\), \(\beta_K+\gamma<1\) and the trends of Assumption 1(i), so that above the floor \(F_K=\beta_KY/K^Y\), \(F_R=\gamma Y/R^e\) and \(F_P=-\kappa Y\). The yield is exponential, \(a\left(x\right)=\bar a\left(1-e^{-\xi x}\right)\) with \(\xi>0\); under the soft ceiling \(a\left(x\right)=1-e^{-\xi x}\), \(a'\left(x\right)=\xi e^{-\xi x}\) and \(\alpha=a-a'x=1-\left(1+\xi x\right)e^{-\xi x}\). Appendix B.6 takes the forms of Section 3.6 “with the marginal extraction cost proportional to \(\left(S_{\mathrm{ref}}/S\right)^{\mu_N}\) as the reserve falls”, which we read as \(C^N_N=c_N\left(N,t\right)\left(S_{\mathrm{ref}}/S\right)^{\mu_N}\) with a factor \(c_N\) that does not depend on \(S\) and tends to a positive limit \(c_{N\infty}\) as \(N\to0\) and \(t\to\infty\). Utility is CRRA, \(u'\left(C\right)=C^{-\eta}\) with \(\eta>0\). Write \(\Gamma\equiv\left(1+g_A\right)\left(1+g_B\right)^{\gamma}\), which exceeds one since \(g_A+g_B>0\), and \(g^{\mathrm{circ}}\) for the rate with \(\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^{1-\beta_K}=\Gamma\). Section 2 has the collection and treatment charges “both charges positive and non-increasing in time”, so the handling cost per handled tonne at full treatment is at most \(c^c\left(0\right)+c^T\left(1,0\right)\).
The first-order conditions of Appendix A used. Besides (C), (G), (KR), (T) and (PP), Appendix A states the conditions in \(\Omega\), \(I\) and \(W\),  \[
\zeta=\sigma\left(p^W-p^M\right),
\tag{$\Omega$}
\]  \[
q=1-\Phi^I\left(1-\sigma\right)\left(p^W-p^M\right),
\tag{I}
\]  \[
p^W_t=-p^{\mathcal W}_t ,
\tag{W}
\] with the storage share \(\sigma\equiv\Phi^IG/R\); the costate recursions of capital, embodied material and the waste stock, with \(1+r_{t+1}\equiv\lambda_t/\left(\beta\lambda_{t+1}\right)\),  \[
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)q_t=\tilde F_{K,t+1}+\left(1-\delta\right)q_{t+1},
\tag{Q}
\]  \[
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^M_t=\delta\,p^W_{t+1}+\left(1-\delta\right)p^M_{t+1},
\tag{M}
\]  \[
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^{\mathcal W}_t=\mu\,h_{t+1}+\left(1-\mu\right)p^{\mathcal W}_{t+1},
\qquad
h\equiv\alpha\varpi\left(\Psi-p^W\right)-c^W\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)-p^P\left[1-\varpi\left(1-d^W\right)-d^W\alpha\varpi\right].
\tag{H}
\] The treatment margin is at its upper corner, \(\varpi=1\), when \(\mathcal G^\varpi\ge\left[c^c+c^{T\prime}\left(1\right)\right]\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)\). Appendix B.6: “Where a balanced price block is used we add two regularity conditions on the preference pair: \(1+r\equiv\left(1+\rho\right)\left(1+g\right)^{\eta}>1+g\), with \(\eta\) the elasticity of marginal utility, which also keeps lifetime utility finite on a path growing at \(g\)”. We use this first condition, which is \(\beta\left(1+g\right)^{1-\eta}<1\).
The circular balanced growth path. Appendix B.6 defines it and says what makes it a candidate configuration: “In full, the circular balanced growth path of Section 3.6 is a path along which, asymptotically, \(R_t\to R_\infty>\bar R\), \(\varpi_t=1\), \(a_t\to1\) with \(x_t\to\infty\), \(N,D\to0\) with \(\sum_tN_t<\infty\), \(P\to0\), and \(C\), \(K\), \(Y\) and every final-good flow grow at the common rate \(g^{\mathrm{circ}}\). […] Deflated by output per effective tonne, the prices of Appendix A solve a linear block in closed form, […]. The block is admissible only if the material value and the consumption wedge stay positive, inequalities that hold for small \(\phi^I\) and are properties of a calibration, not of the primitives. Treatment is full from a finite date on, by Proposition 7(b).” We take \(\varpi_t=1\) from a date \(T_1\) on, and \(C_t/Y_t\) and \(K_t/Y_t\) converging to positive limits \(c_Y\) and \(k\), as Assumption 1(ii) gives for a goods block growing at a common rate. We read “every final-good flow” as the uses of output other than the three cost flows \(C^N\), \(C^D\) and \(C^W\): the handling cost \(C^W\) stays bounded on the path, so the clause cannot cover it. Step 1 of the proof of Lemma W1 shows that \(C^W\) vanishes against output; part (c) of the lemma takes as a premise that the extraction and discovery costs do too, \(\left(C^N_t+C^D_t\right)/Y_t\to0\). We write \(g\) for the common rate until step 3 of the proof of Lemma W1 shows that the production function forces it to be \(g^{\mathrm{circ}}\). Write \(R^e_\infty\equiv R_\infty-\bar R>0\). For a price \(m\) in final goods per tonne, its deflated price is \(\hat m_t\equiv m_tR^e_\infty/Y_t\); and \(\hat\Omega_t\equiv\Omega_tY_t/R^e_\infty\), so that \(\zeta\Omega^j=\hat\zeta\hat\Omega\,\omega^j\) for every use \(j\). Lemma W1 states the block exactly, the two inequalities on its wedges being  \[
\hat\Psi\equiv\lim_t\hat\Psi_t>0,
\qquad
\lim_t\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^C_t\right)>0 .
\tag{WI}
\]

State B (Definition 1): “balanced dematerialization if \(C_t>0\) at every date and, asymptotically, \(C\), \(Y\) and \(K^Y\) grow at a common rate \(g\) with \(Y/C\) bounded above and away from zero, while \(R\) and \(\mathcal W\) decay at a common rate \(\nu\in\left(0,1\right)\)”.
Assumption 1(iii), first half: “\(\theta\left(P\right)\ge\theta_{\min}>0\) for all \(P\)”.
The closure criterion (Proposition 7): at a date with \(\varpi_tH_t>0\), \(x_t=K^R_t/\left(\varpi_tH_t\right)\) and the leakage rate is \(L_t\equiv1-a_t\); along a candidate whose margin (KR) is interior with \(\mathcal G^K_t\ne0\) from a date \(T_0\) on, the criterion is \(\sum_{t\ge T_0}L_t<\infty\).

title: O.1, continued: the workhorse’s balanced paths
text:
The circular balanced growth path
Lemma W1. Take the workhorse under the soft ceiling, and let the regularity condition \(r>g\) hold.
(a) Let a candidate be on the circular balanced growth path, with \(q_t\) and the deflated prices \(\hat\Psi_t\), \(\hat p^W_t\), \(\hat p^M_t\), \(\hat\zeta_t\) convergent, and with the wedges \(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t\) and \(1+\zeta_t\Omega^C_t\) converging to positive limits, which is the wedge provision of Appendix A in the limit. Then \(\left(1+g\right)^{1-\beta_K}=\Gamma\), so \(g=g^{\mathrm{circ}}>0\), and the limits are  \[
\hat\Psi=\frac{\gamma}{1+\Upsilon\left(1-\gamma\hat\Omega\omega^Y\right)},
\quad
\hat\zeta=-\Upsilon\hat\Psi,
\quad
\hat p^W=-\Theta_{\mathcal W}\hat\Psi,
\quad
\hat p^M=\Theta_M\hat p^W,
\quad
q_\infty=1+\phi^I\left(1-\sigma_\infty\right)\Theta_\sigma\hat\Omega\hat\Psi,
\tag{B}
\] with \(\Theta_{\mathcal W}\equiv\mu\left(1+g\right)/\left(r-g\right)\), \(\Theta_M\equiv\delta\left(1+g\right)/\left[1+r-\left(1-\delta\right)\left(1+g\right)\right]\in\left(0,1\right)\), \(\Theta_\sigma\equiv\left(1-\Theta_M\right)\Theta_{\mathcal W}>0\), \(\Upsilon\equiv\Theta_\sigma\sigma_\infty\ge0\), and \(\sigma_\infty\), \(\hat\Omega\) the limits of \(\sigma_t\), \(\hat\Omega_t\). The capital-output ratio satisfies the capital arbitrage \(\left(r+\delta\right)q_\infty k=\beta_K\left(1-\hat\zeta\hat\Omega\omega^Y\right)\). The limit of \(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t\) is positive exactly when \(\hat\Psi>0\), so the two positive limits are the inequalities (WI).
(b) Along the candidate of (a), from a finite date on, the recycling-capital margin (KR) has the unique root \(x_t=\xi^{-1}\ln\left(\xi\mathcal G^K_t/\tilde F_{K,t}\right)>0\); the leakage rate \(L_t\) falls at least geometrically, so the closure criterion holds and the loop closes along the margin; and \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t\to+\infty\), so the condition for the treatment margin’s upper corner holds if the marginal handling charge at full treatment, \(c^c\left(t\right)+c^{T\prime}\left(1,t\right)\), is bounded over \(t\).
(c) Conversely, take \(g=g^{\mathrm{circ}}\) and \(R_\infty>\bar R\), and let the extraction and discovery costs vanish against output, \(\left(C^N_t+C^D_t\right)/Y_t\to0\). The capital arbitrage, with the block (B) and the limits \(\sigma_\infty\) and \(\hat\Omega\) of step 1 below, has a root \(k\) with \(\left(g+\delta\right)k\in\left(0,1\right)\); and at a root where (WI) holds, the limits (B) satisfy the limit forms of (C), (\(\Omega\)), (I), (W), (Q), (M), (H) and of the definition of \(\Psi\).

Proof. Step 1: the intensities and the discount rate. By (C), \(\lambda_t=C_t^{-\eta}/\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^C_t\right)\); with \(C\) growing at \(g\) and the consumption wedge converging to a positive limit, \(1+r_{t+1}=\lambda_t/\left(\beta\lambda_{t+1}\right)\to\left(1+\rho\right)\left(1+g\right)^{\eta}=1+r\). Steps 2 and 3 take only this limit from this step, and step 3 shows that \(g>0\), which the rest of this step uses. Since \(G_t/Y_t=\left[K_{t+1}-\left(1-\delta\right)K_t\right]/Y_t\to\left(g+\delta\right)k>0\), and \(C^W_t/Y_t\to0\) as \(C^W_t=\left[c^c\left(t\right)+c^T\left(1,t\right)\right]H_t\le\left[c^c\left(0\right)+c^T\left(1,0\right)\right]\mu\mathcal B\) for \(t\ge T_1\), by the bound on the charges and Lemma A(b), the goods constraint gives \(c_Y=1-\left(g+\delta\right)k\) under the premise of (c). If \(\phi^I=0\), (\(\Omega\)) gives \(\zeta_t=0\) at every date, every wedge is one and \(\sigma_t=0\), and \(\hat\Omega\) enters what follows only multiplied by \(\hat\zeta\) or by \(\phi^I\). If \(\phi^I>0\), the material stock \(M^K\) converges, as Assumption 1(ii) has it decay at a constant rate or converge, and so does \(\Phi^I_tG_t=M^K_{t+1}-\left(1-\delta\right)M^K_t\), by the transition of embodied material; hence \(\sigma_t=\Phi^I_tG_t/R_t\), which the intensity condition writes as \(\phi^IG_t/\left(\mathcal D_t+\phi^IG_t\right)\in\left[0,1\right]\), converges to some \(\sigma_\infty\in\left[0,1\right]\), and \(\hat\Omega_t=\sigma_tR_tY_t/\left(\phi^IG_tR^e_\infty\right)\) converges to some \(\hat\Omega\ge0\). Under the premise of (c), as \(\mathcal D=\omega^YY+\omega^NC^N+\omega^DC^D+\omega^WC^W+\omega^CC\), \(\left(\mathcal D_t+\phi^IG_t\right)/Y_t\to\bar d\equiv\omega^Y+\omega^Cc_Y+\phi^I\left(g+\delta\right)k\ge\phi^I\left(g+\delta\right)k>0\), so that \(\hat\Omega=R_\infty/\left(\bar dR^e_\infty\right)\) and \(\sigma_\infty=\phi^I\left(g+\delta\right)k/\bar d\). Deflating a recursion of the form (Q), (M) or (H) multiplies its right side by \(Y_{t+1}/Y_t\to1+g\).
Step 2: the material-adjusted marginal product of capital. By (Q), \(\tilde F_{K,t+1}=\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)q_t-\left(1-\delta\right)q_{t+1}\to\left(r+\delta\right)q_\infty\). Let \(\vartheta_Y>0\) be the limit of \(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t\). Since \(K^Y_t\le K_t\), \(\tilde F_{K,t}=\beta_K\left(Y_t/K^Y_t\right)\left(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t\right)\ge\beta_K\left(Y_t/K_t\right)\left(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t\right)\to\beta_K\vartheta_Y/k>0\). So \(\tilde F_{K,t}\ge\underline F\) for a constant \(\underline F>0\) from some date on, and \(\left(r+\delta\right)q_\infty\ge\underline F>0\).
Step 3: the growth rate. By step 2, \(K^Y_t/Y_t=\beta_K\left(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t\right)/\tilde F_{K,t}\to k_Y\equiv\beta_K\vartheta_Y/\left[\left(r+\delta\right)q_\infty\right]>0\), so \(K^Y\) grows at \(g\), and the production function gives \[
\frac{Y_{t+1}}{Y_t}=\Gamma\,e^{-\kappa\left(P_{t+1}-P_t\right)}\left(\frac{K^Y_{t+1}}{K^Y_t}\right)^{\beta_K}\left(\frac{R^e_{t+1}}{R^e_t}\right)^{\gamma}\;\longrightarrow\;\Gamma\left(1+g\right)^{\beta_K},
\] since \(P_t\to0\) and \(R^e_t\to R^e_\infty>0\). The left side tends to \(1+g\), so \(\left(1+g\right)^{1-\beta_K}=\Gamma>1\) and \(g=g^{\mathrm{circ}}>0\): output grows geometrically.
Step 4: the root of (KR) grows at most linearly. Since \(x_t\to\infty\), from some date \(T_2\ge T_1\) on \(x_t\) is defined, finite and positive, so \(\varpi_tH_t>0\) and \(K^R_t>0\); and \(K^R_t<K_t\), since \(Y_t>0\) needs \(K^Y_t>0\). So (KR) holds, \(\xi e^{-\xi x_t}\mathcal G^K_t=\tilde F_{K,t}\); its root is unique, \(a'\) being strictly decreasing; and \(\mathcal G^K_t=\tilde F_{K,t}e^{\xi x_t}/\xi>0\), \(x_t=\xi^{-1}\ln\left(\xi\mathcal G^K_t/\tilde F_{K,t}\right)\). The pollution price grows at most geometrically: by (PP), \(\chi_{t+1}p^P_{t+1}=\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^P_t-\mathcal V_{t+1}\le\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^P_t\), since \(\mathcal V>0\) on a candidate, as the first part of the proof of Lemma P shows; and \(\chi_{t+1}=1-\theta\left(P_{t+1}\right)-\theta'\left(P_{t+1}\right)P_{t+1}\ge1-\theta\left(P_{t+1}\right)\to1-\theta\left(0\right)>0\) as \(P_t\to0\). So \(p^P_{t+1}\le\bar c\,p^P_t\) for a constant \(\bar c\) from some date on. With \(\hat\Psi_t\) and \(\hat p^W_t\) convergent and \(Y_t\) geometric, \(0<\mathcal G^K_t\le\left|\Psi_t\right|+\left|p^W_t\right|+d^Wp^P_t\) grows at most geometrically, and \(x_t\le\xi^{-1}\ln\left(\xi\mathcal G^K_t/\underline F\right)\) grows at most linearly. As \(H_t=\mu\mathcal W_t\le\mu\mathcal B\) by Lemma A(b), \(K^R_t=x_tH_t\) grows at most linearly, \(K^R_t/Y_t\to0\), and \(k_Y=k\): \(\left(r+\delta\right)q_\infty k=\beta_K\vartheta_Y\).
Step 5: the waste price. By (W), \(\hat p^{\mathcal W}_t=-\hat p^W_t\). For \(t\ge T_1\), \(\varpi_t=1\), the last bracket of \(h\) is \(d^W\left(1-\alpha_t\right)\), and \(\alpha_t=1-\left(1+\xi x_t\right)e^{-\xi x_t}\to1\). The handling charge per tonne is at most \(c^c\left(0\right)+c^T\left(1,0\right)\), so its deflated value tends to zero. For the pollution term, Lemma P applies, since \(\varpi_tH_t>0\) from \(T_2\) on, so a handled tonne emits and pollution is positive at a date, and it gives \(p^P_t\ge0\); \(d^Wp^P_t=\mathcal G^K_t-\left(\Psi_t-p^W_t\right)\) by (G), and \(\mathcal G^K_t\left(1-\alpha_t\right)=\left(1+\xi x_t\right)\tilde F_{K,t}/\xi\) by (KR); so \[
0\;\le\;d^W\hat p^P_t\left(1-\alpha_t\right)\;\le\;\frac{\left(1+\xi x_t\right)\tilde F_{K,t}R^e_\infty}{\xi\,Y_t}+\left|\hat\Psi_t-\hat p^W_t\right|\left(1-\alpha_t\right)\;\longrightarrow\;0
\] by steps 2 to 4. So the deflated dividend tends to \(\hat\Psi+\hat p^{\mathcal W}\), and the deflated (H) tends to \(\left(1+r\right)\hat p^{\mathcal W}=\left(1+g\right)\left[\mu\left(\hat\Psi+\hat p^{\mathcal W}\right)+\left(1-\mu\right)\hat p^{\mathcal W}\right]\), that is \(\left(r-g\right)\hat p^{\mathcal W}=\mu\left(1+g\right)\hat\Psi\): \(\hat p^W=-\Theta_{\mathcal W}\hat\Psi\).
Step 6: the block. The deflated (M) tends to \(\left(1+r\right)\hat p^M=\left(1+g\right)\left[\delta\hat p^W+\left(1-\delta\right)\hat p^M\right]\), and \(1+r>1+g>\left(1-\delta\right)\left(1+g\right)\) gives \(\hat p^M=\Theta_M\hat p^W\) with \(\Theta_M\in\left(0,1\right)\). (\(\Omega\)) gives \(\hat\zeta=\sigma_\infty\left(1-\Theta_M\right)\hat p^W=-\Upsilon\hat\Psi\). The definition \(\Psi=F_R\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)+\zeta\) with \(F_R=\gamma Y/R^e\) and \(R^e_t\to R^e_\infty\) gives \(\hat\Psi=\gamma\left(1-\hat\zeta\hat\Omega\omega^Y\right)+\hat\zeta\), so \(\hat\Psi\left[1+\Upsilon\left(1-\gamma\hat\Omega\omega^Y\right)\right]=\gamma\). As \(\gamma>0\) the bracket is not zero, and \(\hat\Psi\) is the first entry of (B). With \(\hat\zeta=-\Upsilon\hat\Psi\) the same identity reads \[
\vartheta_Y\;=\;1-\hat\zeta\hat\Omega\omega^Y\;=\;\frac{\left(1+\Upsilon\right)\hat\Psi}{\gamma},
\] so \(\vartheta_Y>0\) exactly when \(\hat\Psi>0\), and step 4’s relation is the capital arbitrage. Since \(\Phi^I\left(p^W-p^M\right)=\phi^I\hat\Omega\left(\hat p^W-\hat p^M\right)\), (I) in the limit gives \(q_\infty\) of (B), and \(q_\infty\ge1\). This proves (a).
Step 7: part (b). By Lemma P, which applies since \(\varpi_tH_t>0\) from \(T_2\) on, \(p^P_t\ge0\), so \(\mathcal G^K_t\ge\Psi_t-p^W_t=\left(\hat\Psi_t-\hat p^W_t\right)Y_t/R^e_\infty\), where \(\hat\Psi_t-\hat p^W_t\to\left(1+\Theta_{\mathcal W}\right)\hat\Psi>0\). So \(\xi\mathcal G^K_t>\tilde F_{K,t}\) at every late date, the root of step 4 is positive, and \[
L_t\;=\;1-a\left(x_t\right)\;=\;e^{-\xi x_t}\;=\;\frac{\tilde F_{K,t}}{\xi\,\mathcal G^K_t}\;\le\;\frac{\tilde F_{K,t}\,R^e_\infty}{\xi\left(\hat\Psi_t-\hat p^W_t\right)Y_t},
\] whose right side, with \(\tilde F_{K,t}\) convergent and \(Y_t\) growing at \(g>0\), is below \(\bar L\left(1+g/2\right)^{-t}\) for a constant \(\bar L\). So \(\sum_tL_t<\infty\): the closure criterion holds; and as \(\varpi_t=1\) from \(T_1\) on, \(\sum_t\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)<\infty\): the loop closes along the margin. By (G), Lemma P and \(d^W<1\), \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t=\alpha_t\mathcal G^K_t+\left(1-d^W\right)p^P_t\ge\alpha_t\mathcal G^K_t\to+\infty\). If the marginal handling charge at full treatment, \(c^c\left(t\right)+c^{T\prime}\left(1,t\right)\), is bounded over \(t\), as the last clause of (b) supposes, then, since the wedge \(1+\zeta_t\Omega^W_t=1+\hat\zeta_t\hat\Omega_t\omega^W\) converges, by step 1 and the convergence of \(\hat\zeta_t\), the marginal handling cost at full treatment, \(\left[c^c+c^{T\prime}\left(1\right)\right]\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^W_t\right)\), is bounded across dates. So \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t\ge\left[c^c+c^{T\prime}\left(1\right)\right]\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^W_t\right)\) from a finite date on, which is the condition for the upper corner.
Step 8: part (c). At \(\phi^I=0\), \(\sigma_\infty=\Upsilon=0\), (B) gives \(\hat\Psi=\gamma\), \(\hat\zeta=0\) and \(q_\infty=1\), (WI) holds, and the capital arbitrage has the root \(k=\beta_K/\left(r+\delta\right)\), with \(\left(g+\delta\right)k<\beta_K<1\) since \(r>g\). Let \(\phi^I>0\), and write \(s\equiv\left(g+\delta\right)k\). Through \(c_Y=1-s\), step 1 makes \(\bar d\), \(\sigma_\infty\) and \(\hat\Omega\) continuous functions of \(s\in\left(0,1\right]\): \(\bar d\left(s\right)=\omega^Y+\omega^C\left(1-s\right)+\phi^Is\), \(\sigma_\infty\left(s\right)=\phi^Is/\bar d\left(s\right)\le1\) and \(\hat\Omega\left(s\right)=R_\infty/\left[\bar d\left(s\right)R^e_\infty\right]\). Write \(D\left(s\right)\equiv1+\Upsilon\left(1-\gamma\hat\Omega\omega^Y\right)\). Where \(D\ne0\), (B) gives \(1-\hat\zeta\hat\Omega\omega^Y=\left(1+\Upsilon\right)/D\) and \(q_\infty=1+\phi^I\left(1-\sigma_\infty\right)\Theta_\sigma\hat\Omega\gamma/D\), and the capital arbitrage, multiplied by \(\left(g+\delta\right)D\), reads \(f\left(s\right)=0\) with \[
f\left(s\right)\equiv\left(r+\delta\right)s\left[1+\Theta_\sigma\sigma_\infty+E\left(s\right)\right]-\left(g+\delta\right)\beta_K\left(1+\Theta_\sigma\sigma_\infty\right),
\qquad
E\left(s\right)\equiv\frac{\Theta_\sigma\gamma\phi^IR_\infty\left(1-s\right)\left(\omega^Y+\omega^C\right)}{\bar d\left(s\right)^2R^e_\infty}\ge0,
\] because \(\phi^I\left(1-\sigma_\infty\right)-\sigma_\infty\omega^Y=\phi^I\left(1-s\right)\left(\omega^Y+\omega^C\right)/\bar d\). \(f\) is continuous on \(\left(0,1\right]\). If \(\omega^Y+\omega^C>0\), then \(\bar d\left(s\right)\ge\omega^Y+\min\left\{\omega^C,\phi^I\right\}>0\) on \(\left(0,1\right]\) and \(E\) is bounded; otherwise \(E=0\). Either way \(sE\left(s\right)\to0\) as \(s\to0\), and since \(\sigma_\infty\le1\), \(f\left(s\right)\le\left(r+\delta\right)s\left[1+\Theta_\sigma+E\left(s\right)\right]-\left(g+\delta\right)\beta_K<0\) for small \(s\). And \(E\left(1\right)=0\), so \(f\left(1\right)=\left(1+\Theta_\sigma\sigma_\infty\left(1\right)\right)\left[\left(r+\delta\right)-\left(g+\delta\right)\beta_K\right]>0\), since \(r>g\) and \(\beta_K<1\). So \(f\) has a root \(s\in\left(0,1\right)\), and \(k=s/\left(g+\delta\right)\). At a root where (WI) holds, \(D>0\), and \(f=0\) is the capital arbitrage itself. Steps 1 to 6 obtain (B) by solving the limit forms of (C), (\(\Omega\)), (I), (W), (Q), (M), (H) and of the definition of \(\Psi\), one entry at a time, so the limits (B) satisfy each of them: the limit form of (C), \(1+r=\left(1+\rho\right)\left(1+g\right)^{\eta}\), needs the limit consumption wedge \(1-\Upsilon\hat\Psi\hat\Omega\omega^C\) to be positive, which is the second inequality of (WI), and \(c_Y=1-s>0\).

Step 8 shows that the limit system has a solution at a capital-output ratio in the admissible range, and part (b) that along the path the recycling margins are met with the path’s own intensity and, when the marginal handling charge at full treatment is bounded, with full treatment. Of the extraction, exploration and pollution-price margins, the path asks only that extraction and discovery die out, and step 8 asks also that their costs vanish against output.

title: O.2 The closure criterion
text:
The statement
Proposition 7 of the paper (closure criterion) ties the leakage rate of a candidate path to the tail of the yield function. This page proves it in full. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page; a symbol a proof needs beyond them is defined where it is first used. The definitions the proof takes from the paper, the first-order conditions (G), (KR) and (T), Lemma P and Lemma A are on the page of lemmas shared by the long-run proofs.
Proposition 7 (closure criterion). Take a candidate path with \(R_t\to R_\infty>0\) and the recycling-capital margin (KR) interior from a date \(T_0\) on, with \(\mathcal G^K_t\ne0\) there. For \(t\ge T_0\) the margin has a unique solution \(x_t\), and the leakage rate equals the capital cost of recycling per treated tonne, relative to the value of a recovered tonne, divided by the tail elasticity, \[
L_t\;=\;J_t\left(x_t\right)\frac{\tilde F_{K,t}}{\mathcal G^K_t}
\;=\;\frac{\tilde F_{K,t}\,K^R_t}{\mathcal G^K_t\,\varpi_tH_t}\cdot\frac{1}{\epsilon_a\left(x_t\right)} ,
\] and the closure criterion is \(\sum_{t\ge T_0}L_t<\infty\).
(a) If the loop closes, the criterion holds.
(b) If the criterion holds, the loop closes provided either \(\sum_t\left(1-\varpi_t\right)<\infty\), or, under Assumption 1(i), \(\liminf_t\tilde F_{K,t}>0\) and the marginal handling cost at full treatment, \(\left[c^c+c^{T\prime}\left(1\right)\right]\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)\), is bounded across dates. In the second case, moreover, the ceiling is soft, \(x\to\infty\), \(\alpha\to1\), both recycling gains diverge, and treatment is full from a finite date on.
We take the simplest route for the paper’s assumptions. We prove Proposition 7 for general primitives, with no functional form. The margins (KR) and (T) and the gains (G) that they use are restated in The first-order conditions used on the shared page, and \(\epsilon_a\), \(J\) and \(L_t\) at the head of Proof of Proposition 7.

title: O.2 The closure criterion
text:
Proof of Proposition 7
The statement uses, as the paper defines them, the tail elasticity \(\epsilon_a\left(x\right)\equiv xa'\left(x\right)/\left[1-a\left(x\right)\right]\), its inverse measure \(J\left(x\right)\equiv\left[1-a\left(x\right)\right]/a'\left(x\right)=x/\epsilon_a\left(x\right)\), and the leakage rate \(L_t\equiv1-a_t\); \(J_t\) and \(\epsilon_a\) at date \(t\) are formed from \(a\left(\cdot,t\right)\). Assumption 1(i) enters only in step 4.

Proof. Step 1: the margin and the identity. Let \(t\ge T_0\). The margin (KR) holds with \(K^R_t>0\) and \(\varpi_tH_t>0\), so \(x_t=K^R_t/\left(\varpi_tH_t\right)\) is finite and positive. Since \(a'>0\) and \(\mathcal G^K_t\ne0\), (KR) gives \(\tilde F_{K,t}/\mathcal G^K_t=a'\left(x_t,t\right)>0\). Since \(a''<0\), \(a'\left(\cdot,t\right)\) is strictly decreasing, so the equation \(a'\left(x,t\right)\mathcal G^K_t=\tilde F_{K,t}\) has at most one solution in \(x\), and \(x_t\) is one. Then \[
J_t\left(x_t\right)\frac{\tilde F_{K,t}}{\mathcal G^K_t}=\frac{1-a_t}{a'\left(x_t,t\right)}\,a'\left(x_t,t\right)=1-a_t=L_t ,
\] and \(J_t\left(x_t\right)=x_t/\epsilon_a\left(x_t\right)\) with \(x_t=K^R_t/\left(\varpi_tH_t\right)\) gives the second form; \(\epsilon_a\left(x_t\right)\) is finite and positive because \(a'>0\) and \(a<1\) at every finite intensity.
Step 2: part (a). \(0\le a_t\le1\) and \(0\le\varpi_t\le1\) give \(L_t=1-a_t\le1-a_t\varpi_t\), so \(\sum_{t\ge T_0}L_t\le\sum_t\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)<\infty\) when the loop closes.
Step 3: part (b), first case. \(1-a_t\varpi_t=\left(1-a_t\right)+a_t\left(1-\varpi_t\right)\le L_t+\left(1-\varpi_t\right)\), since \(a_t\le1\). Summing over \(t\ge T_0\), and adding the finitely many terms before \(T_0\), each at most one, gives \(\sum_t\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)<\infty\).
Step 4: in the second case the ceiling is soft, \(x_t\to\infty\), \(\alpha_t\to1\) and \(\mathcal G^K_t\to+\infty\). The terms of a convergent series tend to zero, so \(L_t\to0\) and \(a_t\to1\). As \(a\left(x,t\right)<\bar a\) at every finite \(x\), this forces \(\bar a=1\): the ceiling is soft. If \(x_t\le\tilde x<\infty\) along a subsequence, then \(a_t\le a\left(\tilde x,t\right)\le a^\infty\left(\tilde x\right)<1\) along it, by Assumption 1(i), against \(a_t\to1\); so \(x_t\to\infty\). Concavity puts \(a\left(\cdot,t\right)\) below its tangent at \(x_t\), and at \(x_t/2\) this reads \(\tfrac12x_ta'\left(x_t,t\right)\le a\left(x_t,t\right)-a\left(x_t/2,t\right)\). As \(a\le1\) and \(a\) is nondecreasing in \(t\), \[
0\;<\;x_ta'\left(x_t,t\right)\;\le\;2\left[1-a\left(x_t/2,0\right)\right]\;\longrightarrow\;0 ,
\] because \(x_t\to\infty\) and \(a\left(x,0\right)\to\bar a=1\). Hence \(\alpha_t=a_t-x_ta'\left(x_t,t\right)\to1\) and \(a'\left(x_t,t\right)\to0\). By \(\liminf_t\tilde F_{K,t}>0\) there is \(\underline F>0\) with \(\tilde F_{K,t}\ge\underline F\) from some date on, and by step 1 \(\mathcal G^K_t=\tilde F_{K,t}/a'\left(x_t,t\right)\ge\underline F/a'\left(x_t,t\right)\to+\infty\).
Step 5: \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t\to+\infty\). Lemma P applies, since \(H_t>0\) from \(T_0\) on by step 1. By (G), (P) and \(d^W<1\), \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t=\alpha_t\mathcal G^K_t+\left(1-d^W\right)p^P_t\ge\alpha_t\mathcal G^K_t\ge\tfrac12\mathcal G^K_t\) once \(\alpha_t\ge\tfrac12\) and \(\mathcal G^K_t>0\), so \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t\to+\infty\). Both recycling gains diverge. This is the one use of Lemma P, and any bound \(p^P_t\ge\underline p\) with \(\underline p\) independent of \(t\) would serve, (P) being the case \(\underline p=0\).
Step 6: full treatment. Let \(m^{\mathrm{full}}_t\equiv\left[c^c\left(t\right)+c^{T\prime}\left(1,t\right)\right]\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^W_t\right)\), the marginal handling cost at full treatment, which the premise that it is bounded across dates bounds above by some \(\bar m\). Take \(t\ge T_0\) with \(\varpi_t<1\). Then \(\varpi_t>0\) and \(H_t>0\) by step 1, and (T) gives \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t=\left[c^c\left(t\right)+c^{T\prime}\left(\varpi_t,t\right)\right]\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^W_t\right)\). Since \(c^{T\prime}\left(0,t\right)=0\) and \(c^{T\prime\prime}>0\), \(0<c^c\left(t\right)\le c^c\left(t\right)+c^{T\prime}\left(\varpi_t,t\right)\le c^c\left(t\right)+c^{T\prime}\left(1,t\right)\), so \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t\le m^{\mathrm{full}}_t\) when \(1+\zeta_t\Omega^W_t\ge0\) and \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t<0\) otherwise. In both cases \(\mathcal G^\varpi_t\le\max\left\{\bar m,0\right\}\), which step 5 excludes from some date on. So \(\varpi_t=1\) from some date on, \(\sum_t\left(1-\varpi_t\right)<\infty\), and step 3 closes the loop.

The hypothesis \(R_t\to R_\infty>0\) is not used in (a) or (b). With it, Lemma A(c) closes the loop on every feasible candidate, so that on such a path the content of (b) is its list of consequences, full treatment from a finite date above all.

title: O.3 When state C is available: the tail condition and the workhorse’s path
text:
The statement
Section 3.5 of the paper (the closure criterion) states when state C is available at all, and this page proves it in full. That is a question about feasible paths rather than candidates. Under the soft ceiling no feasible path is in state C when the yield tail is too slow, and in the paper’s workhorse, with no new material stored in capital, state C is available exactly when \(\mu\mathcal B>\bar R\), from every initial capital stock above a threshold. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page; a symbol a proof needs beyond them is defined where it is first used. The definitions the proofs take from the paper, the collected ledger (L) and Lemma A are on the page of lemmas shared by the long-run proofs.
The availability of state C.
(a) Let the ceiling be soft and Assumption 1(i) hold, and let the limit yield function \(a^\infty\) have a slow tail, \(\int_1^\infty\left[1-a^\infty\left(x\right)\right]dx/x=\infty\). Then no feasible path is in state C, in either soft-ceiling cell and from any initial stocks. A logarithmic tail, \(1-a^\infty\left(x\right)\sim c\left(\ln\xi x\right)^{-\iota}\), is slow when \(\iota\le1\).
(b) Take the workhorse under the soft ceiling, with \(\phi^I=0\), \(\omega^Y,\omega^C>0\), and extraction and exploration costs that are finite at a positive reserve and below the exhaustion point of discovery. State C is available from some initial capital stock if and only if \(\mu\mathcal B>\bar R\), and then from every initial capital stock above a finite threshold that depends on the primitives and the other initial stocks. On the path constructed, consumption, capital and output grow at the circular rate \(g^{\mathrm{circ}}\), \(\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^{1-\beta_K}=\Gamma\), and its value is finite for \(\eta\ge1\), and for \(\eta<1\) when \(\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^{1-\eta}<1+\rho\).
We prove part (a) of the availability of state C for general primitives, and part (b) by a construction in the workhorse at \(\phi^I=0\), where the material embodied in capital only runs off; the workhorse’s exponential yield makes every intensity schedule explicit. The workhorse is restated at the head of Proof of the availability of state C.

title: O.3 When state C is available: the tail condition and the workhorse’s path
section: Proof of the availability of state C
text:
Proof of the availability of state C
The workhorse (the paper’s long-run section): output \(A_te^{-\kappa P}\left(K^Y\right)^{\beta_K}\left(B_tR^e\right)^{\gamma}\) for \(R\ge\bar R\), and zero below, with \(A_0,B_0>0\) and the trends of Assumption 1(i), \(\kappa\ge0\), \(\beta_K,\gamma>0\) and \(\beta_K+\gamma<1\); the exponential yield \(a\left(x\right)=\bar a\left(1-e^{-\xi x}\right)\), \(\xi>0\), which under the soft ceiling is \(1-e^{-\xi x}\); CRRA utility, \(u\left(C\right)=C^{1-\eta}/\left(1-\eta\right)\) with \(\eta>0\), \(\ln C\) at \(\eta=1\); and \(\Gamma\equiv\left(1+g_A\right)\left(1+g_B\right)^{\gamma}>1\).

(a) A slow tail
No first-order condition is used.

Proof. Suppose a feasible path is in state C. Then \(R_t\to R_\infty>\bar R\ge0\), so by Lemma A(c) there is a date \(T_2\) with \(H_t\ge\underline H\equiv R_\infty/2\) for \(t\ge T_2\), and the loop closes. As \(1-\varpi_t\le1-a_t\varpi_t\to0\), there is \(T_3\ge T_2\) with \(\varpi_t\ge\tfrac12\) for \(t\ge T_3\).
Capital grows at most geometrically. Output grows at the rate \(g>0\) of Definition 1, so for any \(\bar g>g\) there is a date after which \(Y_{t+1}\le\left(1+\bar g\right)Y_t\), and hence \(Y_t\le\bar Y\left(1+\bar g\right)^t\) at every date for some constant \(\bar Y\). The goods constraint, with consumption and the three cost flows nonnegative, gives \(K_{t+1}\le\left(1-\delta\right)K_t+Y_t\), and by induction \(K_t\le\bar K\left(1+\bar g\right)^t\) with \(\bar K\equiv K_0+\bar Y/\left(\bar g+\delta\right)\): if it holds at \(t\), then \(K_{t+1}\le\left(1+\bar g\right)^t\left[\left(1-\delta\right)\bar K+\bar Y\right]\le\left(1+\bar g\right)^t\left[\left(1-\delta\right)\bar K+\left(\bar g+\delta\right)\bar K\right]=\bar K\left(1+\bar g\right)^{t+1}\).
The leakage rate is bounded below. For \(t\ge T_3\), \(K^R_t\le K_t\) gives \(x_t=K^R_t/\left(\varpi_tH_t\right)\le2K_t/\underline H\le c_K\left(1+\bar g\right)^t\) with \(c_K\equiv2\bar K/\underline H\). Write \(L^\infty\equiv1-a^\infty\), which is nonincreasing. Since \(a\left(x,t\right)\le a^\infty\left(x\right)\), \[
1-a_t\varpi_t\;\ge\;1-a_t\;\ge\;L^\infty\left(x_t\right)\;\ge\;L^\infty\!\left(c_K\left(1+\bar g\right)^t\right)
\qquad\left(t\ge T_3\right).
\]
The slow tail. On \(\left[c_K\left(1+\bar g\right)^t,\,c_K\left(1+\bar g\right)^{t+1}\right]\), \(L^\infty\le L^\infty\!\left(c_K\left(1+\bar g\right)^t\right)\) and \(\int dx/x=\ln\left(1+\bar g\right)\), so \[
\int_{c_K\left(1+\bar g\right)^{T_3}}^{\infty}L^\infty\left(x\right)\frac{dx}{x}\;\le\;\ln\left(1+\bar g\right)\sum_{t\ge T_3}L^\infty\!\left(c_K\left(1+\bar g\right)^t\right).
\] The left side is infinite: as \(0\le L^\infty\le1\), it differs from \(\int_1^\infty L^\infty dx/x=\infty\) by at most \(\left|\ln\left[c_K\left(1+\bar g\right)^{T_3}\right]\right|\). So \(\sum_{t\ge T_3}\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)=\infty\), and the loop does not close: a contradiction.
The logarithmic tail. If \(1-a^\infty\left(x\right)\sim c\left(\ln\xi x\right)^{-\iota}\) with \(c>0\), there is \(\check x\) with \(\xi\check x>1\) and \(1-a^\infty\left(x\right)\ge\tfrac c2\left(\ln\xi x\right)^{-\iota}\) for \(x\ge\check x\), and with \(z=\ln\xi x\), \(\int_{\check x}^\infty\left(\ln\xi x\right)^{-\iota}dx/x=\int_{\ln\xi\check x}^\infty z^{-\iota}dz=\infty\) for \(\iota\le1\).



(b) The workhorse
The proof constructs the path. Throughout, the workhorse is under the soft ceiling, \(a\left(x\right)=1-e^{-\xi x}\), and \(\phi^I=0\), so \(\Phi^I=\Omega\phi^I=0\) and the material embodied in capital runs off, \(M^K_{t+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)M^K_t\), whatever the investment. Write \(c^{\mathrm{full}}_t\equiv c^c\left(t\right)+c^T\left(1,t\right)\) for the handling cost per handled tonne at full treatment, nonincreasing in \(t\).

Proof. Step 1: only if. On any feasible path in state C, \(R^R_t=a_t\varpi_t\mu\mathcal W_t\) with \(a_t\varpi_t\to1\) and \(\mathcal W_t\to\mathcal W_\infty\), so \(R_\infty=\lim_tR^R_t=\mu\mathcal W_\infty\le\mu\mathcal B\) by Lemma A(b). With \(R_\infty>\bar R\), \(\mu\mathcal B>\bar R\). This holds from any initial capital stock and for general primitives.
Step 2: closing the loop from a date \(T_1\). Let the stocks at a date \(T_1\), the initial ones if \(T_1=0\) and otherwise those of a path feasible through \(T_1-1\), satisfy \(\mathfrak m\equiv\mu\mathcal W_{T_1}-\bar R>0\). We show that there is \(\underline K_{T_1}<\infty\), depending on the primitives, on \(\left(\mathcal W_{T_1},M^K_{T_1},P_{T_1}\right)\) and on \(A_{T_1}\) and \(B_{T_1}\), such that from every \(K_{T_1}\ge\underline K_{T_1}\) a feasible continuation is in state C, with consumption at least a chosen \(\underline c>0\) at every date.
The intensity schedule. Choose \(\hat x>0\) with \(3e^{-\xi\hat x}\mu\mathcal W_{T_1}\le\mathfrak m/2\), and let \(\hat x_j\equiv\hat x+j/\xi\) for \(j\ge0\), so that \(1-a\left(\hat x_j\right)=e^{-\xi\hat x}e^{-j}\) and \[
\mu\sum_{j\ge0}\left[1-a\left(\hat x_j\right)\right]=\frac{e}{e-1}\,\mu e^{-\xi\hat x}\;\le\;\bar b\equiv2\mu e^{-\xi\hat x} .
\] Since \(\mathfrak m\le\mu\mathcal W_{T_1}\), the choice gives \(\bar b\le\mathfrak m/\left(3\mathcal W_{T_1}\right)<1\). Since \(\mu<1\), \(a\left(\hat x\right)\left(1-\bar b\right)\ge1-e^{-\xi\hat x}-\bar b\ge1-3e^{-\xi\hat x}\), so \(a\left(\hat x\right)\left(1-\bar b\right)\mu\mathcal W_{T_1}\ge\mu\mathcal W_{T_1}-\mathfrak m/2=\bar R+\mathfrak m/2\).
The material block. For \(t=T_1+j\) set \(N_t=D_t=0\), \(\varpi_t=1\) and \(K^R_t=\hat x_j\mu\mathcal W_t\), so that \(x_t=\hat x_j\) while \(\mathcal W_t>0\). Then \(\mathcal N_t=0\), \(R_t=R^R_t=a\left(\hat x_j\right)\mu\mathcal W_t\), the ledger gives \(W_t=R_t+\delta M^K_t\), and the transitions give \[
\mathcal W_{t+1}=\left[1-\mu e^{-\xi\hat x_j}\right]\mathcal W_t+\delta M^K_t,
\qquad
\mathcal M_{t+1}=\mathcal M_t-\mu e^{-\xi\hat x_j}\mathcal W_t,
\qquad
\Xi_t=d^W\mu e^{-\xi\hat x_j}\mathcal W_t .
\] None of this involves capital. Five facts follow, for every \(t\ge T_1\).

(M1) \(\mathcal W_t\ge\left(1-\bar b\right)\mathcal W_{T_1}>0\): the factors \(1-b_s\), \(b_s\equiv\mu e^{-\xi\hat x_s}\in\left[0,1\right]\), give \(\mathcal W_t\ge\mathcal W_{T_1}\prod_{s<j}\left(1-b_s\right)\ge\mathcal W_{T_1}\left(1-\sum_sb_s\right)\), the product bound following by induction from \(\left(1-\Sigma\right)\left(1-b\right)\ge1-\Sigma-b\) for \(\Sigma,b\ge0\).
(M2) \(R_t\ge a\left(\hat x\right)\left(1-\bar b\right)\mu\mathcal W_{T_1}\ge\bar R+\mathfrak m/2\), since \(\hat x_j\ge\hat x\): production runs at every date.
(M3) \(\mathcal M_t\) is nonincreasing, and \(\mathcal W_t\le\mathcal M_t\le\mathcal M_{T_1}\).
(M4) \(0\le P_t\le\bar P\equiv P_{T_1}+\mathcal M_{T_1}\): since \(d^W<1\), \(\Xi_t\le\mathcal M_t-\mathcal M_{t+1}\), and \(P_{t+1}=\left[1-\theta\left(P_t\right)\right]P_t+\Xi_t\) lies in \(\left[0,P_t+\Xi_t\right]\), so \(P_t\le P_{T_1}+\mathcal M_{T_1}-\mathcal M_t\).
(M5) \(M^K_t\to0\); \(\mathcal M_t\) decreases to a limit \(\mathcal M_\infty\ge\left(1-\bar b\right)\mathcal W_{T_1}>0\), and \(\mathcal W_t=\mathcal M_t-M^K_t\to\mathcal M_\infty\); \(x_t=\hat x_j\to\infty\) and \(a_t\to1\), with \(\sum_t\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)<\infty\) over the continuation; \(R_t\to R_\infty=\mu\mathcal M_\infty\ge\bar R+\mathfrak m/2\); and \(P_t\to0\). For the last, \(\theta\) is decreasing, so \(\theta\left(P_t\right)\ge\theta\left(\bar P\right)>0\) and \(P_{t+1}\le\left[1-\theta\left(\bar P\right)\right]P_t+\Xi_t\), with \(\Xi_t\le\mu e^{-\xi\hat x_j}\mathcal M_{T_1}\to0\). For any \(\varepsilon>0\), once \(\Xi_t\le\varepsilon\theta\left(\bar P\right)\), \(P_{t+n}\le\left[1-\theta\left(\bar P\right)\right]^nP_t+\varepsilon\).

The constants. Let \(\underline y\equiv A_{T_1}B_{T_1}^{\gamma}e^{-\kappa\bar P}\left(\mathfrak m/2\right)^{\gamma}>0\). Choose a production core \(k\in\left(0,\left[\underline y/\left(g^{\mathrm{circ}}+\delta\right)\right]^{1/\left(1-\beta_K\right)}\right)\), so that the core surplus \(\mathfrak s\equiv\underline y\,k^{\beta_K}-\left(g^{\mathrm{circ}}+\delta\right)k\) is positive, and any \(\underline c>0\). Since \(g^{\mathrm{circ}}>0\), the left side of  \[
\mathfrak s\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\;\ge\;\mu\mathcal M_{T_1}\left(\hat x_{j+1}+c^{\mathrm{full}}_{T_1}\right)+\underline c
\tag{S}
\] grows geometrically in \(j\) and the right side linearly; let \(j^*\) be the least integer such that (S) holds for every \(j\ge j^*\). Let \(\bar G\equiv\left(g^{\mathrm{circ}}+\delta\right)k\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^{j^*}+\mu\mathcal M_{T_1}\hat x_{j^*}\), \(\vartheta\equiv\min\left\{1,\Gamma\left(1-\delta\right)^{\beta_K}\right\}\), \(\underline E\equiv0\) if \(j^*=0\) and otherwise \[
\underline E\;\equiv\;\left[\frac{\bar G+c^{\mathrm{full}}_{T_1}\mu\mathcal M_{T_1}+\underline c}{\underline y\,\vartheta^{j^*}}\right]^{1/\beta_K},
\qquad
\underline K_{T_1}\;\equiv\;k+\hat x\mu\mathcal W_{T_1}+\underline E .
\]
The goods block. Let \(K_{T_1}\ge\underline K_{T_1}\) and \(E\equiv K_{T_1}-k-\hat x\mu\mathcal W_{T_1}\ge\underline E\), a buffer of production capital that is never replaced. For \(t=T_1+j\) let \[
K^Y_t=k\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j+\left(1-\delta\right)^jE,
\qquad
K_{t+1}=K^Y_{t+1}+K^R_{t+1},
\qquad
I_t=K_{t+1}-K_t,
\] \(C_t\) from the goods constraint, \(\Omega_t\equiv R_t/\mathcal D_t\) and the states from the transitions. At \(j=0\), \(K^Y_{T_1}+K^R_{T_1}=K_{T_1}\). Within a period the material block fixes \(\mathcal W_{t+1}\) before capital is chosen, so \(K^R_{t+1}\) and \(K_{t+1}\) are defined, and the construction is recursive. Since \(A_tB_t^{\gamma}=A_{T_1}B_{T_1}^{\gamma}\Gamma^j\), (M2) and (M4) give \(Y_t\ge\underline y\,\Gamma^j\left(K^Y_t\right)^{\beta_K}\), and with \(\Gamma=\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^{1-\beta_K}\), \[
Y_t\;\ge\;\underline y\,k^{\beta_K}\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
Y_t\;\ge\;\underline y\,E^{\beta_K}\left[\Gamma\left(1-\delta\right)^{\beta_K}\right]^j\;\ge\;\underline y\,E^{\beta_K}\vartheta^j .
\] Gross formation is \(G_t=K_{t+1}-\left(1-\delta\right)K_t=\left(g^{\mathrm{circ}}+\delta\right)k\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j+G^R_t\), the buffer contributing nothing, with \(G^R_t\equiv K^R_{t+1}-\left(1-\delta\right)K^R_t\le\mu\mathcal M_{T_1}\hat x_{j+1}\) by (M3). The cost flows are \(C^N_t=C^D_t=0\) and \(C^W_t=c^{\mathrm{full}}_t\mu\mathcal W_t\le c^{\mathrm{full}}_{T_1}\mu\mathcal M_{T_1}\). For \(j\ge j^*\), \(C_t=Y_t-G_t-C^W_t\ge\mathfrak s\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j-\mu\mathcal M_{T_1}\left(\hat x_{j+1}+c^{\mathrm{full}}_{T_1}\right)\ge\underline c\) by (S). For \(j<j^*\), where \(G_t\le\bar G\) and \(\vartheta^j\ge\vartheta^{j^*}\), \(C_t\ge\underline y\,\underline E^{\beta_K}\vartheta^{j^*}-\bar G-c^{\mathrm{full}}_{T_1}\mu\mathcal M_{T_1}=\underline c\).
Feasibility. The goods constraint holds by the definition of \(C_t\), with \(C_t\ge\underline c>0\). The ledger holds with \(W_t=R_t+\delta M^K_t\ge0\). The intensity condition holds with \(\Omega_t=R_t/\mathcal D_t\ge0\) finite, because \(\phi^IG_t=0\) and \(\mathcal D_t\ge\omega^CC_t>0\). \(N_t=D_t=0\), \(\varpi_t=1\), \(K^R_t\ge0\), \(K^Y_t>0\) so \(K^R_t\le K_t\), and \(K_{t+1}>0\). \(S_t=S_{T_1}\ge0\), \(X_t=X_{T_1}\le\bar X_{\max}\) and \(M^K_t\ge0\).
State C. Extraction and discovery are zero from \(T_1\) on, so \(N,D\to0\) with \(\sum_tN_t<\infty\), the dates before \(T_1\) being finitely many. By (M2) and (M5), \(R_t\to R_\infty>\bar R\) with \(R^R_t=R_t\), \(a_t\varpi_t=a_t\to1\) with \(x_t\to\infty\) and the loop closed, and both stocks converge. For the goods block divide by \(\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\): \(K^Y_t/\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\to k\) because \(1-\delta<1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\), and \(K^R_t/\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\le\mu\mathcal M_{T_1}\hat x_j/\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\to0\), so \(K_t/\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\to k\); with \(P_t\to0\) and \(R_t\to R_\infty\), \[
\frac{Y_t}{\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j}=A_{T_1}B_{T_1}^{\gamma}e^{-\kappa P_t}\left[\frac{K^Y_t}{\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j}\right]^{\beta_K}\left(R_t-\bar R\right)^{\gamma}\;\longrightarrow\;y_\infty\equiv A_{T_1}B_{T_1}^{\gamma}k^{\beta_K}\left(R_\infty-\bar R\right)^{\gamma}\;\ge\;\underline y\,k^{\beta_K};
\] and since \(\left|G^R_t\right|\le\mu\mathcal M_{T_1}\left(\hat x_{j+1}+\hat x_j\right)\) and \(C^W_t\) is bounded, \(C_t/\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\to y_\infty-\left(g^{\mathrm{circ}}+\delta\right)k\ge\mathfrak s>0\). A positive sequence whose ratio to \(\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\) has a positive limit grows at \(g^{\mathrm{circ}}\), so consumption, capital and output grow at the common rate \(g^{\mathrm{circ}}>0\). Every clause of Definition 1(C) holds.
Step 3: filling the waste stock from the initial stocks. We show that, when \(\mu\mathcal B>\bar R\), from every \(K_0\ge\underline K\), the threshold defined below, the following path is feasible and, by step 2, in state C. Let \(\mathfrak m_{\mathcal B}\equiv\mu\mathcal B-\bar R>0\). Choose an integer \(T_1\ge2\) with \(\mu\left(1-\delta\right)^{T_1}\mathcal B\le\mathfrak m_{\mathcal B}/4\), a share \(\upsilon\in\left(0,1\right)\) with \(2\mu\upsilon\mathcal B\le\mathfrak m_{\mathcal B}/4\), an intensity \(x^E>0\) with \(T_1\mu^2e^{-\xi x^E}\mathcal B\le\mathfrak m_{\mathcal B}/4\), and \(\underline c>0\). For \(t<T_1\) the path

discovers \(D_0=\left(1-\upsilon\right)\left(\bar X_{\max}-X_0\right)\), and \(D_t=0\) for \(t\ge1\);
extracts \(N_0=\left(1-\upsilon\right)S_0\) and \(N_1=\left(1-\upsilon\right)S_1\), and \(N_t=0\) for \(t\ge2\);
treats all handled waste, \(\varpi_t=1\), with recycling capital \(K^R_t=x^E\mu\mathcal W_t\);
consumes \(C_t=\underline c\);
accumulates \(K_{t+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)K_t+Y_t-\underline c-C^N_t-C^D_t-C^W_t\), with \(Y_t=F\left(K_t-K^R_t,R_t,P_t,t\right)\), zero at a date with \(R_t<\bar R\);

and takes \(W_t\) from the ledger, \(\Omega_t\equiv R_t/\mathcal D_t\) and the states from the transitions. From \(T_1\) on it is the continuation of step 2.
The material block before \(T_1\) does not involve capital. At \(t<T_1\), \(R^R_t=a\left(x^E\right)\mu\mathcal W_t\), \(R_t=N_t+R^R_t\), the ledger gives \(W_t=R_t+\delta M^K_t\), the displaced mass \(\mathcal N_t=\Omega^{N,S}N_t+\Omega^{D,S}D_t\) of periods 0 and 1 goes to the environment, \(\Xi_t=\Xi^h_t+\mathcal N_t\), and the transitions of \(S\), \(X\), \(P\), \(M^K\) and \(\mathcal W\) use only these. So the stocks at \(T_1\) and the cost flows \(\mathfrak c_t\equiv C^N_t+C^D_t+C^W_t\), \(t<T_1\), are fixed by the initial material stocks and the choices of step 3, whatever \(K_0\). They are finite. \(C^N_0\), \(C^N_1\) and \(C^D_0\) are costs at a positive reserve and below the exhaustion point of discovery, or zero where the reserve is empty or the exhaustion point reached; the other extraction and exploration costs are zero; and \(C^W_t=c^{\mathrm{full}}_t\mu\mathcal W_t\).
The waste stock at \(T_1\) carries the floor. By the reserve transition \(N_0+N_1=S_0+D_0-S_2\), and \(D_0=\left(1-\upsilon\right)\left(\bar X_{\max}-X_0\right)\), so \(\mathcal M_0+\sum_{t<T_1}N_t=\mathcal M_0+\bar N-\mathfrak u=\mathcal B-\mathfrak u\), with the mass left unused \[
\mathfrak u\equiv\upsilon\left(\bar X_{\max}-X_0\right)+S_2\;\le\;2\upsilon\mathcal B ,
\] because \(\bar X_{\max}-X_0\le\bar N\), \(S_2=\upsilon S_1=\upsilon\left(\upsilon S_0+D_0\right)\le\upsilon\bar N\) and \(\bar N\le\mathcal B\). The leakage flow before \(T_1\) is \(\left(1-a\left(x^E\right)\right)\mu\mathcal W_t=e^{-\xi x^E}\mu\mathcal W_t\le e^{-\xi x^E}\mu\mathcal B\) per period, by Lemma A(b), and \(M^K_{T_1}=\left(1-\delta\right)^{T_1}M^K_0\le\left(1-\delta\right)^{T_1}\mathcal B\). Summing (L) over \(t<T_1\), \[
\mu\mathcal W_{T_1}=\mu\left(\mathcal M_{T_1}-M^K_{T_1}\right)\;\ge\;\mu\mathcal B-2\mu\upsilon\mathcal B-T_1\mu^2e^{-\xi x^E}\mathcal B-\mu\left(1-\delta\right)^{T_1}\mathcal B\;\ge\;\bar R+\tfrac14\mathfrak m_{\mathcal B} ,
\] so step 2 applies at \(T_1\) and supplies \(\underline K_{T_1}\), which depends on stocks and technology levels at \(T_1\) that \(K_0\) does not move.
Capital. Let \[
\underline K\;\equiv\;\left(1-\delta\right)^{-T_1}\Big[\max\left\{\underline K_{T_1},\,x^E\mu\mathcal B\right\}+\sum_{t<T_1}\left(\underline c+\mathfrak c_t\right)\Big]
\] and \(K_0\ge\underline K\). Since \(Y_t\ge0\), \(K_{t+1}\ge\left(1-\delta\right)K_t-\left(\underline c+\mathfrak c_t\right)\), and by induction \(K_t\ge\left(1-\delta\right)^{T_1}K_0-\sum_{s<T_1}\left(\underline c+\mathfrak c_s\right)\ge\max\left\{\underline K_{T_1},x^E\mu\mathcal B\right\}\) for \(0\le t\le T_1\).
Feasibility before \(T_1\). The goods constraint holds by the definition of \(K_{t+1}\), with \(C_t=\underline c>0\). \(\mathcal D_t\ge\omega^C\underline c>0\) whether production runs or not, so \(\Omega_t\ge0\) is finite and the intensity condition holds. \(W_t\ge0\); \(N_t,D_t\ge0\); \(\varpi_t=1\); \(K^R_t\le x^E\mu\mathcal B\le K_t\); \(K_{t+1}\ge0\); \(S_1=\upsilon S_0+D_0\ge0\) and \(S_t=S_2=\upsilon S_1\ge0\) for \(t\ge2\); \(X_t\le X_0+D_0\le\bar X_{\max}\); \(M^K_t=\left(1-\delta\right)^tM^K_0\ge0\). Production may be idle at some of these dates; no constraint of Problem 1 requires it to run.
So from every \(K_0\ge\underline K\) the path is feasible, and in state C by step 2, all clauses of Definition 1(C) being asymptotic and \(\sum_tN_t=N_0+N_1\). The threshold depends on the primitives and on \(\left(S_0,X_0,P_0,M^K_0,\mathcal W_0\right)\). With step 1, this proves the equivalence.
Step 4: the value. On the continuation, \(\underline c\le C_t\le\bar c_C\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\) for some \(\bar c_C\), since \(C_t/\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^j\) converges, and \(P_t\in\left[0,\bar P\right]\), on which the continuous \(v\) is bounded. For \(\eta>1\), \(u\left(\underline c\right)\le u\left(C_t\right)<0\). For \(\eta=1\), \(\left|\ln C_t\right|\le c_1+c_2j\) with \(c_1\equiv\left|\ln\underline c\right|+\left|\ln\bar c_C\right|\) and \(c_2\equiv\ln\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)\), and \(\sum_j\beta^j\left(c_1+c_2j\right)<\infty\). For \(\eta<1\), \(0<u\left(C_t\right)\le\bar c_C^{1-\eta}\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^{\left(1-\eta\right)j}/\left(1-\eta\right)\), whose discounted sum is finite when \(\beta\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^{1-\eta}<1\), that is \(\left(1+g^{\mathrm{circ}}\right)^{1-\eta}<1+\rho\). The dates before \(T_1\) add finitely many finite terms. So the value is finite on the stated terms.

title: O.4 Selection against collapse, and when a collapse path has a finite value
text:
The statement
Proposition 5 of the paper (selection against collapse) states that where the collapse ranking condition fails, no optimal path collapses as long as some path has a finite value, and that where the condition holds, a collapse path with a finite value exists. This page proves it in full. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page; a symbol the proof needs beyond them is defined where it is first used.
The paper’s long-run section (Section 3) calls the inequality  \[
\left(1-\delta\right)^{1-\eta}<1+\rho
\tag{R}
\] the collapse ranking condition.
Proposition 5 (selection against collapse). Let \(\bar R>0\) and let \(u\) be CRRA with elasticity \(\eta\).
(i) Where (R) fails, every feasible path in state A has value \(-\infty\); under the hard ceiling every feasible path does.
(ii) Where (R) fails and some feasible path has a finite value, every optimal path has a finite value and an infinite operating set. Under the soft ceiling and Assumption 1(i), an optimal path that converges in the sense of Assumption 1(ii) closes the loop and has \(R_\infty=\mathcal M_\infty/\mathcal T\ge\bar R\); it is in state C exactly when, in addition, \(R_\infty>\bar R\) and its goods block grows at a positive rate.
(iii) Let \(K_0>0\). Where (R) holds, a feasible path in state A with a finite value exists, so the condition holds exactly when some collapse path has a finite value.
We take the simplest route for the paper’s assumptions. No first-order condition is used, and (ii) uses optimality only through a comparison of two values. Technology, yield and costs are general throughout, the proof of (i) covers the general \(u\) of What the proof uses as well as CRRA, and Assumption 1(i) enters only in the last clause of (ii).

title: O.4 Selection against collapse, and when a collapse path has a finite value
text:
What the proof uses
We take from the page of lemmas shared by the long-run proofs what it restates of the paper. A feasible path meets every constraint and domain of Problem 1, the mass restrictions \(S_t\ge0\), \(X_t\le\bar X_{\max}\) and \(M^K_t\ge0\) included, from nonnegative initial stocks, and every cost flow on it is nonnegative. The operating set is \(\mathcal O\equiv\left\{t:R_t\ge\bar R\right\}\), and a path is in state A of Definition 1 exactly when \(\mathcal O\) is finite. The material budget \(\mathcal B\), state C, Assumption 1 and what it means for the loop to close are as quoted there, and Assumption 1(i) gives \(a\left(x,t\right)\le a^\infty\left(x\right)<1\) at every finite \(x\). Its Lemma A bounds what a feasible path extracts, discovers and leaks. The initial stocks meet the mass restrictions at date zero, or no path is feasible.
Section 2 of the paper writes welfare as \(U_0=\sum_{t\ge0}\beta^t\left[u\left(C_t\right)-v\left(P_t\right)\right]\), with \(\beta\equiv1/\left(1+\rho\right)\), \(\rho>0\), \(u'>0\) and \(v'>0\); we take \(v\) real-valued on \(P\ge0\). CRRA utility is \(u\left(C\right)=C^{1-\eta}/\left(1-\eta\right)\) for \(\eta>0\), \(\eta\ne1\), and \(\ln C\) at \(\eta=1\), with \(u\left(0\right)=-\infty\) for \(\eta\ge1\). A general \(u\) is nondecreasing, real-valued at every \(C>0\), and satisfies \(u\left(C\right)\le-cC^{1-\eta}\) on some interval \(\left(0,\bar C\right]\), with \(c>0\) and \(\eta>1\); (R) is then read with that \(\eta\). It has \(u\left(0\right)=-\infty\) too, since \(u\left(0\right)\le u\left(C\right)\le-cC^{1-\eta}\) for every \(C\in\left(0,\bar C\right]\).
The value of a feasible path is the limit, as \(n\to\infty\), of the partial sums \(U_0^n\equiv\sum_{t=0}^{n}\beta^t\left[u\left(C_t\right)-v\left(P_t\right)\right]\), where that limit exists in \(\left[-\infty,\infty\right]\); the value is finite when the limit is a real number. An optimal path is a feasible path whose value exists and is at least the value of every feasible path whose value exists. A collapse path is a feasible path in state A.
From Little’s law, Proposition 3 of the paper, and from the paper’s Appendix A we take the retained material endowment \(\mathcal M_\infty\equiv\lim_t\left(M^K_t+\mathcal W_t\right)\), the storage share \(\sigma\equiv\Phi^IG/R\), and the residence time \(\mathcal T\equiv1/\mu+\sigma_\infty/\delta\), with \(\sigma_\infty\) the limit of \(\sigma_t\).
Pollution is nonnegative. The pollution transition reads \(P_{t+1}=\left[1-\theta\left(P_t\right)\right]P_t+\Xi_t\) with \(\theta\in\left(0,1\right)\), and its inflow \(\Xi=\Xi^h+\mathcal N\) is nonnegative: the emission of the handled stream, \(\Xi^h=\left[1-\varpi+d^W\varpi\left(1-a\right)\right]H\), has nonnegative factors, and the displaced mass \(\mathcal N=\Omega^{N,S}N+\Omega^{D,S}D\) is nonnegative. So \(P_t\ge0\) at every date, from \(P_0\ge0\), and \(v\left(P_t\right)\ge v\left(0\right)\), as \(v\) is increasing.
Lemma V. If \(u\le\bar u\) for a constant \(\bar u\), every feasible path has a value, and it is at most \(\left[\bar u-v\left(0\right)\right]/\left(1-\beta\right)\). CRRA utility with \(\eta>1\) is the case \(\bar u=0\).

Proof. The partial sums split as \[
U_0^n=\sum_{t=0}^{n}\beta^t\Big\{\left[u\left(C_t\right)-\bar u\right]-\left[v\left(P_t\right)-v\left(0\right)\right]\Big\}+\left[\bar u-v\left(0\right)\right]\sum_{t=0}^{n}\beta^t .
\] No term of the first sum is positive, so the first sum is nonincreasing in \(n\) and converges in \(\left[-\infty,0\right]\); the second converges to \(\left[\bar u-v\left(0\right)\right]/\left(1-\beta\right)\). For \(\eta>1\), CRRA gives \(u\left(C\right)=-C^{1-\eta}/\left(\eta-1\right)<0\) at every \(C>0\).

title: O.4 Selection against collapse, and when a collapse path has a finite value
text:
Proof of (i)

Proof. Let (R) fail. Under CRRA this forces \(\eta>1\), since \(\eta\le1\) gives \(\left(1-\delta\right)^{1-\eta}\le1<1+\rho\), and then \(u\left(C\right)=-cC^{1-\eta}\) at every \(C>0\), with \(c=1/\left(\eta-1\right)\). So for CRRA and for a general \(u\) alike: \(\eta>1\), \(\beta\left(1-\delta\right)^{1-\eta}\ge1\), \(u\) is nondecreasing, and \(u\left(C\right)\le-cC^{1-\eta}\) on some interval \(\left(0,\bar C\right]\) with \(c>0\).
Step 1: after the last operating date, consumption is bounded by a stream falling at the factor \(1-\delta\). Let a feasible path be in state A, and let \(T^\dagger\equiv\max\mathcal O\), or \(T^\dagger\equiv-1\) if \(\mathcal O\) is empty. For \(t>T^\dagger\), \(R_t<\bar R\) and \(Y_t=0\), so the goods constraint, with \(I_t=K_{t+1}-K_t\) and nonnegative cost flows, gives \(C_t\le\left(1-\delta\right)K_t-K_{t+1}\). As \(C_t\ge0\), \(K_{t+1}\le\left(1-\delta\right)K_t\); as \(K_{t+1}\ge0\), \(C_t\le\left(1-\delta\right)K_t\). By induction, with \(\bar K\equiv K_{T^\dagger+1}\ge0\) and \(j\equiv t-T^\dagger\), \[
C_t\;\le\;\left(1-\delta\right)^j\bar K\qquad\left(t>T^\dagger\right).
\]
Step 2: the path has value \(-\infty\). If \(\bar K=0\), then \(C_t=0\) and \(u\left(C_t\right)=-\infty\) at every \(t>T^\dagger\), so \(U_0^n=-\infty\) for \(n>T^\dagger\). Let \(\bar K>0\), and take \(j_0\ge1\) with \(\left(1-\delta\right)^{j_0}\bar K\le\bar C\). At \(j\ge j_0\), either \(C_t=0\) and \(u\left(C_t\right)=-\infty\), or \(0<C_t\le\left(1-\delta\right)^j\bar K\le\bar C\), and then, as \(C^{1-\eta}\) decreases in \(C\), \[
\beta^tu\left(C_t\right)\;\le\;-c\bar K^{1-\eta}\beta^{T^\dagger}\Big[\beta\left(1-\delta\right)^{1-\eta}\Big]^j\;\le\;-c\bar K^{1-\eta}\beta^{T^\dagger} ,
\] a negative constant. The finitely many earlier terms are below \(+\infty\), as \(u\) is real-valued at \(C>0\), and the terms \(-\beta^tv\left(P_t\right)\le-\beta^tv\left(0\right)\) add at most \(\left|v\left(0\right)\right|/\left(1-\beta\right)\) to any partial sum. So \(U_0^n\to-\infty\).
Step 3: under the hard ceiling every feasible path is in state A. There \(a_t\varpi_t\le\bar a<1\), so Lemma A(b) gives \(\left(1-\bar a\right)\sum_tH_t\le\sum_t\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)H_t\le\mathcal B\). With \(R_t=N_t+a_t\varpi_tH_t\le N_t+\bar aH_t\) and Lemma A(a), \[
\bar R\cdot\#\mathcal O\;\le\;\sum_{t\ge0}R_t\;\le\;S_0+\bar X_{\max}-X_0+\frac{\bar a\,\mathcal B}{1-\bar a}\;<\;\infty ,
\] the first inequality because \(R_t\ge\bar R\) on \(\mathcal O\). So \(\mathcal O\) is finite, and step 2 applies.
Of \(u\), the proof of (i) uses only that it is nondecreasing with \(u\left(C\right)\le-cC^{1-\eta}\) near zero, for some \(c>0\) and \(\eta>1\).

title: O.4 Selection against collapse, and when a collapse path has a finite value
text:
Proof of (ii)

Proof. Step 4: the first sentence. Let (R) fail, let \(z^\circ\) be a feasible path with a finite value, and let \(z^*\) be optimal. Then \(U_0\left(z^*\right)\ge U_0\left(z^\circ\right)>-\infty\), so \(z^*\) is not in state A, by (i), and its operating set is infinite. As in the proof of (i), (R) fails only for \(\eta>1\), and Lemma V with \(\bar u=0\) gives \(U_0\left(z^*\right)\le-v\left(0\right)/\left(1-\beta\right)\): the value of \(z^*\) is finite. Under the hard ceiling the premise of (ii) never holds, by (i).
Step 5: the loop closes and \(R_\infty\ge\bar R\). Let the ceiling be soft, let Assumption 1(i) hold, and let \(z^*\) converge in the sense of Assumption 1(ii), so that every material flow and stock on it either decays at a constant rate, and then tends to zero, or converges. Material input is bounded, \(R_t\le N_t+\mu\mathcal B\) with \(N_t\to0\) by Lemma A, so either way \(R_t\to R_\infty\) for some finite \(R_\infty\ge0\). As \(\mathcal O\) is infinite, \(R_t\ge\bar R\) at infinitely many dates, so \(R_\infty\ge\bar R>0\). Lemma A(c) then closes the loop, \(\sum_t\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)<\infty\), so \(a_t\varpi_t\to1\), and \(R^R_t=R_t-N_t\to R_\infty\).
Step 6: Little’s law, \(R_\infty=\mathcal M_\infty/\mathcal T\). The two anthropogenic stocks are material stocks, so they converge, to \(M^K_\infty\) and \(\mathcal W_\infty\), and \(\mathcal M_\infty=M^K_\infty+\mathcal W_\infty\). Since \(R^R_t=a_t\varpi_t\mu\mathcal W_t\), step 5 gives \(R_\infty=\mu\mathcal W_\infty\). The transition \(M^K_{t+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)M^K_t+\Phi^I_tG_t\) gives \(\Phi^I_tG_t\to\delta M^K_\infty\), so, as \(R_\infty>0\), \(\sigma_t\to\sigma_\infty=\delta M^K_\infty/R_\infty\). Adding the two stocks, \(\mathcal M_\infty=R_\infty/\mu+\sigma_\infty R_\infty/\delta=R_\infty\mathcal T\), with \(\mathcal T\ge1/\mu>0\). So \(R_\infty=\mathcal M_\infty/\mathcal T\ge\bar R\).
Step 7: state C. We read “its goods block grows at a positive rate” as Definition 1(C) does: output, capital and consumption grow at a common rate \(g>0\). A path in state C has this and \(R_\infty>\bar R\). Every other clause of Definition 1(C) holds on \(z^*\): \(N,D\to0\) with \(\sum_tN_t<\infty\), as the two sums of Lemma A(a) converge; \(R\to R_\infty\) with \(R^R\to R_\infty\), and \(a\varpi\to1\) with the loop closed, by step 5; the two stocks converge, by step 6; and \(x\to\infty\). For the last, \(R^R_t>0\) from some date on, so \(\varpi_tH_t>0\) and \(x_t\) is defined; if \(x_t\le\tilde x<\infty\) at infinitely many dates, then at those dates \(a_t\le a\left(\tilde x,t\right)\le a^\infty\left(\tilde x\right)<1\), against \(a_t\ge a_t\varpi_t\to1\). So \(z^*\) is in state C exactly when, in addition, \(R_\infty>\bar R\) and its goods block grows at a positive rate.
