title: O.8 The planner’s entry margin against open access
text:
What the proof uses
From Section 2 of the paper. Within a date we suppress the time argument and write \(a'\) for \(a_x\). We read the yield as continuous on \(\left[0,\infty\right)\) and twice differentiable on \(\left(0,\infty\right)\), as its derivatives presume. With \(a\left(0\right)=0\), \(a'>0\), \(a''<0\) and \(a\to\bar a\in\left(0,1\right]\), the yield rises strictly from zero towards \(\bar a\), so \(0\le a\left(x\right)<\bar a\le1\); its slope \(a'\) is positive and strictly decreasing, and it tends to zero at infinity, since a limit \(\ell>0\) would make \(a\left(x\right)\ge a\left(1\right)+\ell\left(x-1\right)\) unbounded. The collection charge is positive, \(c^c>0\); \(d^W\in\left(0,1\right)\), \(\Omega^{N,S}\ge0\) and \(C^N_N>0\). The intensities \(\Omega^j=\Omega\omega^j\) are nonnegative, as \(\omega^j\ge0\) and Problem 1 has \(\Omega\ge0\), and the durables coefficient enters as \(\Phi^I=\Omega\phi^I\). Section 2 states \(p^W=-p^{\mathcal W}\), “the social cost of waste is minus the value of a tonne in the waste stock”, and we read the statement’s liability phase as \(p^W>0\), a waste stock in which a tonne has negative value.
From Section 4 of the paper. Raw material trades at \(p^R\) per tonne, capital rents at \(r^K\), the gate fee is \(\tau^W\) and the material-content price \(z\); a unit of the final good put to the current use \(j\) costs the user price \(P^j\equiv1+\left(z+\tau^W\right)\Omega\omega^j\). The emission tax \(\tau^P\) is levied per tonne of \(\Xi\) “on the agent that emits it, the waste sector on the emission \(\Xi^h\) of its handled stream and the mining sector on the mass \(\mathcal N\) it displaces”, and \(\tilde p\equiv p^R+d^W\tau^P\) is the waste sector’s value of a recovered tonne (Section 4.1). Of the mining sector’s conditions “at interior extraction and exploration” the first is the extraction condition  \[
p^R=P^NC^N_N+\tau^P\Omega^{N,S}+p^S ,
\tag{M}
\] and we read “an economy extracts” as (M) holding, as Proposition 9 does for open access: “where it extracts, \(F_R=C^N_N+p^S\)”.
Under open access (Section 4.2) “dumping is free, \(\tau^W=0\), and with \(\tau^P=z=0\) every user price is one, a recovered tonne sells at \(p^R=F_R\) and capital rents at \(r^K=F_K\)”. At the owned stockpile the waste stock is owned and \(\tau^P=z=0\), “and the sector faces \(p^R=F_R\left(1-\tau^W\Omega^Y\right)\) and \(r^K=F_K\left(1-\tau^W\Omega^Y\right)\)”. “In both economies the mining sector emits its displaced mass untaxed.” The recovery value of a treated tonne and the entry margin, “the net gain from the first treated tonne”, are (Section 4.2)  \[
\mathcal G^{x}\!\left(\tilde p,r^K\right)\equiv\max_{x\ge0}\left[a\left(x\right)\tilde p-r^Kx\right],
\qquad
E\equiv\mathcal G^{x}\!\left(\tilde p,r^K\right)+\tau^P\left(1-d^W\right)-P^Wc^c ,
\tag{E}
\] and \(E^{\mathrm{OA}}\) and \(E^{\mathrm{OS}}\) are \(E\) under open access and at the owned stockpile. Proposition 9 defines \(E^{\mathrm{pl}}\) as “\(E\) at the planner’s prices, \(\tilde p=\mathcal G^K\), \(r^K=F_K\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)\), \(\tau^P=p^P\) and \(P^W=1+\zeta\Omega^W\)”.
From Appendix A of the paper. With the gross material value \(\Psi\equiv F_R\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)+\zeta\) and the storage share \(\sigma\equiv\Phi^IG/R\in\left[0,1\right]\), the first-order condition in \(\Omega\) is  \[
\zeta=\sigma\left(p^W-p^M\right),
\tag{Z}
\] and “At \(\phi^I=0\), \(\zeta=0\)”, since \(\Phi^I=\Omega\phi^I\) vanishes and with it \(\sigma\). The wedge conditions are \(1-\zeta\Omega^Y>0\) and \(1+\zeta\Omega^j>0\) for every use \(j\), and “Every flow in final goods is grossed up by \(1\pm\zeta\Omega^j\) for the material it carries”. The gain on the recycling-capital margin is \(\mathcal G^K\equiv\Psi-p^W+d^Wp^P\). At interior extraction the extraction condition is  \[
\Psi=C^N_N\left(1+\zeta\Omega^N\right)+p^S+p^W+p^P\Omega^{N,S},
\tag{N}
\] and “While extraction is interior, (N) gives \(\Psi\)”, so that with the virgin displacement value  \[
V\equiv\Psi-p^W+d^Wp^P=C^N_N\left(1+\zeta\Omega^N\right)+p^S+\left(\Omega^{N,S}+d^W\right)p^P,
\qquad
\mathcal G^K=V,
\tag{V}
\] the second form being (N) substituted into the first, in which \(p^W\) cancels.
The margins at a vector. Where the planner extracts, (V) gives \(\mathcal G^K=V\), and the planner’s prices in (E) give \[
E^{\mathrm{pl}}=\mathcal G^{x}\!\left(V,\tilde F_K\right)+p^P\left(1-d^W\right)-\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)c^c .
\] Under open access \(\tilde p=p^R=F_R\), \(r^K=F_K\), \(\tau^P=0\) and \(P^W=1\); where it extracts, (M) with \(P^N=1\) and \(\tau^P=0\) gives \(F_R=C^N_N+p^S=V_0\), so \[
E^{\mathrm{OA}}=\mathcal G^{x}\!\left(V_0,F_K\right)-c^c .
\] At the owned stockpile with the fee \(\tau^W\), \(\tilde p=p^R\), \(r^K=r^{\mathrm{OS}}\equiv F_K\left(1-\tau^W\Omega^Y\right)\), \(\tau^P=0\) and \(P^W=1+\tau^W\Omega^W\); where it extracts, (M) with \(P^N=1+\tau^W\Omega^N\) and \(\tau^P=0\) gives \(p^R=V^{\mathrm{OS}}\equiv C^N_N\left(1+\tau^W\Omega^N\right)+p^S\), so \[
E^{\mathrm{OS}}=\mathcal G^{x}\!\left(V^{\mathrm{OS}},r^{\mathrm{OS}}\right)-\left(1+\tau^W\Omega^W\right)c^c .
\] A vector of the statement is one at which the planner and open access extract, with \(F_K>0\), \(p^P>0\), the wedge inequalities \(1-\zeta\Omega^Y>0\) and \(1+\zeta\Omega^j>0\) for \(j\in\left\{N,W\right\}\), and (Z) for some \(\sigma\in\left[0,1\right]\) and some \(p^M\). In the statement’s last sentence the owned stockpile extracts in place of open access, at the same vector extended by the fee. The yield, \(c^c\), \(d^W\), \(\Omega^{N,S}\) and the relative intensities \(\omega^j\) are primitives, common to the three economies.

title: O.8 The planner’s entry margin against open access
text:
The recovery value
Lemma R. Let \(r>0\) and \(\tilde p\) be real, and \(f\left(x\right)\equiv a\left(x\right)\tilde p-rx\) on \(\left[0,\infty\right)\).
(a) \(f\) attains its maximum at exactly one point \(x^*\left(\tilde p,r\right)\), and the maximum, \(\mathcal G^x\left(\tilde p,r\right)\) of (E), is nonnegative and at least \(a\left(x\right)\tilde p-rx\) for every \(x\ge0\).
(b) For real \(\tilde p_0,\tilde p_1\) and \(r_0,r_1>0\), with \(x_i\equiv x^*\left(\tilde p_i,r_i\right)\), \[
a\left(x_0\right)\left(\tilde p_1-\tilde p_0\right)-x_0\left(r_1-r_0\right)\;\le\;\mathcal G^x\left(\tilde p_1,r_1\right)-\mathcal G^x\left(\tilde p_0,r_0\right)\;\le\;a\left(x_1\right)\left(\tilde p_1-\tilde p_0\right)-x_1\left(r_1-r_0\right).
\]
(c) If \(\tilde p>0\), \(\hat x>0\) and \(r\ge\bar a\tilde p/\hat x\), then \(\mathcal G^x\left(\tilde p,r\right)\le a\left(\hat x\right)\tilde p\).

Proof. 

\(f\) is continuous with \(f\left(0\right)=0\). If \(\tilde p\le0\), then \(f\left(x\right)\le-rx<0\) for \(x>0\), as \(a\ge0\), so the maximiser is \(0\). Let \(\tilde p>0\). On \(\left(0,\infty\right)\), \(f'=a'\tilde p-r\) is continuous and strictly decreasing, with limit \(-r<0\) at infinity. If \(f'<0\) throughout, \(f\), continuous at \(0\), falls strictly on \(\left[0,\infty\right)\) and the maximiser is \(0\). Otherwise \(f'\) is nonnegative somewhere and negative far out, so by the intermediate value theorem it vanishes at exactly one point \(x^*>0\), positive before it and negative after; \(f\) rises strictly on \(\left[0,x^*\right]\) and falls strictly on \(\left[x^*,\infty\right)\), and the maximiser is \(x^*\). Either way it is unique. The maximum is at least \(f\left(0\right)=0\) and at least \(f\left(x\right)\) for every \(x\).
By (a), \(\mathcal G^x\left(\tilde p_1,r_1\right)\ge a\left(x_0\right)\tilde p_1-r_1x_0\), while \(\mathcal G^x\left(\tilde p_0,r_0\right)=a\left(x_0\right)\tilde p_0-r_0x_0\); subtracting gives the lower bound. Likewise \(\mathcal G^x\left(\tilde p_0,r_0\right)\ge a\left(x_1\right)\tilde p_0-r_0x_1\) and \(\mathcal G^x\left(\tilde p_1,r_1\right)=a\left(x_1\right)\tilde p_1-r_1x_1\) give the upper bound.
For \(x\le\hat x\), \(f\left(x\right)\le a\left(\hat x\right)\tilde p\), as \(a\) is increasing and \(rx\ge0\). For \(x>\hat x\), \(f\left(x\right)\le\bar a\tilde p-rx<\bar a\tilde p-r\hat x\le0\le a\left(\hat x\right)\tilde p\).

title: O.8 The planner’s entry margin against open access
text:
Proof of Proposition 12

Proof. Step 1: the identity (I) holds. At a vector of the statement \(F_K>0\) and \(\tilde F_K=F_K\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)>0\), so both maxima exist by Lemma R(a). Subtracting \(E^{\mathrm{OA}}\) from \(E^{\mathrm{pl}}\), the collection terms leave \(-\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)c^c+c^c=-\zeta\Omega^Wc^c\), which is the first part of (I), and (V) less \(V_0=C^N_N+p^S\) is its second part. Neither margin depends on \(p^W\).
Step 2: the bracket lies between the recovery gap at the two best intensities. Let \(x^{\mathrm{OA}}\equiv x^*\left(V_0,F_K\right)\) and \(x^{\mathrm{pl}}\equiv x^*\left(V,\tilde F_K\right)\) be the best intensities of open access and of the planner, and call the recovery gap at an intensity \(x\) the amount \(a\left(x\right)\left(V-V_0\right)-x\left(\tilde F_K-F_K\right)\) by which the planner’s objective in (E) exceeds open access’s when both use \(x\). Lemma R(b) at \(\left(\tilde p_0,r_0\right)=\left(V_0,F_K\right)\) and \(\left(\tilde p_1,r_1\right)=\left(V,\tilde F_K\right)\) gives  \[
a\left(x^{\mathrm{OA}}\right)\left(V-V_0\right)-x^{\mathrm{OA}}\left(\tilde F_K-F_K\right)
\;\le\;\mathcal G^{x}\!\left(V,\tilde F_K\right)-\mathcal G^{x}\!\left(V_0,F_K\right)\;\le\;
a\left(x^{\mathrm{pl}}\right)\left(V-V_0\right)-x^{\mathrm{pl}}\left(\tilde F_K-F_K\right),
\tag{B}
\] with \(\tilde F_K-F_K=-\zeta\Omega^YF_K\).
Step 3: with \(\zeta\ge0\) and the collection condition the planner’s threshold is lower, and at \(\phi^I=0\) it is lower with no condition. Let \(\zeta\ge0\). Each term of \(V-V_0\) is nonnegative and \(d^Wp^P>0\), by \(\Omega^N\ge0\), \(C^N_N>0\), \(\Omega^{N,S}\ge0\), \(d^W>0\) and \(p^P>0\), so \(V>V_0\). And \(-x\left(\tilde F_K-F_K\right)=x\zeta\Omega^YF_K\ge0\) for \(x\ge0\). So the left side of (B) is nonnegative, as \(a\ge0\), and (I) gives \[
E^{\mathrm{pl}}-E^{\mathrm{OA}}\;\ge\;p^P\left(1-d^W\right)-\zeta\Omega^Wc^c .
\] Hence \(E^{\mathrm{pl}}>E^{\mathrm{OA}}\) when the diversion gain covers the collection wedge, which is the claim at \(\phi^I>0\). At \(\phi^I=0\), \(\zeta=0\) by Appendix A, the collection wedge vanishes and the bound is \(p^P\left(1-d^W\right)>0\), by \(p^P>0\) and \(d^W<1\). So the planner’s threshold is lower at every vector of the statement with \(\zeta=0\), whatever \(p^W\), which appears in neither margin.
Step 4: with \(\zeta<0\) in the liability phase the ordering can reverse. A condition is needed when dropping it lets the conclusion fail at some vector of the statement. Each of the two families of steps 4 and 5 fixes the relative intensities \(\omega^j\), which Section 2 leaves free in \(\left[0,\infty\right)\), and works whatever the yield, \(c^c\), \(d^W\) and \(\Omega^{N,S}\); each has \(\sigma>0\), so it belongs to an economy with \(\phi^I>0\).
Take \(\omega^Y>0\) and every other relative intensity zero, so \(\Omega^j=0\) for \(j\ne Y\). Choose \(p^W>0\), \(F_K>0\), \(p^S>0\), \(p^P>0\) with \(p^P\left(1-d^W\right)<c^c\), and \(C^N_N>0\) with \(a\left(1\right)V_0-F_K>c^c\), possible as \(a\left(1\right)>0\). Then \(\varepsilon\equiv c^c-p^P\left(1-d^W\right)>0\) and \(V=V_0+\left(\Omega^{N,S}+d^W\right)p^P>0\), whatever \(\zeta\) and \(\Omega\). As \(a\) is continuous at zero with \(a\left(0\right)=0\), there is \(\hat x>0\) with \(a\left(\hat x\right)V<\varepsilon\). Set \(\zeta=-1\), which (Z) gives at \(\sigma=\tfrac12\) and \(p^M=p^W+2\), and \(\Omega=\bar aV/\left(\hat xF_K\omega^Y\right)\), so that \(\tilde F_K=F_K\left(1+\Omega^Y\right)>\bar aV/\hat x\). The wedge conditions hold for every use, \(1-\zeta\Omega^Y=1+\Omega^Y\) and \(1+\zeta\Omega^j=1\) for \(j\ne Y\), and so does the collection condition, \(\zeta\Omega^Wc^c=0<p^P\left(1-d^W\right)\). By Lemma R(c), \(\mathcal G^x\left(V,\tilde F_K\right)\le a\left(\hat x\right)V<\varepsilon\), so \(E^{\mathrm{pl}}<\varepsilon+p^P\left(1-d^W\right)-c^c=0\), while Lemma R(a) at \(x=1\) gives \(E^{\mathrm{OA}}\ge a\left(1\right)V_0-F_K-c^c>0\). So \(E^{\mathrm{pl}}<0<E^{\mathrm{OA}}\): the ordering reverses, and the two margins have opposite signs. Both prices of raw material are positive, as at a date at which production runs: \(F_R=V_0\) under open access, and for the planner, by the definition of \(\Psi\), \(F_R=\left(\Psi-\zeta\right)/\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)=\left(\Psi+1\right)/\left(1+\Omega^Y\right)\), with \(\Psi=C^N_N+p^S+p^W+p^P\Omega^{N,S}>0\) by (N).
Step 5: with a large collection wedge the ordering can reverse. Take \(\omega^N=\omega^Y=0<\omega^W\), so \(\Omega^N=\Omega^Y=0\) and \(\tilde F_K=F_K\). Choose \(C^N_N\), \(p^S\), \(F_K\), \(p^P\) and \(p^W\) positive; set \(\zeta=p^W/2\), which (Z) gives at \(\sigma=\tfrac12\) and \(p^M=0\); and choose \(\Omega\) with \(\zeta\Omega^Wc^c>\left(1+\Omega^{N,S}\right)p^P\), possible as \(\omega^W>0\) and \(c^c>0\). The wedge conditions hold for every use, \(1-\zeta\Omega^Y=1\) and \(1+\zeta\Omega^j\ge1\), as \(\zeta>0\), and \(\zeta\ge0\) gives \(V\ge V_0\) by step 3; only the collection condition fails. Here \(V-V_0=\left(\Omega^{N,S}+d^W\right)p^P\) and \(\tilde F_K-F_K=0\), so the right side of (B) is at most \(\left(\Omega^{N,S}+d^W\right)p^P\), as \(a<1\), and (I) gives \[
E^{\mathrm{pl}}-E^{\mathrm{OA}}\;\le\;\left(\Omega^{N,S}+d^W\right)p^P+p^P\left(1-d^W\right)-\zeta\Omega^Wc^c=\left(1+\Omega^{N,S}\right)p^P-\zeta\Omega^Wc^c<0 .
\] The planner’s price of raw material is \(\Psi-\zeta=C^N_N+p^S+p^P\Omega^{N,S}+p^W/2>0\), and open access’s is \(V_0>0\).
Step 6: against the owned stockpile the identity holds with \(\zeta-\tau^W\) in the three wedges. Take a vector of the statement with the owned stockpile extracting in place of open access, extended by a fee with \(1-\tau^W\Omega^Y>0\) and \(1+\tau^W\Omega^W>0\). With \(F_K>0\), the first condition on the fee makes \(r^{\mathrm{OS}}\) positive, and \(1-\zeta\Omega^Y>0\) makes \(\tilde F_K\) positive, so both maxima exist; the second condition makes the handling wedge \(P^W=1+\tau^W\Omega^W\) positive, and the identity does not use it. Subtracting \(E^{\mathrm{OS}}\) from \(E^{\mathrm{pl}}\), the collection terms leave \(-\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)c^c+\left(1+\tau^W\Omega^W\right)c^c=-\left(\zeta-\tau^W\right)\Omega^Wc^c\), and \[
E^{\mathrm{pl}}-E^{\mathrm{OS}}=\Big[\mathcal G^{x}\!\left(V,\tilde F_K\right)-\mathcal G^{x}\!\left(V^{\mathrm{OS}},r^{\mathrm{OS}}\right)\Big]+p^P\left(1-d^W\right)-\left(\zeta-\tau^W\right)\Omega^Wc^c,
\] \[
V-V^{\mathrm{OS}}=\left(\zeta-\tau^W\right)\Omega^NC^N_N+\left(\Omega^{N,S}+d^W\right)p^P,
\qquad
\tilde F_K-r^{\mathrm{OS}}=-\left(\zeta-\tau^W\right)\Omega^YF_K .
\] In (I) the three wedges are those on the extraction effort, \(\zeta\Omega^NC^N_N\) in \(V-V_0\), on the rental, \(\tilde F_K-F_K=-\zeta\Omega^YF_K\) inside the bracket, and on the collection charge, \(\zeta\Omega^Wc^c\). Against the owned stockpile each carries \(\zeta-\tau^W\) in place of \(\zeta\), while the overburden term \(\Omega^{N,S}p^P\) is unchanged, as are \(d^Wp^P\) and the diversion gain: the owned stockpile’s mine, like open access’s, pays nothing on the mass it displaces. At \(\tau^W=0\) the owned stockpile’s margin is open access’s, and the identity is (I).

title: O.9 The planner’s allocation as a competitive equilibrium
text:
The statement
Proposition 6 of the paper (decentralisation), in Section 4.3, states that where the planner’s economy operates in every period and its final-goods sector breaks even at the supporting prices, the planner’s allocation is a competitive equilibrium once the waste stock is owned and an emission tax, a discovery tax and a material-content price are set at the planner’s shadow prices. This page proves it in full. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page; a symbol the proof needs beyond them is defined where it is first used.
Proposition 6 (decentralisation). Let a path solve Problem 1 with multipliers \(\left\{\lambda,\zeta,p^W\right\}\) and costates (CS), and suppose that in every period the planner operates, \(R_t\ge\bar R\), with \(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t>0\), and that the final-goods sector participates at the prices (SP),  \[
\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)\left(Y-F_RR-F_KK^Y\right)\Big|_t\;\ge\;0 ,
\tag{PA}
\] which for the workhorse of Section 3.6, with output elasticities \(\beta_K\) and \(\gamma\) summing to \(\mu_F\), reads \(R^e_t\ge\gamma\bar R/\left(1-\mu_F\right)\). Suppose the waste stock is owned, displaced mass is emitted by the mining sector and charged the emission tax as part of \(\Xi\), and the instruments are  \[
\tau^P_t = p^P_t,
\qquad
\tau^X_t = -p^X_t\;\ge\;0,
\qquad
z_t = \zeta_t-p^W_t .
\tag{IN}
\] Then the planner’s allocation is a competitive equilibrium of Definition 2, supported by  \[
\tau^W_t = p^W_t=-p^{\mathcal W}_t,
\qquad
p^R_t = \Psi_t-p^W_t,
\qquad
r^K_t = F_K\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)\Big|_t,
\tag{SP}
\] with the private valuations \(\left(q,p^S,p^M,p^{\mathcal W}\right)\) equal to the planner’s costates, the household’s multiplier equal to \(\lambda\) and the same interest rate. Under unified ownership of the exploration frontier \(\tau^X\equiv0\), and \(p^X\) arises inside the mining sector.
The costates (CS), the planner’s first-order conditions, the market economy and Definition 2 are restated in What the proof uses.
We take the simplest route for the paper’s assumptions: we substitute (IN) and (SP) into each agent’s problem and show that the planner’s choices solve it, each market condition becoming a condition of the planner’s, and that the markets clear because the planner’s constraints hold. No functional form is used except in step 8, the workhorse’s threshold.

title: O.9 The planner’s allocation as a competitive equilibrium
text:
What the proof uses
From the paper’s model (Section 2). Problem 1 chooses \(C,I,N,D,\varpi,K^R,W,\Omega\) subject to the goods constraint, the ledger, the intensity condition \(R=\Omega\left(\mathcal D+\phi^IG\right)\) and the transitions, with \(K^Y=K-K^R\), \(R=N+R^R\), \(R^R=\mathcal R\left(\varpi H,K^R\right)\), \(H=\mu\mathcal W\), \(G=I+\delta K\), \(C^W=c^W\left(\varpi\right)H\) with \(c^W\left(\varpi\right)\equiv c^c\varpi+c^T\left(\varpi\right)\), and \(\Xi=\Xi^h+\mathcal N\). Appendix A.2 writes the costates of the six transitions as  \[
\underbrace{\lambda q}_{K},\quad
\underbrace{\lambda p^S}_{S},\quad
\underbrace{\lambda p^X}_{X},\quad
\underbrace{-\lambda p^P}_{P},\quad
\underbrace{-\lambda p^M}_{M^K},\quad
\underbrace{\lambda p^{\mathcal W}}_{\mathcal W},
\tag{CS}
\] each attached in the period in which the transition it prices is chosen, with \(\lambda\) the multiplier on the goods constraint, \(\lambda p^W\) that on the ledger written with \(W\) on the left, and \(\lambda\zeta\) that on the intensity condition written with \(R\) on the left. Of the primitives we use: \(C^N_{NN}\ge0\) and \(C^D_{DD}\ge0\), so each cost is convex in its flow; \(C^D_X>0\) where \(D>0\) and \(C^D\left(0,X,t\right)=0\), so \(C^D_X\ge0\), with \(C^D_X=0\) at \(D=0\); \(c^{T\prime\prime}>0\), so \(c^W\) is convex; \(\mathcal F_K>0\) and \(\mathcal F_{R^e}>0\), “with \(\mathcal F\) concave in \(\left(K^Y,R^e\right)\) at each \(\left(P,t\right)\) and the Inada condition in capital, \(\mathcal F_K\to\infty\) as \(K^Y\to0\) at any \(R^e>0\), maintained”, two clauses Section 2.1 states with the output equation; and the yield \(a\), increasing and concave with \(a\left(0\right)=0\) and \(a<\bar a\), with \(\mathcal R\left(T,K^R\right)=a\left(K^R/T\right)T\) at \(T>0\) and \(\mathcal R\left(0,K^R\right)=0\), a treated flow of zero recovering nothing.
From the paper’s Appendix A: what the hypothesis provides. We read the hypothesis as Appendix A reads a solution with its multipliers and costates, and as the page of shared lemmas reads a candidate: at every date the first-order system of Appendix A holds, with its wedge conditions \(1-\zeta\Omega^Y>0\) and \(1+\zeta\Omega^j>0\) for every use \(j\) maintained, and for each stock \(Z\) with costate \(m\) in (CS) the transversality condition \(\lim_{t\to\infty}\beta^t\lambda_tm_tZ_{t+1}=0\) holds. The system uses \(\Psi\equiv F_R\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)+\zeta\), the storage share \(\sigma\equiv\Phi^IG/R\), the discount rate \(1+r_{t+1}\equiv\lambda_t/\left(\beta\lambda_{t+1}\right)\), the material-adjusted marginal product of capital \(\tilde F_K\equiv F_K\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)\), where “\(F_R\) is \(\mathcal F_{R^e}\) at the prevailing \(R\ge\bar R\)”, and the gains (G), \(\mathcal G^K\equiv\Psi-p^W+d^Wp^P\) and \(\mathcal G^\varpi\equiv\alpha\mathcal G^K+\left(1-d^W\right)p^P\). In Appendix A’s order:

the four unbounded controls: \(\zeta=\sigma\left(p^W-p^M\right)\), condition (Ω); \(u'\left(C\right)=\lambda\left(1+\zeta\Omega^C\right)\), condition (C); \(q=1-\Phi^I\left(1-\sigma\right)\left(p^W-p^M\right)\), condition (I); and \(p^W_t=-p^{\mathcal W}_t\), condition (W);
extraction and exploration, as branch systems,  \[
\Psi=C^N_N\left(1+\zeta\Omega^N\right)+p^S+p^W+p^P\Omega^{N,S}\ \text{ where }N>0,
\qquad
p^S+p^X=C^D_D\left(1+\zeta\Omega^D\right)+p^P\Omega^{D,S}\ \text{ where }D>0,
\tag{ND}
\] of which Appendix A says that “each corner holds when its inequality goes the other way”: where \(N=0\) the right side of the first, at \(N=0\), is at least \(\Psi\), and where \(D=0\) the right side of the second, at \(D=0\), is at least \(p^S+p^X\);
the conditions on the treated share and recycling capital, which we read together with Appendix A’s remarks on the pair;
the costate recursions  \[
\begin{aligned}
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)q_t&=\tilde F_{K,t+1}+\left(1-\delta\right)q_{t+1},
&
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^S_t&=\left|C^N_S\right|\left(1+\zeta\Omega^N\right)\big|_{t+1}+p^S_{t+1},
\\
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^X_t&=-C^D_X\left(1+\zeta\Omega^D\right)\big|_{t+1}+p^X_{t+1},
&
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^M_t&=\delta\,p^W_{t+1}+\left(1-\delta\right)p^M_{t+1},
\\
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^{\mathcal W}_t&=\mu\,h_{t+1}+\left(1-\mu\right)p^{\mathcal W}_{t+1},
&
h&\equiv\alpha\varpi\left(\Psi-p^W\right)-c^W\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)-p^P\left[1-\varpi\left(1-d^W\right)-d^W\alpha\varpi\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{CR}
\]

Appendix A states the conditions on the pair \(\left(\varpi,K^R\right)\), (T) and (KR) where the pair is interior, as branch systems, notes that “The upper bound \(K^R\le K\) never binds, since \(F_K\to\infty\) as \(K^Y\to0\)”, and adds that “At \(\varpi=0\) the ratio \(x=K^R/\left(\varpi H\right)\) is undefined, so entry into treatment and into recycling capital is one joint decision, tested over the best available pair \(\left(\varpi,x\right)\).” We read these first-order conditions as one requirement on the pair: at the planner’s pair \(\left(\varpi_t,K^R_t\right)\), with every other control and every multiplier at the planner’s values, the one-sided derivative of the braces of the shared page, \[
B_t\left(\varpi,K^R\right)\equiv Y-C^W-p^W_tR+\zeta_t\left[R-\Omega_t\left(\mathcal D+\phi^IG_t\right)\right]-p^P_t\Xi ,
\] is nonpositive along every direction \(\left(d\varpi,dK^R\right)\) that keeps the pair in \(\left[0,1\right]\times\left[0,K_t\right]\) for small steps, \(\mathcal F\) being differentiable at the date’s input, as the shared page’s derivatives presume. In \(B_t\), \(Y=F\left(K_t-K^R,N_t+\mathcal R\left(\varpi H_t,K^R\right),P_t,t\right)\), and \(C^W\), \(R\), \(\mathcal D\) and \(\Xi\) move with the pair through \(C^W\), \(R^R\) and \(Y\). Where the pair is interior the requirement is (KR) and (T), at a bound the inequality of its branch, and at \(\varpi=0\) the joint test. By (C), \(u'>0\) and the wedge condition \(1+\zeta\Omega^C>0\), \(\lambda_t>0\) at every date.
Production capital is positive. At every date \(K^Y_t>0\), so \(K^R_t<K_t\), as Appendix A’s sentence on the upper bound states. Section 2’s Inada clause is its reason: \(\tilde F_{K,t}\) is a real number in (CR) and (KR), while \(\mathcal F_K\to\infty\) as \(K^Y\to0\) at any \(R^e>0\).
From the paper’s market economy (Section 4.1 and Appendix C). Four price-taking agents with perfect foresight share the technology, preferences and accounting of Section 2: a household, which consumes, owns the capital stock and rents it out, owns the three sectors and receives all profits and net tax revenue as lump sums; a final-goods sector; a mining sector that owns the reserve \(S\); and a waste sector that owns the waste stock \(\mathcal W\). The final good is the numeraire. Raw material sells at \(p^R\) per tonne, one price for a secondary and a virgin tonne; capital rents at \(r^K\); handing over a tonne of waste costs the gate fee \(\tau^W\); and the matter embodied in the final good is priced at \(z\) per tonne, the material-content price. A unit of the final good put to a current use \(j\in\left\{Y,N,D,W,C\right\}\) releases \(\Omega\omega^j\) tonnes, on which its buyer pays the fee at once, and put to capital formation it stores \(\Phi^I\) tonnes, so the user prices are  \[
P^j\equiv1+\left(z+\tau^W\right)\Omega\omega^j,
\qquad
P^I\equiv1+z\,\Phi^I .
\tag{UP}
\] The instruments are an emission tax \(\tau^P\) per tonne of \(\Xi\), levied on the agent that emits it, the waste sector on \(\Xi^h\) and the mining sector on the mass \(\mathcal N\) it displaces; a discovery tax \(\tau^X\) per tonne discovered; and \(z\), “with revenue returned as a lump sum”. Agents discount at the market interest rate \(r\) and take the paths of prices, instruments, \(P\) and \(\Omega\) as given; nobody chooses \(\Omega\).

The final-goods sector rents \(K^Y\), buys \(R\) tonnes and sells \(Y\); the \(\Omega^YY\) tonnes that diffuse in production go to the waste sector at the fee, and the rest leaves inside the good and sells at \(z\). Its profit is \[
\Pi^Y\equiv Y+z\left(R-\Omega^YY\right)-p^RR-\tau^W\Omega^YY-r^KK^Y=\left[1-\left(z+\tau^W\right)\Omega^Y\right]Y-\left(p^R-z\right)R-r^KK^Y ,
\] with the first-order conditions \(F_R\left[1-\left(z+\tau^W\right)\Omega^Y\right]=p^R-z\) and \(F_K\left[1-\left(z+\tau^W\right)\Omega^Y\right]=r^K\), together (FY).
The mining sector sells what it extracts at \(p^R\), buys extraction and exploration effort at \(P^N\) and \(P^D\), and pays the emission tax on the mass it displaces and the discovery tax, so its cash flow is \(\Pi^N\equiv p^RN-P^NC^N-P^DC^D-\tau^P\mathcal N-\tau^XD\). With \(p^S\) its valuation of a tonne left in the ground, at interior extraction and exploration  \[
p^R=P^NC^N_N+\tau^P\Omega^{N,S}+p^S,
\qquad
p^S=P^DC^D_D+\tau^P\Omega^{D,S}+\tau^X,
\qquad
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^S_t=\left|C^N_S\right|P^N\big|_{t+1}+p^S_{t+1}.
\tag{M}
\] Cumulative discovery has no owner, the common-pool reading, “so that \(p^X\) enters no private condition”; under unified ownership of the exploration frontier the sector owns \(X\) as well.
The waste sector takes in \(W\) at the fee, draws \(H=\mu\mathcal W\) from its stock, chooses \(\varpi\in\left[0,1\right]\) and \(K^R\ge0\), rented at \(r^K\), sells \(R^R\) at \(p^R\) and pays the emission tax on \(\Xi^h\). Its operating profit (Appendix C) is \[
\Pi^W\left(\varpi,K^R\right)\equiv p^R\mathcal R\left(\varpi H,K^R\right)-P^Wc^W\left(\varpi\right)H-r^KK^R-\tau^P\Xi^h,
\qquad
\Xi^h=\left(1-\varpi+d^W\varpi\right)H-d^W\mathcal R\left(\varpi H,K^R\right).
\] Its value \(J^W_t\) “is the fee on what it accepts, plus its operating profit, plus the discounted value of the stock it carries into the next period”, with \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W_t+W_t\). With \(p^{\mathcal W}_t\equiv\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)^{-1}\partial J^W_{t+1}/\partial\mathcal W_{t+1}\) its valuation of a tonne taken in at \(t\), acceptance at an interior quantity requires \(\tau^W_t=-p^{\mathcal W}_t\), condition (GF), and the valuation follows  \[
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^{\mathcal W}_t=\mu\,h^{\mathrm{mkt}}_{t+1}+\left(1-\mu\right)p^{\mathcal W}_{t+1},
\qquad
h^{\mathrm{mkt}}\equiv\alpha\varpi\,p^R-P^Wc^W-\tau^P\left[1-\varpi\left(1-d^W\right)-d^W\alpha\varpi\right].
\tag{WS}
\] The value of a recovered tonne to the sector is \(\tilde p\equiv p^R+d^W\tau^P\).
The household (Appendix C) maximises \(U_0\) subject to, at every date,  \[
P^C_tC_t+P^I_tG_t+\tau^W_t\delta M^K_t=r^K_tK_t+\Pi_t+T_t ,
\tag{HB}
\] with \(G_t=I_t+\delta K_t\), the transitions of \(K\) and \(M^K\) of Section 2, \(\Pi_t\) the profits of the three sectors and \(T_t\) the lump sum. With \(\Lambda_t\) its multiplier on (HB), \(q_t\) the value of a unit of \(K_{t+1}\) in goods and \(p^M_t\) the cost of a tonne of \(M^K_{t+1}\), its conditions are  \[
u'\left(C_t\right)=\Lambda_tP^C_t,
\quad
q_t=P^I_t+\Phi^I_tp^M_t,
\quad
1+r_{t+1}\equiv\frac{\Lambda_t}{\beta\Lambda_{t+1}},
\quad
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)q_t=r^K_{t+1}+\left(1-\delta\right)q_{t+1},
\quad
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^M_t=\delta\,\tau^W_{t+1}+\left(1-\delta\right)p^M_{t+1},
\tag{H}
\] “with the usual transversality conditions”.

Definition 2 (competitive equilibrium with instruments). “Given the initial stocks, instrument paths \(\left\{z_t,\tau^P_t,\tau^X_t\right\}\) and the rule that displaced mass is emitted by the mining sector as part of \(\Xi\), a competitive equilibrium is a set of quantity paths, price paths \(\left\{p^R,\tau^W,r^K,r\right\}\) and private valuations \(\left\{q,p^S,p^X,p^M,p^{\mathcal W}\right\}\) such that each agent solves its problem taking prices, \(P\) and \(\Omega\) as given; in each period the final-goods sector either operates, choosing \(\left(K^Y,R\right)\) at a maximum of its profit over \(\left[0,\infty\right)^2\), or is idle, \(Y=R=0\), with \(r^K=0\) and capital not rented held idle; the government budget balances period by period; the stocks follow” the transitions of Problem 1; “and in every period the markets for goods, capital, material, disposal and embodied material clear,”  \[
Y=C+I+\delta K+C^N+C^D+C^W,
\quad
K^Y+K^R=K,
\quad
R=N+R^R,
\quad
W=\Omega\mathcal D+\delta M^K,
\quad
R-\Omega\omega^YY=\Omega\left(\omega^NC^N+\omega^DC^D+\omega^WC^W+\omega^CC\right)+\Phi^IG ,
\tag{MC}
\] “capital clearing as \(K^Y+K^R\le K\) at an idle date.”
What it is for an agent to solve its problem. Definition 2 asks each agent to solve its problem at given prices and counts the private valuations among the objects of an equilibrium. The final-goods sector’s problem is static, and Definition 2 states it: a maximum of its profit over \(\left[0,\infty\right)^2\). The household, the mining sector and the waste sector each carry a stock into the next date, and Section 4.1 and Appendix C state their problems through their valuations of those stocks, in (M), in (GF) with (WS), and in (H). Section 4.1 says, in the sentence after Definition 2, what solving its problem means for these three: “For the household, the mining sector and the waste sector, which carry a stock from one date to the next, solving its problem means meeting the conditions that Section 4.1 and Appendix C state for it: at each date its choices attain the maximum of its payoff plus the stocks it carries forward at its own valuations, its valuations follow its asset equations, and each stock it carries meets its transversality condition.” We call that maximum, over the choices open to the agent at the date, its date problem; its asset equations are the last of (M), (WS) and the last two of (H). The payoff is the mining sector’s cash flow \(\Pi^N_t\), the waste sector’s \(\tau^W_tW_t+\Pi^W_t\), and the household’s \(u\left(C_t\right)\) under its budget (HB) at \(t\), its stocks valued at \(\Lambda_tq_t\) and \(-\Lambda_tp^M_t\). For the waste sector the date problem is the maximum that defines \(J^W_t\), with the stock it carries valued at \(p^{\mathcal W}_t\) a tonne. This is the sense of the paper’s text after Proposition 6, that the proof “finds a planner condition of Appendix A in each, so the proposition reaches as far as those conditions characterise the optimum”.
Lemma Q. The recovery \(\mathcal R\left(T,K\right)\), on \(T,K\ge0\), is concave, nondecreasing in \(K\), and \(0\le\mathcal R\left(T,K\right)\le\bar aT\).

Proof. Take \(\left(T_i,K_i\right)\), \(i=1,2\), and \(\vartheta\in\left(0,1\right)\), with \(T\equiv\vartheta T_1+\left(1-\vartheta\right)T_2\) and \(K\equiv\vartheta K_1+\left(1-\vartheta\right)K_2\). If \(T_1,T_2>0\), the weights \(w_1\equiv\vartheta T_1/T\) and \(w_2\equiv\left(1-\vartheta\right)T_2/T\) sum to one and \(K/T=w_1K_1/T_1+w_2K_2/T_2\), so concavity of \(a\) gives \(T\,a\left(K/T\right)\ge\vartheta T_1a\left(K_1/T_1\right)+\left(1-\vartheta\right)T_2a\left(K_2/T_2\right)\). If \(T_2=0<T_1\), then \(T=\vartheta T_1\) and \(K\ge\vartheta K_1\), and as \(a\) is increasing, \(\mathcal R\left(T,K\right)\ge\vartheta T_1a\left(K_1/T_1\right)=\vartheta\mathcal R\left(T_1,K_1\right)+\left(1-\vartheta\right)\mathcal R\left(T_2,K_2\right)\); the case \(T_1=0<T_2\) is the same, and if \(T_1=T_2=0\) both sides are zero. The rest holds because \(a\) is increasing with \(0=a\left(0\right)\le a<\bar a\).

title: O.9 The planner’s allocation as a competitive equilibrium
text:
Proof of Proposition 6

Proof. Step 1: the supporting prices. As \(\lambda_t>0\), the interest rate \(1+r_{t+1}=\lambda_t/\left(\beta\lambda_{t+1}\right)\) is positive and \(\beta^t\lambda_t>0\). Take the household’s multiplier \(\Lambda_t\equiv\lambda_t\), so its interest rate in (H) is the planner’s, and the private valuations \(q\), \(p^S\), \(p^X\), \(p^M\), \(p^{\mathcal W}\) equal to the costates. Under (IN) and (SP), \(z+\tau^W=\zeta\), so (UP) gives \[
P^j=1+\zeta\Omega^j\quad\left(j\in\left\{Y,N,D,W,C\right\}\right),
\qquad
P^I=1+\left(\zeta-p^W\right)\Phi^I ,
\] with \(P^N,P^D,P^W,P^C>0\) by the wedge conditions and \(1-\left(z+\tau^W\right)\Omega^Y=1-\zeta\Omega^Y>0\) by hypothesis. The sectors face \[
p^R-z=\Psi-\zeta=F_R\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right),
\qquad
r^K=\tilde F_K,
\qquad
\tilde p=\Psi-p^W+d^Wp^P=\mathcal G^K,
\qquad
p^R-\tau^P\Omega^{N,S}=\Psi-p^W-p^P\Omega^{N,S},
\] the first two positive at every date, as the planner operates and \(\mathcal F_K,\mathcal F_{R^e}>0\).
Step 2: the discovery tax is nonnegative. Since \(\beta^t\lambda_t/\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)=\beta^{t+1}\lambda_{t+1}\), the recursion for \(p^X\) in (CR) reads \[
\beta^t\lambda_tp^X_t=\beta^{t+1}\lambda_{t+1}p^X_{t+1}-\beta^{t+1}\lambda_{t+1}C^D_X\left(1+\zeta\Omega^D\right)\big|_{t+1}\;\le\;\beta^{t+1}\lambda_{t+1}p^X_{t+1},
\] as \(C^D_X\ge0\) and \(1+\zeta\Omega^D>0\), so \(\beta^t\lambda_tp^X_t\le\beta^s\lambda_sp^X_s\) for every \(s>t\). Cumulative discovery does not fall, \(X_{s+1}=X_s+D_s\ge X_s\). If \(X_{t'}>0\) at some date \(t'\), then \(X_{s+1}\ge X_{t'}>0\) for \(s\ge t'\), and the transversality condition \(\beta^s\lambda_sp^X_sX_{s+1}\to0\) gives \(\beta^s\lambda_sp^X_s\to0\). Hence \(\beta^t\lambda_tp^X_t\le0\), and \(\tau^X_t=-p^X_t\ge0\) at every date. If \(X_t=0\) at every date, nothing is ever discovered, every dividend in the recursion is zero and the transversality condition is silent, so \(p^X_t=\lambda_0p^X_0/\left(\beta^t\lambda_t\right)\) keeps the sign of \(p^X_0\), which the first-order system leaves free; the sign in (IN) is then what the statement supposes of the instrument. The steps that follow use \(\tau^X=-p^X\) and not its sign, so the equilibrium holds whichever sign \(p^X_0\) takes.
Step 3: the markets clear, the stocks follow their transitions, and the government’s and the household’s budgets hold. The allocation is the planner’s, so the goods constraint is the goods market of (MC), \(K^Y=K-K^R\) the capital market and \(R=N+R^R\) the material market. The ledger \(W_t=R_t-\Delta M^K_{t+1}\), the transition \(\Delta M^K_{t+1}=\Phi^I_tG_t-\delta M^K_t\) and the intensity condition give the disposal market, \(W=R-\Phi^IG+\delta M^K=\Omega\mathcal D+\delta M^K\), and the embodied-material market is the intensity condition with \(\Omega^YY=\Omega\omega^YY\) moved to the left. The stocks follow the transitions of Problem 1 because they are the planner’s, the flow \(\Xi=\Xi^h+\mathcal N\) being emitted by the waste sector and by the mining sector as Definition 2’s rule has it. Let the lump sum be the tax revenue, \[
T_t\equiv\tau^P_t\left(\Xi^h_t+\mathcal N_t\right)+\tau^X_tD_t .
\] The material-content price is paid by the buyers of the good to the final-goods sector for the matter it sells inside the good, and the embodied-material market makes the tonnes paid for the tonnes sold, so it leaves the government nothing to return, whether or not its payments pass through it. The government budget balances. For (HB), let \(\Pi_t\equiv\Pi^Y_t+\Pi^N_t+\tau^W_tW_t+\Pi^W_t\). Collecting the cash flows with (UP), the emission and discovery taxes cancelling against \(T\), gives at every date \[
\begin{aligned}
r^KK+\Pi+T-\left(P^CC+P^IG+\tau^W\delta M^K\right)
={}&\left(Y-C-G-C^N-C^D-C^W\right)+r^K\left(K-K^Y-K^R\right)+p^R\left(N+R^R-R\right)
\\
&+z\left(R-\Omega\mathcal D-\Phi^IG\right)+\tau^W\left(W-\Omega\mathcal D-\delta M^K\right),
\end{aligned}
\] with \(\mathcal D=\omega^YY+\omega^NC^N+\omega^DC^D+\omega^WC^W+\omega^CC\). Each bracket is zero by (MC), the fourth being the embodied-material market. So (HB) holds along the planner’s allocation.
Step 4: the household solves its problem. By Step 1, (C) is \(u'\left(C_t\right)=\lambda_t\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^C_t\right)=\Lambda_tP^C_t\). By (Ω), \(\zeta-p^W+p^M=-\left(1-\sigma\right)\left(p^W-p^M\right)\), so (I) reads \(q=1+\left(\zeta-p^W\right)\Phi^I+\Phi^Ip^M=P^I+\Phi^Ip^M\). The recursions of \(q\) and \(p^M\) in (CR) are those of (H) at \(r^K=\tilde F_K\) and \(\tau^W=p^W\). So (H) holds with \(\Lambda=\lambda\), and the household’s transversality conditions, \(\beta^t\Lambda_tq_tK_{t+1}\to0\) and \(\beta^t\Lambda_tp^M_tM^K_{t+1}\to0\), are the planner’s for \(K\) and \(M^K\). For the date problem, take any \(\left(C,G\right)\) with \(C\ge0\) that meets (HB) at \(t\), with \(K_{t+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)K_t+G\) and \(M^K_{t+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)M^K_t+\Phi^I_tG\). Using \(q_t-\Phi^I_tp^M_t=P^I_t\) and then (HB), \[
u\left(C\right)+\Lambda_t\left[q_tK_{t+1}-p^M_tM^K_{t+1}\right]
=u\left(C\right)+\Lambda_tP^I_tG+\left(1-\delta\right)\Lambda_t\left[q_tK_t-p^M_tM^K_t\right]
=u\left(C\right)-\Lambda_tP^C_tC+\varkappa_t ,
\] with \(\varkappa_t\) the same for every such choice. As \(u\) is concave and \(u'\left(C_t\right)=\Lambda_tP^C_t\), \(u\left(C\right)-\Lambda_tP^C_tC\le u\left(C_t\right)-\Lambda_tP^C_tC_t\), and the planner’s \(\left(C_t,G_t\right)\), which meets (HB) by step 3 with \(C_t\ge0\) and \(K_{t+1}\ge0\), attains the date problem.
Step 5: the mining sector solves its problem. Under the common-pool reading the sector carries the reserve alone, \(S_{t+1}=S_t+D-N\). By (IN), (SP) and step 1, its payoff plus the reserve at its valuation is \[
\Pi^N_t+p^S_tS_{t+1}=g^N_t\left(N\right)+g^D_t\left(D\right)+p^S_tS_t ,
\] \[
g^N_t\left(N\right)\equiv\left(\Psi_t-p^W_t-p^P_t\Omega^{N,S}-p^S_t\right)N-\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^N_t\right)C^N\left(N,S_t,t\right),
\qquad
g^D_t\left(D\right)\equiv\left(p^S_t+p^X_t-p^P_t\Omega^{D,S}\right)D-\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^D_t\right)C^D\left(D,X_t,t\right),
\] both concave on \(\left[0,\infty\right)\), the costs being convex in the flow and their factors positive. The derivative of \(g^N_t\) is zero at \(N_t\) where \(N_t>0\), by (ND), and nonpositive at zero where \(N_t=0\), by its corner; a concave function lies below its tangent, so \(N_t\) maximises \(g^N_t\) over \(N\ge0\), and likewise \(D_t\) maximises \(g^D_t\). The planner’s \(\left(N_t,D_t\right)\) meets the mass restrictions, \(S_{t+1}\ge0\) among them, so it attains the date problem over any set of choices that contains it. The first two conditions of (M) are those of (ND), through \(p^R-\tau^P\Omega^{N,S}=\Psi-p^W-p^P\Omega^{N,S}\) and \(P^N=1+\zeta\Omega^N\), and through \(\tau^X=-p^X\) and \(P^D=1+\zeta\Omega^D\); the reserve’s equation in (M) is that of (CR) at \(P^N=1+\zeta\Omega^N\); and the transversality condition \(\beta^t\lambda_tp^S_tS_{t+1}\to0\) is the planner’s.
Step 6: the waste sector solves its problem. By (SP) and (W), \(\tau^W_t+p^{\mathcal W}_t=p^W_t+p^{\mathcal W}_t=0\), so (GF) holds, and the date problem maximises \[
\left(\tau^W_t+p^{\mathcal W}_t\right)W+\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi,K^R\right)+\left(1-\mu\right)p^{\mathcal W}_t\mathcal W_t ,
\] in which \(W\) no longer appears: the planner’s \(W_t\) attains it, and a pair attains it exactly when it maximises \(\Pi^W_t\). At the supporting prices, by step 1 and with \(\Xi^h\) substituted, \[
\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi,K^R\right)=\mathcal G^K_t\,\mathcal R\left(\varpi H_t,K^R\right)-\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^W_t\right)c^W\left(\varpi\right)H_t-\tilde F_{K,t}K^R-p^P_t\left[1-\left(1-d^W\right)\varpi\right]H_t .
\] Collecting the terms of \(B_t\) that move with the pair, \(Y\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)-C^W\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)+\left(\zeta-p^W+d^Wp^P\right)R^R\) and the untreated stream’s \(-p^P\left[1-\left(1-d^W\right)\varpi\right]H\), and using \(\Psi-\zeta=F_R\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)\), \[
\Pi^W_t-B_t=\left(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t\right)\left[F_{R,t}\,\mathcal R-F_{K,t}K^R-F\left(K_t-K^R,N_t+\mathcal R,P_t,t\right)\right]+c_t ,
\] with \(\mathcal R=\mathcal R\left(\varpi H_t,K^R\right)\), \(F_{R,t}\) and \(F_{K,t}\) at the planner’s input, and \(c_t\) the same for every pair.
Capital without a treated flow. Where \(\varpi_tH_t=0\), the planner’s pair has \(K^R_t=0\): capital then recovers nothing, and were \(K^R_t>0\) the derivative of \(B_t\) along \(\left(0,-1\right)\) would be \(\tilde F_{K,t}>0\), against the requirement on the pair.
If \(\mathcal G^K_t\le0\), the pair maximises. For \(K^R>0\), \(\mathcal G^K_t\mathcal R\left(\varpi H_t,K^R\right)\le0=\mathcal G^K_t\mathcal R\left(\varpi H_t,0\right)\) and \(\tilde F_{K,t}K^R>0\), so \(\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi,K^R\right)<\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi,0\right)\) at every \(\varpi\). The planner’s pair has \(K^R_t=0\): otherwise \(\varpi_tH_t>0\), by capital without a treated flow, so \(\mathcal R\) has the derivative \(a'\left(x_t\right)\) in \(K^R\) there, the derivative of \(B_t\) along \(\left(0,-1\right)\) is \(\tilde F_{K,t}-\mathcal G^K_ta'\left(x_t\right)>0\), against the requirement. Along \(\left(\pm1,0\right)\) from \(\left(\varpi_t,0\right)\), \(\mathcal R=0\) does not move, so \(\Pi^W_t\left(\cdot,0\right)-B_t\left(\cdot,0\right)\) is constant and the requirement makes the one-sided derivatives of the concave \(\Pi^W_t\left(\cdot,0\right)\) at \(\varpi_t\) nonpositive: \(\varpi_t\) maximises it over \(\left[0,1\right]\). So \(\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi,K^R\right)\le\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi,0\right)\le\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi_t,K^R_t\right)\).
If \(\mathcal G^K_t>0\), the pair maximises. Then \(\Pi^W_t\) is concave on \(\left[0,1\right]\times\left[0,\infty\right)\), by Lemma Q, the convexity of \(c^W\) with \(1+\zeta\Omega^W>0\), and linearity of the rest. The pair is not at \(K^R_t=0\) with \(\varpi_tH_t>0\) and \(a'\!\left(0^+\right)=\infty\): along \(\left(0,1\right)\), \(\mathcal R\left(\varpi_tH_t,s\right)/s\to\infty\) as \(s\downarrow0\), and differentiability of \(F\) at the planner’s input gives \(B_t\left(\varpi_t,s\right)-B_t\left(\varpi_t,0\right)=\mathcal G^K_t\mathcal R\left(\varpi_tH_t,s\right)-\tilde F_{K,t}s+o\left(s+\mathcal R\left(\varpi_tH_t,s\right)\right)\), whose ratio to \(s\) tends to \(+\infty\), against the requirement. So \(\mathcal R\) has a finite one-sided derivative \(\mathcal R'\) at the planner’s pair along each direction \(\left(d\varpi,dK^R\right)\) into \(\left[0,1\right]\times\left[0,\infty\right)\): it is differentiable where \(\varpi_tH_t>0\) and \(K^R_t>0\); it has \(\mathcal R'=a'\!\left(0^+\right)dK^R\) where \(K^R_t=0<\varpi_tH_t\) and \(a'\!\left(0^+\right)<\infty\); and where \(\varpi_tH_t=0\), so \(K^R_t=0\), it is \(s\,\mathcal R\left(d\varpi H_t,dK^R\right)\) along the direction, linear in the step \(s\). The chain rule at the planner’s input then gives the bracket of \(\Pi^W_t-B_t\) the one-sided derivative \(F_{R,t}\mathcal R'-F_{K,t}dK^R-\left(-F_{K,t}dK^R+F_{R,t}\mathcal R'\right)=0\), so the one-sided derivatives of \(\Pi^W_t\) equal those of \(B_t\), nonpositive along every direction that keeps the pair in \(\left[0,1\right]\times\left[0,K_t\right]\). As \(K^R_t<K_t\), by production capital is positive, these are all the directions into the sector’s set \(\left[0,1\right]\times\left[0,\infty\right)\). For a concave function the difference quotient along a segment does not rise as the step grows, so \(\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi,K^R\right)-\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi_t,K^R_t\right)\) is at most the one-sided derivative along \(\left(\varpi-\varpi_t,K^R-K^R_t\right)\), which is nonpositive.
The valuation. With the sector’s choices the planner’s, (SP) and step 1 give \(h^{\mathrm{mkt}}=\alpha\varpi\left(\Psi-p^W\right)-\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)c^W-p^P\left[1-\varpi\left(1-d^W\right)-d^W\alpha\varpi\right]=h\), so (WS) is the recursion of \(p^{\mathcal W}\) in (CR), and the transversality condition \(\beta^t\lambda_tp^{\mathcal W}_t\mathcal W_{t+1}\to0\) is the planner’s.
Step 7: the final-goods sector operates at a maximum of its profit. Every period operates, so Definition 2 asks that the planner’s \(\left(K^Y_t,R_t\right)\) maximise \(\Pi^Y_t\) over \(\left[0,\infty\right)^2\). By step 1, at any \(\left(K,R\right)\), \[
\Pi^Y_t\left(K,R\right)=\left(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t\right)\left[F\left(K,R,P_t,t\right)-F_{R,t}R-F_{K,t}K\right],
\] with \(F_{R,t}\) and \(F_{K,t}\) at the planner’s input. So (FY) holds there, by the definitions of \(\Psi\) and \(\tilde F_K\), and \(\Pi^Y_t\left(K^Y_t,R_t\right)\) is the left side of (PA), nonnegative by hypothesis. Below the floor \(F=0\), and \(\Pi^Y_t\left(K,R\right)\le0\le\Pi^Y_t\left(K^Y_t,R_t\right)\), as \(F_{R,t},F_{K,t}>0\). On and above the floor, with \(R^e=R-\bar R\), \[
\Pi^Y_t\left(K,R\right)-\Pi^Y_t\left(K^Y_t,R_t\right)=\left(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t\right)\left[\mathcal F\left(K,R^e,P_t,t\right)-\mathcal F\left(K^Y_t,R^e_t,P_t,t\right)-F_{K,t}\left(K-K^Y_t\right)-F_{R,t}\left(R^e-R^e_t\right)\right],
\] which is nonpositive, as Section 2.1 takes \(\mathcal F\left(\cdot,\cdot,P_t,t\right)\) concave in \(\left(K^Y,R^e\right)\), so that its graph lies below its tangent plane at the planner’s input. The workhorse of Section 3.6 is an example: its output \(A_te^{-\kappa P}\left(K^Y\right)^{\beta_K}\left(B_tR^e\right)^{\gamma}\), with \(\beta_K,\gamma>0\), as \(\mathcal F_K,\mathcal F_{R^e}>0\), and \(\beta_K+\gamma<1\), is concave in \(\left(K^Y,R^e\right)\) at every \(P\) and \(t\).
Step 8: the workhorse’s threshold. In the workhorse, above the floor \(F=A_te^{-\kappa P}\left(K^Y\right)^{\beta_K}\left(B_tR^e\right)^{\gamma}\) with \(A_t,B_t>0\) and \(\mu_F\equiv\beta_K+\gamma<1\). At the planner’s input \(K^Y_t>0\), by production capital is positive, and \(R^e_t>0\), as \(F_R=\gamma Y/R^e\) is finite there, so \(Y_t>0\), \(F_RR^e=\gamma Y\) and \(F_KK^Y=\beta_KY\). Then \[
Y-F_RR-F_KK^Y=Y-F_R\left(R^e+\bar R\right)-\beta_KY=Y\left[\left(1-\mu_F\right)-\frac{\gamma\bar R}{R^e}\right],
\] and with \(Y_t>0\) and \(1-\zeta_t\Omega^Y_t>0\), (PA) holds at \(t\) exactly when \(R^e_t\ge\gamma\bar R/\left(1-\mu_F\right)\).
Step 9: unified ownership. The sector now owns \(X\) as well, with valuation \(p^X_t\) of a unit of \(X_{t+1}\), and \(\tau^X\equiv0\). Its date problem adds \(p^X_tX_{t+1}=p^X_t\left(X_t+D\right)\) and drops \(\tau^X_tD\), so \(g^D_t\) is the function of step 5 and the planner’s \(\left(N_t,D_t\right)\) still attains it. The exploration condition of (M) at \(\tau^X=0\), with \(p^X\) added to the sector’s own value of a discovered tonne, is \(p^S+p^X=P^DC^D_D+\tau^P\Omega^{D,S}\), the exploration condition of (ND). The valuation follows the asset equation \(\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^X_t=-P^DC^D_X\big|_{t+1}+p^X_{t+1}\), what a unit of \(X_{t+1}\) adds to the next date’s payoff and to the stock it carries, as the reserve’s equation in (M) is for \(S\); at \(P^D=1+\zeta\Omega^D\) it is the recursion of \(p^X\) in (CR), and its transversality condition is the planner’s. The tax leaves the government budget, \(T_t=\tau^P_t\left(\Xi^h_t+\mathcal N_t\right)\), and step 3 is otherwise unchanged. So \(p^X\) arises inside the sector.
Conclusion. Every period operates, with the final-goods sector at a maximum of its profit (step 7); the household, the mining sector and the waste sector solve their problems (steps 4 to 6) at the prices (SP), with the private valuations \(\left(q,p^S,p^M,p^{\mathcal W}\right)\) equal to the costates, the household’s multiplier \(\Lambda=\lambda\) and the planner’s interest rate; the government budget balances and the markets clear (step 3); and the stocks are the planner’s. So the planner’s allocation is a competitive equilibrium of Definition 2, with (IN) and the sign of \(\tau^X\) of step 2.

title: O.10 The discovery tax and the retained endowment: an exact split with no sign
text:
The statement
Proposition 13 of the paper, stated in Appendix C, compares the retained material endowment of two feasible paths, which it calls the untaxed and the taxed path. It splits the difference exactly into a direct term, from extraction, and an indirect term, from the rates at which the two paths lose matter, signs each term under its premises, and shows that the accounting does not sign their sum. This page proves it in full. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page; a symbol the proof needs beyond them is defined where it is first used.
Proposition 13 (the discovery tax and the retained endowment). General primitives. For any two feasible paths from the same initial stocks, each with nonnegative gross investment, the difference in the retained endowment decomposes exactly into a direct term, the extraction difference weighted by the untaxed path’s retention probabilities, and an indirect term, the change in the leakage of the taxed path’s inflows and of the initial stocks when the untaxed retention schedule replaces the taxed one. The direct term is nonnegative when the untaxed path extracts at least as much at every date; the indirect term is nonpositive when the untaxed path’s loss rates are at least as high at every date and the storage shares coincide, which they do at \(\phi^I=0\). The accounting does not sign the sum: there are two feasible paths meeting all three premises with the untaxed one retaining less.
The names of the two paths come from Section 4.5 of the paper, which reads the proposition as the effect of the discovery tax \(\tau^X\), levied per tonne discovered (Section 4.1). The proposition holds for any two feasible paths, and we label them 0, the untaxed path, and 1, the taxed path. We take the simplest route for the paper’s assumptions. The decomposition and the two signs are accounting on the constraints of Problem 1 and hold for general primitives; no price, tax or equilibrium condition enters. The example of the last sentence is built in the Cobb-Douglas form of the paper’s workhorse, without a floor, under the soft ceiling and with \(\phi^I=0\).

title: O.10 The discovery tax and the retained endowment: an exact split with no sign
text:
What the proof uses
From Section 2 of the paper. A feasible path meets every constraint of Problem 1, the goods constraint, the ledger, the intensity condition and the transitions, with the flows as Section 2 defines them, the domains \(C,N,D,K^R,W,\Omega\ge0\), \(K_{t+1}\ge0\) and \(\varpi_t\in\left[0,1\right]\), and the mass restrictions \(S_t\ge0\), \(X_t\le\bar X_{\max}\) and \(M^K_t\ge0\), from given initial stocks with \(\mathcal W_0\ge0\). On it \(\mathcal W_t\ge0\) at every date, by \(W_t\ge0\) and \(\mu<1\), so the handled flow \(H_t=\mu\mathcal W_t\) is nonnegative. Every cost flow is nonnegative: \(C^N\left(0,S,t\right)=0\) with \(C^N_N>0\), likewise \(C^D\), and \(c^c>0\) and \(c^T\ge0\), as \(c^T\left(0\right)=0\) with \(c^{T\prime}>0\). The yield rises from \(a\left(0,t\right)=0\) towards \(\bar a\), so \(0\le a<\bar a\le1\). Recovered material is \(R^R_t=a_t\varpi_tH_t\) with \(a_t\equiv a\left(x_t,t\right)\); at a date with no treated flow, \(\varpi_tH_t=0\), nothing is recovered, and we set \(a_t\varpi_t\equiv0\). The displaced mass \(\mathcal N=\Omega^{N,S}N+\Omega^{D,S}D\) goes to the environment and enters neither \(M^K\) nor \(\mathcal W\), so the inflow of the two anthropogenic stocks is extraction alone.
From Section 3 and Appendices A and B. With \(\mathcal M_t\equiv M^K_t+\mathcal W_t\), the collected ledger of Section 2 reads \(\Delta\mathcal M_{t+1}=N_t-\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)H_t\), and summed over the periods before a date \(\bar t\) it is the summed ledger of Appendix B.1,  \[
\mathcal M_{\bar t}=\mathcal M_0+\sum_{t<\bar t}N_t-\sum_{t<\bar t}\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)H_t .
\tag{L}
\] Proposition 1(i) bounds the inflow: summing the transitions of \(S\) and \(X\), \(\sum_{t<\bar t}N_t=S_0-S_{\bar t}+X_{\bar t}-X_0\), which \(S_{\bar t}\ge0\) and \(X_{\bar t}\le\bar X_{\max}\) bound by the virgin budget \(\bar N\equiv S_0+\bar X_{\max}-X_0\); so \(\sum_tN_t\le\bar N\). Proposition 3 calls \(\mathcal M_\infty\equiv\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathcal M_t\) the retained material endowment and states that it exists on every feasible path; Lemma M derives this again on the paths the proposition concerns. Appendix B calls \(\ell_t\equiv\mu\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)\) the loss rate of the waste stock, “the share of the stock at the start of period \(t\) that is handled and not recovered”; so \(\ell_t\in\left[0,\mu\right]\), with \(\ell_t=\mu\) at a date with no treated flow. Appendix A calls \(\sigma\equiv\Phi^IG/R\), with \(\Phi^I=\Omega\phi^I\), the storage share, “the fraction of the material entering production that new capital embodies”; we set \(\sigma_t\equiv0\) at a date with \(R_t=0\). With a superscript naming the path, the three premises of the proposition read, at every date \(t\), \[
\text{(P1)}\ \ N^0_t\ge N^1_t,
\qquad
\text{(P2)}\ \ \ell^0_t\ge\ell^1_t,
\qquad
\text{(P3)}\ \ \sigma^0_t=\sigma^1_t .
\]

title: O.10 The discovery tax and the retained endowment: an exact split with no sign
text:
Retention probabilities
Lemma M. Let a feasible path have \(G_t\ge0\) at every date.
(a) At every date \(\sigma_t\in\left[0,1\right]\) and \(\Phi^I_tG_t=\sigma_tR_t\), and with \(\mathbf z_t\equiv\left(M^K_t,\mathcal W_t\right)^\top\)  \[
\mathbf z_{t+1}=\mathbf Q_t\mathbf z_t+\mathbf b_tN_t,
\qquad
\mathbf Q_t\equiv\begin{pmatrix}1-\delta&\sigma_t\left(\mu-\ell_t\right)\\[2pt]\delta&1-\mu+\left(1-\sigma_t\right)\left(\mu-\ell_t\right)\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf b_t\equiv\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_t\\[2pt]1-\sigma_t\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{Z}
\]
(b) For \(t\le\bar t\) let \(\varrho_{t,\bar t}^\top\equiv\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf Q_{\bar t-1}\mathbf Q_{\bar t-2}\cdots\mathbf Q_t\), with \(\mathbf 1\equiv\left(1,1\right)^\top\) and \(\varrho_{\bar t,\bar t}\equiv\mathbf 1\). Its entries lie in \(\left[0,1\right]\) and do not increase with \(\bar t\), so the limit \(\varrho_t\equiv\lim_{\bar t\to\infty}\varrho_{t,\bar t}\equiv\left(\varrho^M_t,\varrho^{\mathcal W}_t\right)^\top\) exists in \(\left[0,1\right]^2\).
(c) The retained endowment exists, and with \(\varrho^N_s\equiv\varrho_{s+1}^\top\mathbf b_s\in\left[0,1\right]\),  \[
\mathcal M_\infty=\varrho^M_0M^K_0+\varrho^{\mathcal W}_0\mathcal W_0+\sum_{s\ge0}\varrho^N_sN_s ,
\tag{R}
\] the series converging.
We call \(\varrho^M_t\) and \(\varrho^{\mathcal W}_t\) the retention probabilities of a tonne in \(M^K_t\) and in \(\mathcal W_t\), and \(\varrho^N_s\) that of a tonne extracted at \(s\); a path’s retention schedule is the sequence of them. They depend on the path only through its loss rates and storage shares. (Z) says how a tonne moves: one in \(M^K_t\) is released into the waste stock with probability \(\delta\), and one in \(\mathcal W_t\) is lost with probability \(\ell_t\) and is otherwise, at \(t+1\), in the waste stock or, recovered and stored, in capital; \(\varrho_{t,\bar t}\) is the probability that a tonne held at \(t\) is still held at \(\bar t\). The proof uses only the algebra.

Proof. 

Every term of \(\mathcal D_t\) is a relative intensity \(\omega^j\ge0\) times a nonnegative flow: consumption, a cost flow, or output, which is nonnegative because the goods constraint gives \(Y_t=C_t+G_t+C^N_t+C^D_t+C^W_t\ge0\) when \(G_t\ge0\). In the intensity condition \(R_t=\Omega_t\mathcal D_t+\Phi^I_tG_t\) both terms are then nonnegative, as \(\Omega_t\ge0\) and \(\phi^I\ge0\), so \(0\le\Phi^I_tG_t\le R_t\). This gives \(\sigma_t\in\left[0,1\right]\), and where \(R_t=0\) it gives \(\Phi^I_tG_t=0=\sigma_tR_t\). The transition of \(M^K\) becomes \(M^K_{t+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)M^K_t+\sigma_tR_t\), the ledger \(W_t=R_t-\Delta M^K_{t+1}=\left(1-\sigma_t\right)R_t+\delta M^K_t\), and the transition of the waste stock \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W_t+\delta M^K_t+\left(1-\sigma_t\right)R_t\). Substituting \(R_t=N_t+a_t\varpi_t\mu\mathcal W_t=N_t+\left(\mu-\ell_t\right)\mathcal W_t\) gives (Z).
As \(0\le\ell_t\le\mu<1\), \(0\le\sigma_t\le1\) and \(0<\delta<1\), \(\mathbf Q_t\) and \(\mathbf b_t\) are entrywise nonnegative, with column sums \(\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf Q_t=\left(1,\,1-\ell_t\right)\le\mathbf 1^\top\) and \(\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf b_t=1\). So \(\varrho_{t,\bar t}\ge0\), and for \(\bar t>t\) \[
\varrho_{t,\bar t}^\top=\left(\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf Q_{\bar t-1}\right)\mathbf Q_{\bar t-2}\cdots\mathbf Q_t\;\le\;\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf Q_{\bar t-2}\cdots\mathbf Q_t=\varrho_{t,\bar t-1}^\top ,
\] the matrices being nonnegative and an empty product being the identity. By induction \(\varrho_{t,\bar t}\le\varrho_{t,t}=\mathbf 1\), and a nonincreasing sequence in \(\left[0,1\right]\) converges.
Iterating (Z) from \(0\) to \(\bar t\) and multiplying by \(\mathbf 1^\top\), since \(\mathcal M_{\bar t}=\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf z_{\bar t}\), \[
\mathcal M_{\bar t}=\varrho_{0,\bar t}^\top\mathbf z_0+\sum_{s<\bar t}f_s\left(\bar t\right),
\qquad
f_s\left(\bar t\right)\equiv\varrho_{s+1,\bar t}^\top\mathbf b_sN_s .
\] By (b), \(f_s\left(\bar t\right)\in\left[0,N_s\right]\) and \(f_s\left(\bar t\right)\to\varrho^N_sN_s\) as \(\bar t\to\infty\), with \(\varrho^N_s\in\left[0,1\right]\). Since \(\sum_sN_s\le\bar N\), for every \(\upsilon>0\) there is a date \(s_\upsilon\) with \(\sum_{s\ge s_\upsilon}N_s<\upsilon\), and for \(\bar t>s_\upsilon\) \[
\Big|\sum_{s<\bar t}f_s\left(\bar t\right)-\sum_{s\ge0}\varrho^N_sN_s\Big|\;\le\;\sum_{s<s_\upsilon}\big|f_s\left(\bar t\right)-\varrho^N_sN_s\big|+2\upsilon ,
\] where the finite sum tends to zero. As \(\varrho_{0,\bar t}^\top\mathbf z_0\to\varrho_0^\top\mathbf z_0\) too, \(\mathcal M_{\bar t}\) converges, to the right side of (R).


At fixed loss rates and storage shares the right side of (R) is linear in the initial stocks and the inflow. And what is not retained leaks: letting \(\bar t\to\infty\) in (L), the cumulated leakage \(\sum_t\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)H_t\) equals \(\mathcal M_0+\sum_tN_t-\mathcal M_\infty\), which by (R) is the initial stocks and the inflow each weighted by one minus its retention probability.

title: O.10 The discovery tax and the retained endowment: an exact split with no sign
text:
Proof of Proposition 13
Let paths 0 and 1 be feasible from the same initial stocks, so with a common \(\mathbf z_0=\left(M^K_0,\mathcal W_0\right)^\top\ge0\), and let each have \(G_t\ge0\) at every date; write \(\Delta Z\equiv Z^0-Z^1\). For a mass made of initial stocks \(\mathbf z\ge0\) and a nonnegative summable inflow \(e\), let \[
\mathcal E^j\left(\mathbf z,e\right)\equiv\left(\varrho^j_0\right)^\top\mathbf z+\sum_{s\ge0}\varrho^{N,j}_se_s ,
\] the part of it that path \(j\)’s retention schedule retains, at most \(\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf z+\sum_se_s\); the rest, \(\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf z+\sum_se_s-\mathcal E^j\left(\mathbf z,e\right)\), is the part that schedule lets leak. By Lemma M, \(\mathcal M^j_\infty=\mathcal E^j\left(\mathbf z_0,N^j\right)\), and by the paragraph after it the leakage of path 1’s own mass \(\left(\mathbf z_0,N^1\right)\) under its own schedule is what path 1 actually loses, \(\sum_t\left(1-a^1_t\varpi^1_t\right)H^1_t\).

Proof. Step 1: the decomposition is exact. Adding and subtracting \(\mathcal E^0\left(\mathbf z_0,N^1\right)\),  \[
\Delta\mathcal M_\infty
=\underbrace{\sum_{s\ge0}\varrho^{N,0}_s\,\Delta N_s}_{\text{direct}}
+\underbrace{\big(\varrho^0_0-\varrho^1_0\big)^\top\mathbf z_0+\sum_{s\ge0}\big(\varrho^{N,0}_s-\varrho^{N,1}_s\big)N^1_s}_{\text{indirect}} ,
\tag{D}
\] every series converging absolutely, its terms being bounded by \(N^0_s+N^1_s\). The direct term is the extraction difference weighted by the untaxed path’s retention probabilities. The indirect term is \(\mathcal E^0\left(\mathbf z_0,N^1\right)-\mathcal E^1\left(\mathbf z_0,N^1\right)\), which is the leakage of the taxed path’s inflow and of the initial stocks under the taxed schedule less their leakage under the untaxed schedule. It is the change in that leakage when the untaxed retention schedule replaces the taxed one, counted as what it does to the endowment, that is with a minus sign: more leakage, less endowment.
Step 2: under (P1) the direct term is nonnegative. Every weight \(\varrho^{N,0}_s\) is nonnegative by Lemma M, and every \(\Delta N_s\) is nonnegative under (P1).
Step 3: under (P2) and (P3) the indirect term is nonpositive. At a common \(\sigma_t\) the two entries of the second column of \(\mathbf Q_t\), \(\sigma_t\left(\mu-\ell_t\right)\) and \(1-\mu+\left(1-\sigma_t\right)\left(\mu-\ell_t\right)\), are nonincreasing in \(\ell_t\), and the first column does not involve \(\ell_t\); so (P2) and (P3) give \(\mathbf Q^0_t\le\mathbf Q^1_t\) entrywise. Backward from \(\varrho^0_{\bar t,\bar t}=\varrho^1_{\bar t,\bar t}=\mathbf 1\), if \(\varrho^0_{t+1,\bar t}\le\varrho^1_{t+1,\bar t}\), then \[
\varrho^0_{t,\bar t}=\left(\mathbf Q^0_t\right)^\top\varrho^0_{t+1,\bar t}\;\le\;\left(\mathbf Q^0_t\right)^\top\varrho^1_{t+1,\bar t}\;\le\;\left(\mathbf Q^1_t\right)^\top\varrho^1_{t+1,\bar t}=\varrho^1_{t,\bar t},
\] the first inequality because \(\mathbf Q^0_t\ge0\) and the second because \(\varrho^1_{t+1,\bar t}\ge0\). In the limit \(\varrho^0_t\le\varrho^1_t\), and with the common \(\mathbf b_s\), \(\varrho^{N,0}_s\le\varrho^{N,1}_s\). As \(\mathbf z_0\ge0\) and \(N^1_s\ge0\), every term of the indirect term is nonpositive. At \(\phi^I=0\), \(\Phi^I=\Omega\phi^I=0\), so \(\sigma_t=0\) on every path and (P3) holds.

The last sentence of the proposition is proved in Two paths on which the untaxed one retains less. Discovery appears in neither (R) nor (D): its displaced mass goes to the environment, so exploration reaches the endowment only through the extraction of the reserves it finds, in the direct term, and through whatever differences in loss rates and storage shares accompany it, in the indirect one.

title: O.10 The discovery tax and the retained endowment: an exact split with no sign
section: Two paths on which the untaxed one retains less
text:
Two paths on which the untaxed one retains less
The example needs a loop that closes, and the economy below lets one be built from any date at which the waste stock is positive and capital is large enough.
The economy. There is no floor, \(\bar R=0\), and output is \[
\mathcal F\left(K^Y,R^e,P,t\right)=A_0\Gamma^te^{-\kappa P}\left(K^Y\right)^{\beta_K}\left(R^e\right)^{\gamma},
\qquad A_0>0,\ \ \Gamma>1,\ \ \kappa>0,\ \ \beta_K,\gamma>0,\ \ \beta_K+\gamma<1 ,
\] the Cobb-Douglas form of the paper’s workhorse with \(B_t\equiv1\) and \(A_t=A_0\Gamma^t\). It has the signs of Section 2, is concave in \(\left(K^Y,R^e\right)\), its Hessian there having negative diagonal and determinant proportional to \(\beta_K\gamma\left(1-\beta_K-\gamma\right)>0\), and has \(\mathcal F_K\to\infty\) as \(K^Y\to0\) at any \(R^e>0\). The yield is \(a\left(x\right)=1-e^{-x}\), which has the properties of Section 2 under the soft ceiling \(\bar a=1\); \(\phi^I=0\) and \(\omega^Y>0\). Every other primitive is any that Section 2 allows. The initial stocks are \(M^K_0=0\), \(\mathcal W_0>0\), \(S_0>0\), \(X_0\le\bar X_{\max}\), \(P_0\ge0\) and a capital stock \(K_0\) chosen below, as \(A_0\) is. With \(\phi^I=0\) the transition of \(M^K\) keeps \(M^K_t=0\), so \(\mathcal M_t=\mathcal W_t\), the ledger gives \(W_t=R_t\), and \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\left(1-\ell_t\right)\mathcal W_t+N_t\). Fix \(\hat x\) with \(e^{-\hat x}\le\min\left\{\delta,\tfrac14\right\}\), let \(\hat x_t\equiv\hat x+t\), and let \(c^{\mathrm{full}}\equiv c^c\left(0\right)+c^T\left(1,0\right)\), which bounds the handling cost per handled tonne at full treatment at every date, both charges being nonincreasing in time.
Lemma K. In this economy take the stocks at a date \(t_0\ge0\), the initial ones if \(t_0=0\) and otherwise those left by a path that meets every constraint, domain and mass restriction of Problem 1 at the dates before \(t_0\), and let them have \(M^K_{t_0}=0\), \(S_{t_0}\ge0\), \(X_{t_0}\le\bar X_{\max}\), \(P_{t_0}\ge0\), \(w\equiv\mathcal W_{t_0}>0\) and \(K_{t_0}>\hat x_{t_0}\mu w\); let \(k\equiv K_{t_0}-\hat x_{t_0}\mu w\). For \(t\ge t_0\) set \(N_t=D_t=0\), \(\varpi_t=1\), \(K^R_t=\hat x_t\mu\mathcal W_t\), \(K_{t+1}=k+K^R_{t+1}\) and \(I_t\equiv K_{t+1}-K_t\), and take \(C_t\) from the goods constraint, \(\Omega_t\equiv R_t/\mathcal D_t\), \(W_t\) from the ledger and the other states from the transitions. Then for \(t\ge t_0\), \(\ell_t=\mu e^{-\hat x_t}\) and \(\mathcal W_t\) is nonincreasing with \(\tfrac12w\le\mathcal W_t\le w\), so \(\tfrac12w\le\mathcal M_\infty\le w\). If moreover  \[
A_0\,\underline y\;\ge\;\max\Big\{\delta k+\left(\hat x+1+c^{\mathrm{full}}\right)\mu w,\ \frac{\mu w}{\ln\Gamma}\Big\},
\qquad
\underline y\equiv e^{-\kappa\left(P_{t_0}+w\right)}k^{\beta_K}\left(\tfrac38\mu w\right)^{\gamma},
\tag{K}
\] every constraint, domain and mass restriction of Problem 1 holds at every \(t\ge t_0\), with \(G_t>0\), so that the path continued in this way is feasible.

Proof. The material block does not involve capital. At \(t\ge t_0\) the treated flow is \(\varpi_tH_t=\mu\mathcal W_t\), positive by induction, so capital per treated tonne is \(x_t=K^R_t/\left(\varpi_tH_t\right)=\hat x_t\), \(R_t=R^R_t=\left(1-e^{-\hat x_t}\right)\mu\mathcal W_t\), \(\ell_t=\mu e^{-\hat x_t}\) and \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\left(1-\ell_t\right)\mathcal W_t\). So \(\mathcal W_{t+1}\), and with it \(K_{t+1}\), is fixed at \(t\), and the construction is recursive. As \(\hat x_s\ge\hat x+\left(s-t_0\right)\), \(\sum_{s\ge t_0}\ell_s\le\mu e^{-\hat x}\sum_{j\ge0}e^{-j}<2e^{-\hat x}\le\tfrac12\), and \(\prod_s\left(1-\ell_s\right)\ge1-\sum_s\ell_s\) by induction, so \(w\ge\mathcal W_t\ge\tfrac12w\) and \(R_t\ge\left(1-e^{-\hat x}\right)\tfrac12\mu w\ge\tfrac38\mu w\). No mass is displaced, and the handled stream emits \(\Xi_t=d^We^{-\hat x_t}\mu\mathcal W_t=d^W\ell_t\mathcal W_t\le\mathcal W_t-\mathcal W_{t+1}\), so from \(0\le P_{t+1}\le P_t+\Xi_t\), as \(\theta\in\left(0,1\right)\) and \(P_{t_0}\ge0\), \(0\le P_t\le P_{t_0}+w\).
Capital. \(K_t=k+K^R_t\) at every \(t\ge t_0\), at \(t_0\) by the definition of \(k\), so \(K^Y_t=k>0\) and \(K^R_t<K_t\). Since \(\ell_t<e^{-\hat x}\le\delta\) and \(\hat x_{t+1}=\hat x_t+1\), \[
G_t=K_{t+1}-\left(1-\delta\right)K_t=\delta k+\mu\mathcal W_t\Big[\left(\hat x_t+1\right)\left(1-\ell_t\right)-\left(1-\delta\right)\hat x_t\Big]\;\ge\;\delta k>0 ,
\] and \(G_t\le\delta k+\hat x_{t+1}\mu\mathcal W_{t+1}\le\delta k+\left(\hat x+t+1\right)\mu w\).
Consumption. By the bounds on \(R_t\) and \(P_t\), \(Y_t\ge A_0\Gamma^t\underline y\). Extraction and exploration cost nothing, and \(C^W_t=\left[c^c\left(t\right)+c^T\left(1,t\right)\right]\mu\mathcal W_t\le c^{\mathrm{full}}\mu w\). With \(\Gamma^t\ge1+t\ln\Gamma\), \[
C_t=Y_t-G_t-C^W_t\;\ge\;\Big[A_0\underline y-\delta k-\left(\hat x+1+c^{\mathrm{full}}\right)\mu w\Big]+t\Big[A_0\underline y\ln\Gamma-\mu w\Big]\;\ge\;0
\] by (K).
The rest. \(\mathcal D_t\ge\omega^YY_t>0\), so \(\Omega_t\ge0\) is finite and the intensity condition holds; the ledger gives \(W_t=R_t\ge0\); \(N_t=D_t=0\), \(\varpi_t=1\), \(K^R_t\ge0\) and \(K_{t+1}>0\); \(S\) and \(X\) do not move and \(M^K=0\), so the mass restrictions hold; and the goods constraint holds by the definition of \(C_t\).

Proof of the last sentence of Proposition 13. Take the economy above. Choose \(n\in\left(0,S_0\right]\), an integer \(T_0\) with \(\left(1-\mu\right)^{T_0}\left(\mathcal W_0+n\right)<\tfrac12\mathcal W_0\), then \(K_0>\left(1-\delta\right)^{-T_0-1}\left(\hat x+T_0+1\right)\mu\left(\mathcal W_0+n\right)\), and last \(A_0\) large enough for the three inequalities named below, none of whose other terms involves \(A_0\).

Proof. Path 1, the taxed path, is Lemma K’s continuation from date 0, with \(w=\mathcal W_0\) and \(K_0>\hat x\mu\mathcal W_0\) by the choice of \(K_0\); (K) for it is the first inequality. It never extracts, has \(\ell^1_t=\mu e^{-\hat x_t}\) at every date, and retains \(\mathcal M^1_\infty\ge\tfrac12\mathcal W_0\).
Path 0, the untaxed path, extracts \(N^0_0=n\) at date 0 and treats nothing: \(D^0_0=0\), \(\varpi^0_0=0\), \(K^{R,0}_0=0\), \(G^0_0=0\), so \(K^0_1=\left(1-\delta\right)K_0\), and, \(C^D\) and \(C^W\) being zero, \(C^0_0=Y^0_0-C^N\left(n,S_0,0\right)\) with \(Y^0_0=A_0e^{-\kappa P_0}K_0^{\beta_K}n^{\gamma}\), nonnegative under the second inequality, \(A_0e^{-\kappa P_0}K_0^{\beta_K}n^{\gamma}\ge C^N\left(n,S_0,0\right)\). Then \(\mathcal D^0_0\ge\omega^YY^0_0>0\) and \(\Omega^0_0=n/\mathcal D^0_0\); \(S^0_1=S_0-n\ge0\); the ledger gives \(W^0_0=n\), and \(\mathcal W^0_1=\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W_0+n\). At the dates \(1\le t\le T_0\) the path is idle: it extracts, discovers and treats nothing, so \(R^0_t=0\), output, every cost flow, \(\mathcal D^0_t\), consumption and gross investment are zero, \(\Omega^0_t=0\), \(K^0_{t+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)K^0_t\) and \(\mathcal W^0_{t+1}=\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W^0_t\), and every constraint holds. From \(T_0+1\) on it is Lemma K’s continuation from \(w^0\equiv\mathcal W^0_{T_0+1}=\left(1-\mu\right)^{T_0}\left[\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W_0+n\right]\), with \(K^0_{T_0+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)^{T_0+1}K_0>\hat x_{T_0+1}\mu w^0\) by the choice of \(K_0\), \(M^K_{T_0+1}=0\), \(S^0_{T_0+1}=S_0-n\ge0\), \(X^0_{T_0+1}=X_0\) and \(P^0_{T_0+1}\ge0\), pollution staying nonnegative from \(P_0\ge0\) as \(\Xi\ge0\) and \(\theta<1\). (K) for it is the third inequality, in which \(P^0_{T_0+1}\) is fixed by the material choices before \(T_0+1\).
Both paths are feasible from the same initial stocks, with \(G\ge0\) at every date. (P1): \(N^0_0=n>0=N^1_0\), and neither path extracts later. (P2): \(\ell^0_t=\mu>\ell^1_t\) at \(t\le T_0\), where path 0 treats nothing, and \(\ell^0_t=\mu e^{-\hat x_t}=\ell^1_t\) after. (P3): \(\phi^I=0\). Yet, by Lemma K and the choice of \(T_0\), \[
\mathcal M^0_\infty\;\le\;w^0\;<\;\left(1-\mu\right)^{T_0}\left(\mathcal W_0+n\right)\;<\;\tfrac12\mathcal W_0\;\le\;\mathcal M^1_\infty .
\] The untaxed path retains less although its direct term is positive. The definition of Lemma M(b) gives \(\varrho_{t,\bar t}=\mathbf Q_t^\top\varrho_{t+1,\bar t}\), whose second entry at \(\sigma\equiv0\) is \(\left(1-\ell_t\right)\varrho^{\mathcal W}_{t+1,\bar t}\); with \(\mathbf b_s=\left(0,1\right)^\top\) this gives \(\varrho^{N,0}_0=\prod_{t\ge1}\left(1-\ell^0_t\right)=\left(1-\mu\right)^{T_0}\prod_{t>T_0}\left(1-\ell^0_t\right)\ge\tfrac12\left(1-\mu\right)^{T_0}\), by the bound on \(\sum_{t>T_0}\ell^0_t\) in the proof of Lemma K. So the direct term is \(n\varrho^{N,0}_0>0\): path 0 keeps part of what it extracts, but its idle dates lose the initial stock that path 1 keeps.

The hard ceiling. Under the hard ceiling the proposition is empty, every retention probability being zero. If \(\bar a<1\), then \(\ell_t\ge\underline\ell\equiv\mu\left(1-\bar a\right)>0\) at every date, as \(a_t\varpi_t\le a_t<\bar a\) where a flow is treated and \(a_t\varpi_t=0\) where none is. Multiplying out, \[
\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf Q_{t+1}\mathbf Q_t=\Big(1-\delta\ell_{t+1},\ \ 1-\ell_t-\ell_{t+1}\left[1-\mu+\left(1-\sigma_t\right)\left(\mu-\ell_t\right)\right]\Big)\;\le\;\left(1-\delta\underline\ell\right)\mathbf 1^\top ,
\] the bracket being nonnegative, and since every \(\mathbf Q_t\) is nonnegative with \(\mathbf 1^\top\mathbf Q_t\le\mathbf 1^\top\), taking the factors of \(\varrho_{t,\bar t}^\top\) two at a time gives \(\varrho_{t,\bar t}\le\left(1-\delta\underline\ell\right)^{\lfloor\left(\bar t-t\right)/2\rfloor}\mathbf 1\to0\). So \(\varrho_t=0\) at every date, both terms of (D) vanish, and \(\mathcal M_\infty=0\) on every feasible path with nonnegative gross investment.

title: O.11 A laissez-faire collapse where the planner survives
text:
The statement
Theorem 1 of the paper (a laissez-faire collapse where the planner survives) states that the floor and soft-ceiling cell contains primitives under which no optimal path of the planner collapses, while every open-access path does. This page proves it in full by constructing such primitives. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page; a symbol the proof needs beyond them is defined where it is first used. Three lemmas about the economy the proof constructs, Lemmas Z, W and E, are proved on the continuation of this page.
Section 3.7 of the paper calls the inequality  \[
\left(1-\delta\right)^{1-\eta}<1+\rho
\tag{R}
\] the collapse ranking condition.
Theorem 1 (a laissez-faire collapse where the planner survives). There are primitives in the floor and soft-ceiling cell, in the workhorse family of Section 3.6 with the exponential yield at \(\bar a=1\), \(\phi^I=0\), \(\eta>1\) and the collapse ranking condition (R) failing, under which the planner’s problem has an optimal path; every optimal path has a finite value and an infinite operating set, so is not in state A, and keeps \(\mu\) times its remaining budget at or above \(\bar R\) at every date; while every open-access path recycles nothing before a date \(t^*\), holds its remaining budget below \(\bar R/\mu\) from then on, and is in state A. The open-access part uses no property of preferences, of the household or of the mining sector.
We take the simplest route for the paper’s assumptions. Problem 1 takes the initial stocks as given, so the primitives we exhibit include them. In the economy we construct, all the material left is in the waste stock, enough to carry the floor if the loop is closed from the first period. The collection charge lies above any price an operating final-goods sector pays for a tonne of material at date \(0\), and below what a path that closes the loop from the first period can afford. The open-access part is then accounting on the constraints of Problem 1, with the two sector conditions that define an open-access path applied at date \(0\). The planner’s part combines Proposition 5 of the paper with Lemmas B, W and E and uses no first-order condition. What the proof uses restates what the proof takes from the paper beyond its Section 2.
