title: O.11 A laissez-faire collapse where the planner survives
text:
What the proof uses
From Section 2 of the paper. A feasible path meets every constraint of Problem 1: the goods constraint, the ledger \(W_t=R_t-\Delta M^K_{t+1}\), the intensity condition and the transitions, with the flows as Section 2 defines them, the domains \(C,N,D,K^R,W,\Omega\ge0\), \(K_{t+1}\ge0\) and \(\varpi_t\in\left[0,1\right]\), and the mass restrictions \(S_t\ge0\), \(X_t\le\bar X_{\max}\) and \(M^K_t\ge0\). Capital is split between production and recycling, \(K=K^Y+K^R\), so \(K^R_t\le K_t\), and \(K^Y_t=K_t-K^R_t\) is the capital input of \(F\). The waste-stock transition \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W_t+W_t\), with \(W_t\ge0\) and \(\mathcal W_0\ge0\), keeps \(\mathcal W_t\ge0\), so the handled flow \(H_t=\mu\mathcal W_t\) is nonnegative. The treated flow is \(T_t\equiv\varpi_tH_t\). Where \(T_t>0\), recovered material is \(R^R_t=a\left(x_t,t\right)T_t\) with \(x_t=K^R_t/T_t\); where \(T_t=0\), nothing is recovered. Either way \(0\le R^R_t\le\bar aT_t\), as \(a<\bar a\), and with \(T_t\le H_t\) this is the throughput cap of Section 2.3, \(R^R_t\le\bar a\mu\mathcal W_t\). Raw material input is \(R_t=N_t+R^R_t\). Every cost flow is nonnegative: \(C^N\left(0,S,t\right)=0\) with \(C^N_N>0\), likewise \(C^D\), and \(c^c>0\) and \(c^T\ge0\), as \(c^T\left(0\right)=0\) with \(c^{T\prime}>0\).
Welfare is \(U_0=\sum_{t\ge0}\beta^t\left[u\left(C_t\right)-v\left(P_t\right)\right]\), with \(\beta\equiv1/\left(1+\rho\right)\) and \(\rho>0\). The value of a feasible path is the limit, as \(n\to\infty\), of the partial sums \(\sum_{t=0}^{n}\beta^t\left[u\left(C_t\right)-v\left(P_t\right)\right]\), where that limit exists in \(\left[-\infty,\infty\right]\); the value is finite when the limit is a real number. An optimal path is a feasible path whose value exists and is at least the value of every feasible path whose value exists.
From Section 3. The material budget (Section 3.2) is \(\mathcal B\equiv\bar N+M^K_0+\mathcal W_0\), with the virgin budget \(\bar N\equiv S_0+\bar X_{\max}-X_0\). The operating set (Section 3.3) is \(\mathcal O\equiv\left\{t:R_t\ge\bar R\right\}\), and Definition 1 calls a path in state A, “collapse if \(\mathcal O\) is finite: production ceases after a finite total number of operating periods, output is zero thereafter, and consumption, financed from the capital stock alone, converges to zero”. A feasible path with a finite operating set meets the whole clause: after its last operating date output is zero, so the goods constraint, with every cost flow nonnegative, \(C_t\ge0\) and \(K_{t+1}\ge0\), gives \(K_{t+1}\le\left(1-\delta\right)K_t\) and \(C_t\le\left(1-\delta\right)K_t\), and capital and consumption tend to zero. So a feasible path is in state A exactly when its operating set is finite.
The workhorse (Section 3.6) “is the Cobb-Douglas case of the specification the quantitative model of Section 5 implements: output \(A_te^{-\kappa P}\left(K^Y\right)^{\beta_K}\left(B_tR^e\right)^{\gamma}\) with \(\beta_K+\gamma<1\), a marginal extraction cost rising with the elasticity \(\mu_N\) as the reserve falls, the exponential yield \(a\left(x\right)=\bar a\left(1-e^{-\xi x}\right)\), and CRRA utility”. Appendix B.6 takes “the marginal extraction cost proportional to \(\left(S_{\mathrm{ref}}/S\right)^{\mu_N}\) as the reserve falls”. The trends are those of Assumption 1(i), \(A_{t+1}/A_t=1+g_A\) and \(B_{t+1}/B_t=1+g_B\) with \(g_A,g_B\ge0\) and \(g_A+g_B>0\), and Section 3.6 writes \(\Gamma\equiv\left(1+g_A\right)\left(1+g_B\right)^{\gamma}>1\). CRRA utility with elasticity \(\eta>1\) is \(u\left(C\right)=C^{1-\eta}/\left(1-\eta\right)\), negative and increasing on \(\left(0,\infty\right)\), with \(u\left(0\right)=-\infty\).
Proposition 5 (selection against collapse) is stated in Section 3.7 and proved in full in O.4 of this appendix. We use it as the paper states it, and only this part of it: “Let \(\bar R>0\) and let \(u\) be CRRA with elasticity \(\eta\). […] (ii) Where (R) fails and some feasible path has a finite value, every optimal path has a finite value and an infinite operating set.” Value and optimal path are read in it as defined in From Section 2 of the paper.
From Section 4 and Appendix C. A unit of the final good put to the current use \(j\) costs the user price \(P^j\equiv1+\left(z+\tau^W\right)\Omega\omega^j\), with \(\tau^W\) the gate fee and \(z\) the material-content price; \(p^R\) is the price of a tonne of raw material, \(r^K\) the rental of capital, \(\tau^P\) the emission tax, and \(\tilde p\equiv p^R+d^W\tau^P\) the waste sector’s value of a recovered tonne (Section 4.1). Section 4.2: “Under open access the waste stock has no owner: dumping is free, \(\tau^W=0\), and with \(\tau^P=z=0\) every user price is one, a recovered tonne sells at \(p^R=F_R\) and capital rents at \(r^K=F_K\); since nobody values the stock, the waste sector chooses its treated share and recycling capital against its operating profit alone.” Appendix C.1 writes that operating profit as \(\Pi^W\left(\varpi,K^R\right)\equiv\tilde p\,\mathcal R\left(\varpi H,K^R\right)+\tau^P\left(1-d^W\right)\varpi H-P^W\left[c^c\varpi+c^T\left(\varpi\right)\right]H-r^KK^R-\tau^PH\). At open access’s prices, \(\tilde p=p^R\), \(\tau^P=0\) and \(P^W=1\), so at date \(t\)  \[
\Pi^W_t\left(\varpi,K^R\right)=p^R_t\,\mathcal R\left(\varpi H_t,K^R,t\right)-\left[c^c\varpi+c^T\left(\varpi\right)\right]H_t-r^K_tK^R .
\tag{$\Pi^W$}
\] The final-goods sector “rents \(K^Y\), buys \(R\) tonnes and sells \(Y\). The \(\Omega^YY\) tonnes that diffuse in production go to the waste sector at the fee, and the rest leaves inside the good and sells at \(z\)” (Section 4.1). The fee and \(z\) are zero at open access, so there its profit at date \(t\) is  \[
\Pi^Y_t\left(K,R\right)=F\left(K,R,P_t,t\right)-p^R_tR-r^K_tK .
\tag{$\Pi^Y$}
\] Definition 2 has the sector either operate, “choosing \(\left(K^Y,R\right)\) at a maximum of its profit over \(\left[0,\infty\right)^2\)”, or be idle, “\(Y=R=0\), with \(r^K=0\)”.
Appendix C.9 defines the class of paths the theorem speaks of: “An open-access path is a feasible allocation with prices that takes every generated tonne into the waste stock at a zero fee, has the waste sector maximising its operating profit at open access’s prices, and has the final-goods sector either operating at a global maximum of its profit, hence participating, or idle; nothing is required of the household or the mine”. We read the definition as three conditions on a path with prices \(\left(p^R_t,r^K_t\right)_{t\ge0}\), at every date \(t\):

(OA1) the allocation is a feasible path, its waste-stock transition taking every generated tonne into \(\mathcal W\), at a zero fee;
(OA2) the waste sector’s pair \(\left(\varpi_t,K^R_t\right)\) maximises (\(\Pi^W\)) over \(\left[0,1\right]\times\left[0,\infty\right)\);
(OA3) either the date is idle, \(Y_t=R_t=0\), or the final-goods sector operates: \(\left(K^Y_t,R_t\right)\) maximises (\(\Pi^Y\)) over \(\left[0,\infty\right)^2\).

The proof uses no price at an idle date, so it covers the reading of idle with \(r^K=0\) as well. At an operating date it derives open access’s prices, \(p^R=F_R\) and \(r^K=F_K\), and participation, from (OA3).
Appendix C.9 also defines the remaining budget: “The remaining budget is the virgin material still to be extracted, \(S_t+\bar X_{\max}-X_t\), plus the two anthropogenic stocks; it falls each period by exactly the leakage flow and, once below \(\bar R/\left(\bar a\mu\right)\), leaves the economy only finitely many operating periods.” We write it  \[
\mathcal B_t\equiv S_t+\bar X_{\max}-X_t+M^K_t+\mathcal W_t ,
\tag{B}
\] so that \(\mathcal B_0=\mathcal B\). The leakage flow is the left side of the collected ledger of Section 2.3, \(\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)H_t=H_t-R^R_t\). Lemma B proves the two claims of the definition.

title: O.11 A laissez-faire collapse where the planner survives
text:
The remaining budget
Lemma B. On every feasible path:
(a) \(\mathcal B_{t+1}=\mathcal B_t-\left(H_t-R^R_t\right)\) with \(H_t-R^R_t\ge0\), so the remaining budget is nonincreasing; and \(0\le\mathcal W_t\le\mathcal B_t\);
(b) if \(\bar a\mu\mathcal B_{t_1}<\bar R\) at some date \(t_1\), then at most \(\left(S_{t_1}+\bar X_{\max}-X_{t_1}\right)/\left(\bar R-\bar a\mu\mathcal B_{t_1}\right)\) dates \(t\ge t_1\) have \(R_t\ge\bar R\), and the operating set is finite. Equivalently, a feasible path with an infinite operating set has \(\bar a\mu\mathcal B_t\ge\bar R\) at every date.

Proof. 

The waste-stock transition and the ledger give \(\mathcal W_{t+1}-\mathcal W_t=W_t-H_t=R_t-\left(M^K_{t+1}-M^K_t\right)-H_t\), and the transitions of reserves and discovery give \(\left(S_{t+1}-X_{t+1}\right)-\left(S_t-X_t\right)=\left(D_t-N_t\right)-D_t=-N_t\). Adding the change in \(M^K\) and using \(R_t=N_t+R^R_t\), \(\mathcal B_{t+1}-\mathcal B_t=-N_t+R_t-H_t=R^R_t-H_t\), which is nonpositive as \(R^R_t\le\bar aT_t\le H_t\). The mass restrictions make \(S_t\), \(\bar X_{\max}-X_t\) and \(M^K_t\) nonnegative, so \(\mathcal B_t\ge\mathcal W_t\ge0\).
Let \(t\ge t_1\). The throughput cap and (a) give \(R_t=N_t+R^R_t\le N_t+\bar a\mu\mathcal W_t\le N_t+\bar a\mu\mathcal B_t\le N_t+\bar a\mu\mathcal B_{t_1}\), so at a date with \(R_t\ge\bar R\) extraction is at least the positive gap \(\bar R-\bar a\mu\mathcal B_{t_1}\). Summing the transitions of reserves and discovery from \(t_1\) to any \(n\ge t_1\) gives \(\sum_{t=t_1}^{n}N_t=S_{t_1}-S_{n+1}+X_{n+1}-X_{t_1}\le S_{t_1}+\bar X_{\max}-X_{t_1}\), by \(S_{n+1}\ge0\) and \(X_{n+1}\le\bar X_{\max}\). As \(N_t\ge0\), the gap times the number of dates \(t\ge t_1\) with \(R_t\ge\bar R\) is at most this sum, which is the bound; finitely many dates precede \(t_1\). The second sentence is the contrapositive of the first.

title: O.11 A laissez-faire collapse where the planner survives
text:
The economy
We prove the theorem for the primitives and initial stocks that follow. Every primitive is constant in time except the two trends, and the constants left open in the list are fixed in The constants that separate the two economies.

Technology. \(\beta_K,\gamma>0\) with \(\mu_F\equiv\beta_K+\gamma<1\); \(g_A,g_B\ge0\) with \(g_A+g_B>0\), and \(B_0=1\); for \(R\ge\bar R\) the workhorse’s output \(\mathcal F=A_te^{-\kappa P}\left(K^Y\right)^{\beta_K}\left(B_tR^e\right)^{\gamma}\), so that \(A_tB_t^{\gamma}=A_0\Gamma^t\), with \(\kappa>0\) and \(A_0>0\) left open.
Floor and yield. \(\bar R>0\), and the exponential yield at \(\bar a=1\), \(a\left(x\right)=1-e^{-\xi x}\) with \(\xi>0\).
Waste and handling. \(\mu\in\left(\mu_F,1\right)\); \(d^W\in\left(0,1\right)\); any treatment cost \(c^T\) with the properties of Section 2, for instance \(c^T\left(\varpi\right)=\varpi^2\); and a collection charge \(c^c>0\) left open.
Materials accounting. \(\phi^I=0\); \(\omega^j\ge0\) for every use, with \(\omega^C>0\); any \(\Omega^{N,S},\Omega^{D,S}\ge0\).
Pollution. Any decay rate \(\theta\) with the properties of Section 2, for instance \(\theta\left(P\right)=\left(1+e^{-P}\right)/4\).
Extraction and exploration. The workhorse’s extraction cost and any exploration cost with the properties of Section 2, each zero at a zero flow for every \(S\ge0\) and \(X\le\bar X_{\max}\). By Lemma Z they enter only there.
Preferences. \(\delta\in\left(0,1\right)\); CRRA utility with \(\eta>1\); \(\rho\in\left(0,\left(1-\delta\right)^{1-\eta}-1\right]\), an interval that is not empty as \(\left(1-\delta\right)^{1-\eta}>1\), so that (R) fails; and the workhorse’s disutility \(v\left(P\right)=\psi_vP^{1+\varphi}/\left(1+\varphi\right)\) with \(\psi_v,\varphi>0\), or any \(v\) with the properties of Section 2 that is real-valued on \(P\ge0\).
Initial stocks. \(S_0=0\), \(X_0=\bar X_{\max}\), \(M^K_0=0\), \(\mathcal W_0=\bar R/\left[\mu\left(1-\mu_F\right)\right]\), \(P_0>0\), and \(K_0\) left open.

With \(\bar R>0\) and \(\bar a=1\), the economy is in the floor and soft-ceiling cell. Its output function has the signs of Section 2.1 wherever \(K^Y,R^e>0\), \(\mathcal F_P=-\kappa\mathcal F<0\) among them. It is concave in \(\left(K^Y,R^e\right)\), its Hessian at \(K^Y,R^e>0\) having a negative diagonal and a determinant proportional to \(\beta_K\gamma\left(1-\beta_K-\gamma\right)>0\), and \(\mathcal F_K=\beta_K\mathcal F/K^Y\to\infty\) as \(K^Y\to0\) at any \(R^e>0\): these are the two clauses Section 2.1 states after the output function. Where \(K^Y,R^e>0\), \(F_K=\beta_KY/K^Y\) and \(F_R=\gamma Y/R^e\). Pollution is positive at every date of every feasible path, as \(P_{t+1}\ge\left[1-\theta\left(P_t\right)\right]P_t\) and \(P_0>0\), and at a positive stock the workhorse’s \(v\) has \(v'>0\) and \(v''>0\). Every \(v\) admitted is continuous and nondecreasing on \(P\ge0\).
The constants that separate the two economies. Write \(\bar P\equiv P_0+\mathcal W_0\), and take \(\kappa>0\) so small that  \[
s\;\equiv\;\left(\frac{\gamma}{\mu_F}\right)^{\gamma}e^{\kappa\bar P}\;<\;1 ,
\tag{S}
\] which is possible because \(\beta_K>0\) makes \(\mu_F>\gamma\). Then choose, in this order:

\(x_0\ge1/\xi\) so large that \(b\equiv\mu e^{-\xi x_0}/\left(1-\Gamma^{-1}\right)<1\), that \(\underline R\equiv\left(1-e^{-\xi x_0}\right)\left(1-b\right)\mu\mathcal W_0>\bar R\), and that \(\left[\left(1-\mu_F\right)\left(\underline R-\bar R\right)/\left(\mu_F\bar R\right)\right]^{\gamma}>\sqrt s\). This is possible: as \(x_0\to\infty\), \(b\to0\) and \(\underline R\to\mu\mathcal W_0=\bar R/\left(1-\mu_F\right)\), so the bracket tends to one, while \(\sqrt s<1\).
\(k>0\) so large that \(\left[k/\left(k+x_0\mu\mathcal W_0\right)\right]^{\beta_K}>\sqrt s\), which is possible as the ratio tends to one, and \(K_0\equiv k+x_0\mu\mathcal W_0\).
\(A_0\), given the rest. Write \[
\underline Y\equiv A_0e^{-\kappa\bar P}\left(\underline R-\bar R\right)^{\gamma}k^{\beta_K},
\qquad
\bar p^R\equiv\gamma A_0K_0^{\beta_K}\left(\frac{\gamma\bar R}{1-\mu_F}\right)^{\gamma-1},
\] both proportional to \(A_0\). Substituting \(\mu\mathcal W_0=\bar R/\left(1-\mu_F\right)\) and collecting powers of \(\gamma\bar R\), then using (S), \[
\frac{\underline Y}{\mu\mathcal W_0\,\bar p^R}
=e^{-\kappa\bar P}\left[\frac{\left(1-\mu_F\right)\left(\underline R-\bar R\right)}{\gamma\bar R}\right]^{\gamma}\left(\frac{k}{K_0}\right)^{\beta_K}
=\frac1s\left[\frac{\left(1-\mu_F\right)\left(\underline R-\bar R\right)}{\mu_F\bar R}\right]^{\gamma}\left(\frac{k}{K_0}\right)^{\beta_K}
\;>\;\frac{\sqrt s\,\sqrt s}{s}=1 ,
\] by steps 1 and 2. So \(\underline Y-\mu\mathcal W_0\bar p^R\) is positive and proportional to \(A_0\), and we take \(A_0\) so large that \[
\underline Y-\mu\mathcal W_0\,\bar p^R\;>\;\delta k+\mu\mathcal W_0\left(\delta x_0+\frac{\ln\Gamma}{\xi}\right)+c^T\left(1\right)\mu\mathcal W_0 .
\]
\(c^c\equiv\bar p^R\), which is positive.

By steps 3 and 4, \[
\underline C\;\equiv\;\underline Y-\delta k-\mu\mathcal W_0\left(\delta x_0+\frac{\ln\Gamma}{\xi}\right)-\left[c^c+c^T\left(1\right)\right]\mu\mathcal W_0\;>\;0 .
\] So the economy is in the floor and soft-ceiling cell and in the workhorse family, with the exponential yield at \(\bar a=1\), \(\phi^I=0\), \(\eta>1\) and (R) failing, and with \(\kappa>0\), so that output falls with pollution as Section 2.1 requires.

title: O.11 A laissez-faire collapse where the planner survives
text:
Proof of Theorem 1
Take the economy of The economy and let \(t^*\equiv1\). It is one of the economies (E) of the continuation page: above the floor its output is \(A_0\Gamma^te^{-\kappa P}\left(K^Y\right)^{\beta_K}\left(R^e\right)^{\gamma}\), as \(A_tB_t^{\gamma}=A_0\Gamma^t\), and its other primitives and initial stocks are among those (E) admits. So Lemma Z applies to its feasible paths: none extracts or explores, \(S_t=0\), \(X_t=\bar X_{\max}\) and \(M^K_t=0\) at every date, so the remaining budget (B) is the waste stock, \(\mathcal B_t=\mathcal W_t\).

Proof. Step 1: a feasible path has a finite value. The constants \(x_0\ge1/\xi\) and \(k>0\) of The economy, with \(K_0=k+x_0\mu\mathcal W_0\), \(b<1\), \(\underline R>\bar R\) and \(\underline C>0\), meet the hypotheses of Lemma W. So the economy has a feasible path with \(C_t\ge\underline C>0\) at every date, and its value is finite.
Step 2: the planner’s problem has an optimal path. By step 1 and Lemma E.
Step 3: every optimal path has a finite value and an infinite operating set, so is not in state A. Here \(\bar R>0\), \(u\) is CRRA with elasticity \(\eta>1\), (R) fails, and by step 1 some feasible path has a finite value. Part (ii) of Proposition 5 gives the two claims, and a path in state A has a finite operating set.
Step 4: every optimal path keeps \(\mu\mathcal B_t\ge\bar R\) at every date. Its operating set is infinite by step 3, so Lemma B(b), at \(\bar a=1\), gives \(\mu\mathcal B_t\ge\bar R\) at every date.
Step 5: an open-access path recycles nothing before \(t^*\). Take an open-access path and suppose \(R^R_0>0\). By Lemma Z, \(N_0=0\), so \(R_0=R^R_0>0\): the date is not idle, and by (OA3) \(\left(K^Y_0,R_0\right)\) maximises \(\Pi^Y_0\) over \(\left[0,\infty\right)^2\).
Both prices are positive. If \(r^K_0\le0\), then \(\Pi^Y_0\left(K,\bar R+1\right)\ge A_0e^{-\kappa P_0}K^{\beta_K}-p^R_0\left(\bar R+1\right)\), which grows without bound in \(K\) as \(\beta_K>0\). If \(p^R_0\le0\), then \(\Pi^Y_0\left(1,R\right)\ge A_0e^{-\kappa P_0}\left(R-\bar R\right)^{\gamma}-r^K_0\), which grows without bound in \(R\) as \(\gamma>0\). Either way \(\Pi^Y_0\) would have no maximum.
The sector produces and participates. The choice \(\left(0,0\right)\) gives \(\Pi^Y_0\left(0,0\right)=0\), output being zero below the floor, so \(\Pi^Y_0\left(K^Y_0,R_0\right)\ge0\). Were \(Y_0=0\), this profit would be \(-p^R_0R_0-r^K_0K^Y_0<0\). So \(Y_0>0\), which in the workhorse needs \(K^Y_0>0\) and \(R^e_0=R_0-\bar R>0\).
Open access’s prices. \(\Pi^Y_0\) is differentiable on the open set where \(K>0\) and \(R>\bar R\), and its maximiser lies there, so its partial derivatives vanish: \(r^K_0=F_K=\beta_KY_0/K^Y_0\) and \(p^R_0=F_R=\gamma Y_0/R^e_0\).
Participation caps the price of material. At these prices \[
0\;\le\;\Pi^Y_0\left(K^Y_0,R_0\right)=Y_0-\frac{\gamma Y_0}{R^e_0}\left(R^e_0+\bar R\right)-\beta_KY_0=Y_0\left[\left(1-\mu_F\right)-\frac{\gamma\bar R}{R^e_0}\right],
\] so \(R^e_0\ge\gamma\bar R/\left(1-\mu_F\right)\). As \(\kappa P_0\ge0\), \(K^Y_0\le K_0\) and \(\gamma<1\), \[
p^R_0=\gamma A_0e^{-\kappa P_0}\left(K^Y_0\right)^{\beta_K}\left(R^e_0\right)^{\gamma-1}\;\le\;\gamma A_0K_0^{\beta_K}\left(\frac{\gamma\bar R}{1-\mu_F}\right)^{\gamma-1}=\bar p^R .
\]
The recycler cannot cover the collection charge. As \(R^R_0>0\) and nothing is recovered without a treated flow, \(T_0=\varpi_0H_0>0\), and \(R^R_0=\left(1-e^{-\xi x}\right)T_0<T_0\) with \(x=K^R_0/T_0\). By (OA2) the pair does at least as well as \(\left(0,0\right)\), at which (\(\Pi^W\)) is zero. With \(p^R_0>0\), \(c^T\ge0\) and \(r^K_0K^R_0\ge0\), \[
0\;\le\;\Pi^W_0\left(\varpi_0,K^R_0\right)=p^R_0R^R_0-c^cT_0-c^T\left(\varpi_0\right)H_0-r^K_0K^R_0\;<\;\left(p^R_0-c^c\right)T_0 ,
\] so \(c^c<p^R_0\le\bar p^R=c^c\), a contradiction. Hence \(R^R_0=0\): the path recycles nothing at date \(0\), the one date before \(t^*\). The inequality \(c^c<p^R_0\) is the necessary condition in item 2 of Proposition 9 of the paper, that the open-access economy treats only if \(\bar aF_R>c^c\), reached here from the operating profit alone.
Step 6: from \(t^*\) on the remaining budget stays below \(\bar R/\mu\). As \(\mathcal B_t=\mathcal W_t\) and \(R^R_0=0\), Lemma B(a) gives \(\mathcal B_1=\mathcal B_0-H_0=\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W_0\). So \[
\mu\mathcal B_1=\left(1-\mu\right)\mu\mathcal W_0=\frac{1-\mu}{1-\mu_F}\,\bar R\;<\;\bar R ,
\] as \(\mu>\mu_F\), and by Lemma B(a), \(\mathcal B_t\le\mathcal B_1<\bar R/\mu\) at every date \(t\ge t^*\).
Step 7: the open-access path is in state A. At date \(0\), \(R_0=N_0+R^R_0=0<\bar R\). At every date \(t\ge1\), \(N_t=0\), so the throughput cap and step 6 give \(R_t=R^R_t\le\mu\mathcal W_t=\mu\mathcal B_t<\bar R\). No date operates: the operating set is empty, hence finite, and the path is in state A.
What the open-access part uses. Steps 5 to 7 use the constraints of Problem 1, the conditions (OA2) and (OA3), the output function, the yield, the collection and treatment charges and the initial stocks, and of extraction and exploration only that the initial stocks leave nothing to extract or discover, by Lemma Z(a). They use nothing about \(u\), \(v\), \(\rho\) or \(\eta\), and no condition on the household’s or the mine’s choices: the open-access part holds for every preference pair.

Three further facts show how the economy works; the theorem does not use them. First, the class of open-access paths is not empty. The path with, at every date, \(N_t=D_t=0\), \(\varpi_t=0\), \(K^R_t=0\), \(\Omega_t=0\), \(K_{t+1}=\tfrac12\left(1-\delta\right)K_t\), \(C_t=\tfrac12\left(1-\delta\right)K_t\) and \(p^R_t=r^K_t=0\), the states following the transitions, is one. Its material input, output and cost flows are zero, so \(C_t+K_{t+1}-\left(1-\delta\right)K_t=0\) is its goods constraint, \(W_t=0\) its ledger and \(\Omega_t=0\) its intensity condition; every date is idle; and at zero prices (\(\Pi^W\)) is at most zero, its value at \(\left(0,0\right)\). Second, every open-access path of the economy is idle at every date: a date with \(R_t>0\) operates, and the argument of step 5 then gives \(R_t>\bar R\), which step 7 excludes. Third, the open-access economy fails for want of a recycler, not of a producer. By the choice of \(x_0\), \(\left(1-\mu_F\right)\left(\underline R-\bar R\right)/\left(\mu_F\bar R\right)>s^{1/\left(2\gamma\right)}\ge\left(\gamma/\mu_F\right)^{1/2}>\gamma/\mu_F\), so along the path of Lemma W, \(R^e_t\ge\underline R-\bar R>\gamma\bar R/\left(1-\mu_F\right)\): a final-goods sector paid its marginal products there would participate, by the computation of step 5. Yet at date \(0\) no recycler covers the collection charge that this path pays on every handled tonne.
crumbs: 14  O.11 A laissez-faire collapse where the planner survives

title: O.11, continued: the planner’s side, a path with a finite value and an optimal path
text:
What the lemmas use
The proof of Theorem 1 of the paper (a laissez-faire collapse where the planner survives) needs two facts about the planner’s problem in the economy it constructs: a feasible path with a finite value, and an optimal path. This page proves both, as Lemmas W and E, for a class of economies that contains that one, together with Lemma Z on what every feasible path of such an economy does. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page. We take the simplest route: the path of Lemma W closes the loop from the first period along an explicit schedule of recycling capital, and Lemma E finds an optimal path by compactness, with no first-order condition.
From Section 2 of the paper. A feasible path meets every constraint of Problem 1: the goods constraint \(Y=C+I+\delta K+C^N+C^D+C^W\), the ledger \(W_t=R_t-\Delta M^K_{t+1}\), the intensity condition \(R=\Omega\left(\mathcal D+\phi^IG\right)\) with \(\mathcal D\equiv\omega^YY+\omega^NC^N+\omega^DC^D+\omega^WC^W+\omega^CC\) and \(G\equiv I+\delta K\), and the transitions, with the flows as Section 2 defines them; the domains \(C,N,D,K^R,W,\Omega\ge0\), \(K_{t+1}\ge0\) and \(\varpi_t\in\left[0,1\right]\); and the mass restrictions \(S_t\ge0\), \(X_t\le\bar X_{\max}\) and \(M^K_t\ge0\). Capital is split as \(K=K^Y+K^R\), so \(0\le K^R_t\le K_t\). The handled flow is \(H_t\equiv\mu\mathcal W_t\) and the treated flow \(T_t\equiv\varpi_tH_t\); recovered material is \(R^R_t=\mathcal R\left(T_t,K^R_t\right)\), where \(\mathcal R\left(T,K\right)=a\left(K/T\right)T\) for \(T>0\) and nothing is recovered at \(T=0\), \(\mathcal R\left(0,K\right)=0\); and \(R=N+R^R\). The handled stream emits \(\Xi^h\equiv\left[1-\varpi+d^W\varpi\left(1-a\right)\right]H\), which reads \(\Xi^h=H-R^R-\left(1-d^W\right)\left(T-R^R\right)\), the displaced mass is \(\mathcal N\equiv\Omega^{N,S}N+\Omega^{D,S}D\), and pollution follows \(P_{t+1}=\left[1-\theta\left(P_t\right)\right]P_t+\Xi^h_t+\mathcal N_t\). Welfare is \(U_0=\sum_{t\ge0}\beta^t\left[u\left(C_t\right)-v\left(P_t\right)\right]\), with \(\beta\equiv1/\left(1+\rho\right)\). The value of a feasible path is the limit, as \(n\to\infty\), of the partial sums of \(U_0\) up to date \(n\), where that limit exists in \(\left[-\infty,\infty\right]\), and is finite when the limit is a real number; an optimal path is a feasible path whose value exists and is at least the value of every feasible path whose value exists.
The economies (E). An economy (E) is Problem 1 with these primitives and initial stocks, every other primitive being any that Section 2 allows: a floor \(\bar R>0\); for \(R\ge\bar R\), output \(\mathcal F=A_0\Gamma^te^{-\kappa P}\left(K^Y\right)^{\beta_K}\left(R^e\right)^{\gamma}\) with \(A_0>0\), \(\Gamma>1\), \(\kappa\ge0\), \(\beta_K,\gamma>0\) and \(\beta_K+\gamma<1\), and \(F=0\) below the floor; the yield \(a\left(x\right)=1-e^{-\xi x}\) with \(\xi>0\); \(\phi^I=0\) and \(\omega^C>0\); a collection charge \(c^c>0\) and a treatment cost \(c^T\), both constant in time; a decay rate \(\theta\) continuous with values in \(\left(0,1\right)\); CRRA utility \(u\left(C\right)=C^{1-\eta}/\left(1-\eta\right)\) with \(\eta>1\), so that \(u<0\) on \(\left(0,\infty\right)\) and \(u\left(0\right)=-\infty\); a disutility \(v\) real-valued, continuous and nondecreasing on \(P\ge0\); and the initial stocks \(S_0=0\), \(X_0=\bar X_{\max}\), \(M^K_0=0\), \(\mathcal W_0>0\), \(P_0\ge0\) and \(K_0>0\). Write \(\bar P\equiv P_0+\mathcal W_0\). As \(\gamma>0\), \(\mathcal F\) vanishes at \(R^e=0\), so \(F\) is continuous in \(\left(K^Y,R,P\right)\) on \(\left[0,\infty\right)^3\) at every date; and \(c^T\), being differentiable, is continuous.
Lemma Z. Take an economy (E) and a path that meets the transitions and the ledger of Problem 1, the domains \(N,D,K^R,W\ge0\) and \(\varpi_t\in\left[0,1\right]\), and the mass restrictions; every feasible path does. At every date:
(a) \(N_t=D_t=0\), \(S_t=0\), \(X_t=\bar X_{\max}\) and \(M^K_t=0\), so \(C^N_t=C^D_t=0\), \(\mathcal N_t=0\) and \(W_t=R_t=R^R_t\);
(b) \(0\le R^R_t\le T_t\le H_t\) and \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\mathcal W_t-\left(H_t-R^R_t\right)\), so \(\mathcal W_t\) is nonnegative and nonincreasing;
(c) \(0\le\Xi^h_t\le\mathcal W_t-\mathcal W_{t+1}\) and \(0\le P_t\le\bar P\).
crumbs: 15  O.11, continued: the planner's side, a path with a finite value and an optimal path

title: O.11, continued: the planner’s side, a path with a finite value and an optimal path
text:
Proof. 

As \(X_{t+1}=X_t+D_t\le\bar X_{\max}\) with \(D_t\ge0\) and \(X_0=\bar X_{\max}\), induction gives \(D_t=0\) and \(X_t=\bar X_{\max}\). Then \(S_{t+1}=S_t-N_t\ge0\) with \(N_t\ge0\) and \(S_0=0\) gives \(N_t=0\) and \(S_t=0\). Section 2 sets \(C^N\left(0,S,t\right)=C^D\left(0,X,t\right)=0\), and \(\mathcal N=\Omega^{N,S}N+\Omega^{D,S}D=0\). With \(\phi^I=0\) the transition of embodied material reads \(M^K_{t+1}=\left(1-\delta\right)M^K_t\), so \(M^K_t=0\), and the ledger gives \(W_t=R_t\), which is \(R^R_t\) as \(N_t=0\).
With \(W_t=R^R_t\), the waste-stock transition reads \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W_t+R^R_t=\mathcal W_t-\left(H_t-R^R_t\right)\). Let \(\mathcal W_t\ge0\), as at \(t=0\). Then \(H_t\ge0\) and \(T_t=\varpi_tH_t\in\left[0,H_t\right]\), and \(R^R_t\in\left[0,T_t\right]\), as \(\mathcal R\left(T,K\right)=\left(1-e^{-\xi K/T}\right)T\le T\) for \(T>0\) and \(\mathcal R\left(0,K\right)=0\). So \(\mathcal W_{t+1}\ge\left(1-\mu\right)\mathcal W_t\ge0\) and \(\mathcal W_{t+1}\le\mathcal W_t\), and induction completes (b).
By (b), \(\Xi^h_t=H_t-T_t+d^W\left(T_t-R^R_t\right)\ge0\), and \(\Xi^h_t=H_t-R^R_t-\left(1-d^W\right)\left(T_t-R^R_t\right)\le H_t-R^R_t=\mathcal W_t-\mathcal W_{t+1}\), as \(d^W<1\). As \(\theta\in\left(0,1\right)\) and \(\mathcal N_t=0\), \(P_{t+1}=\left[1-\theta\left(P_t\right)\right]P_t+\Xi^h_t\) lies between \(0\) and \(P_t+\Xi^h_t\) when \(P_t\ge0\). By induction \(0\le P_t\le P_0+\sum_{s<t}\left(\mathcal W_s-\mathcal W_{s+1}\right)=P_0+\mathcal W_0-\mathcal W_t\le\bar P\).

title: O.11, continued: the planner’s side, a path with a finite value and an optimal path
section: A feasible path with a finite value
text:
A feasible path with a finite value
Lemma W. Let an economy (E) have constants \(x_0\ge1/\xi\) and \(k>0\) with \(K_0=k+x_0\mu\mathcal W_0\), \[
b\equiv\frac{\mu e^{-\xi x_0}}{1-\Gamma^{-1}}<1,
\qquad
\underline R\equiv\left(1-e^{-\xi x_0}\right)\left(1-b\right)\mu\mathcal W_0>\bar R ,
\] and \[
\underline C\equiv A_0e^{-\kappa\bar P}\left(\underline R-\bar R\right)^{\gamma}k^{\beta_K}-\delta k-\mu\mathcal W_0\left(\delta x_0+\frac{\ln\Gamma}{\xi}\right)-\left[c^c+c^T\left(1\right)\right]\mu\mathcal W_0\;>\;0 .
\] Then Problem 1 has a feasible path with \(R_t\ge\underline R\) and \(C_t\ge\underline C\) at every date, so that every date operates, and its value is finite.

Proof. The path. Let \(x_t\equiv x_0+t\ln\Gamma/\xi\), so that \(e^{-\xi x_t}=e^{-\xi x_0}\Gamma^{-t}\). At every date set \(N_t=D_t=0\), \(\varpi_t=1\), \(K^R_t=x_t\mu\mathcal W_t\) and \(K_{t+1}=k+x_{t+1}\mu\mathcal W_{t+1}\), with \(I_t\equiv K_{t+1}-K_t\), \(C_t\) from the goods constraint, \(W_t=R_t\), \(\Omega_t\equiv R_t/\mathcal D_t\), and the states from the transitions. With \(\varpi_t=1\) the treated flow is \(H_t=\mu\mathcal W_t\) and capital per treated tonne is \(x_t\), so \(R_t=R^R_t=\left(1-e^{-\xi x_t}\right)\mu\mathcal W_t\) and \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\left(1-\mu e^{-\xi x_t}\right)\mathcal W_t\), which is positive as \(\mu e^{-\xi x_t}<1\). So \(\mathcal W_{t+1}\), and with it \(K_{t+1}\), is fixed at date \(t\), and the construction is recursive. As \(K_0=k+x_0\mu\mathcal W_0\), \(K_t=k+K^R_t\) and \(K^Y_t=k>0\) at every date. The path meets the transitions, the ledger, the domains of \(N\), \(D\), \(K^R\), \(W\) and \(\varpi\), and the mass restrictions, \(S\), \(X\) and \(M^K\) staying at their initial values; so Lemma Z applies to it.
The waste stock and material input. With \(b_s\equiv\mu e^{-\xi x_s}\in\left(0,1\right)\), \(\sum_{s\ge0}b_s=\mu e^{-\xi x_0}\sum_{s\ge0}\Gamma^{-s}=b\). As \(\prod_{s<t}\left(1-b_s\right)\ge1-\sum_{s<t}b_s\), by induction from \(\left(1-B\right)\left(1-b_t\right)\ge1-B-b_t\) for \(B\ge0\), \(\left(1-b\right)\mathcal W_0\le\mathcal W_t\le\mathcal W_0\). As \(x_t\ge x_0\), \(R_t\ge\left(1-e^{-\xi x_0}\right)\left(1-b\right)\mu\mathcal W_0=\underline R>\bar R\): every date operates, with \(R^e_t\ge\underline R-\bar R>0\).
Output, handling and capital formation. By Lemma Z(c), \(P_t\le\bar P\), so \(Y_t=A_0\Gamma^te^{-\kappa P_t}k^{\beta_K}\left(R^e_t\right)^{\gamma}\ge\underline Y\Gamma^t\), with \(\underline Y\equiv A_0e^{-\kappa\bar P}\left(\underline R-\bar R\right)^{\gamma}k^{\beta_K}\). By Lemma Z(a), \(C^N_t=C^D_t=0\), and the handling cost is \(C^W_t=\left[c^c+c^T\left(1\right)\right]\mu\mathcal W_t\le\left[c^c+c^T\left(1\right)\right]\mu\mathcal W_0\). Gross capital formation is \(G_t=K_{t+1}-\left(1-\delta\right)K_t=\delta k+\mu\left[x_{t+1}\mathcal W_{t+1}-\left(1-\delta\right)x_t\mathcal W_t\right]\). As \(\mathcal W_{t+1}\le\mathcal W_t\) and \(x_{t+1}=x_t+\ln\Gamma/\xi\), \[
G_t\;\le\;\delta k+\mu\mathcal W_t\left(\delta x_t+\frac{\ln\Gamma}{\xi}\right)\;\le\;\delta k+\mu\mathcal W_0\left(\delta x_0+\frac{\ln\Gamma}{\xi}\right)+t\,\delta\mu\mathcal W_0\frac{\ln\Gamma}{\xi} .
\]
Consumption is at least \(\underline C\). The goods constraint gives \(C_t=Y_t-G_t-C^W_t\). With \(\Gamma^t\ge1+t\ln\Gamma\), \[
C_t\;\ge\;\underline C+t\ln\Gamma\left(\underline Y-\frac{\delta\mu\mathcal W_0}{\xi}\right).
\] The hypothesis \(\underline C>0\) gives \(\underline Y>\delta\mu\mathcal W_0x_0\ge\delta\mu\mathcal W_0/\xi\), as \(x_0\ge1/\xi\), so the second term is nonnegative and \(C_t\ge\underline C>0\).
The path is feasible. The goods constraint holds by the definition of \(C_t\), and the ledger by \(W_t=R_t\ge0\) with \(M^K=0\). The intensity condition is \(R_t=\Omega_t\mathcal D_t\), as \(\phi^I=0\); every term of \(\mathcal D_t\) is nonnegative, so \(\mathcal D_t\ge\omega^CC_t>0\), and \(\Omega_t=R_t/\mathcal D_t\ge0\) meets it. The domains hold, with \(C_t>0\), \(0\le K^R_t<K_t\) and \(K_{t+1}>0\); the transitions and the mass restrictions hold by construction.
The value is finite. As \(u\) is increasing and negative, \(u\left(\underline C\right)\le u\left(C_t\right)<0\), and \(v\left(0\right)\le v\left(P_t\right)\le v\left(\bar P\right)\). So both \(\sum_t\beta^tu\left(C_t\right)\) and \(\sum_t\beta^tv\left(P_t\right)\) converge absolutely, and the value is a real number.
crumbs: 15  O.11, continued: the planner's side, a path with a finite value and an optimal path

title: O.11, continued: the planner’s side, a path with a finite value and an optimal path
text:
An optimal path
Lemma E. If some feasible path of an economy (E) has a finite value, Problem 1 has an optimal path.

Proof. Every feasible path has a value. By Lemma Z(c), \(0\le P_t\le\bar P\), so with \(\bar v\equiv\max_{\left[0,\bar P\right]}\left|v\right|\), finite as \(v\) is continuous, \(\sum_t\beta^tv\left(P_t\right)\) converges absolutely. As \(u<0\) on \(\left(0,\infty\right)\) and \(u\left(0\right)=-\infty\), the partial sums of \(\sum_t\beta^tu\left(C_t\right)\) are nonincreasing and converge in \(\left[-\infty,0\right]\). So the value exists, and it is at most \(-v\left(0\right)/\left(1-\beta\right)\), as \(v\) is nondecreasing.
A relaxed problem. A programme is a sequence of reals \(\pi=\left(C_t,K_{t+1},\varpi_t,K^R_t\right)_{t\ge0}\). Given \(\pi\) and the initial stocks, \(K_0\) among them and \(K_t\) for \(t\ge1\) a coordinate of \(\pi\), define date by date \(H_t=\mu\mathcal W_t\), \(T_t=\varpi_tH_t\), \(R_t=\mathcal R\left(T_t,K^R_t\right)\), \(\mathcal W_{t+1}=\mathcal W_t-\left(H_t-R_t\right)\), \(\Xi^h_t=H_t-R_t-\left(1-d^W\right)\left(T_t-R_t\right)\), \(P_{t+1}=\left[1-\theta\left(P_t\right)\right]P_t+\Xi^h_t\), \(Y_t=F\left(K_t-K^R_t,R_t,P_t,t\right)\) and \(C^W_t=\left[c^c\varpi_t+c^T\left(\varpi_t\right)\right]H_t\). Let \(\mathbb S\) be the set of programmes that satisfy, at every date, \[
C_t\ge0,\quad K_{t+1}\ge0,\quad\varpi_t\in\left[0,1\right],\quad0\le K^R_t\le K_t,\quad C_t\le g_t\left(\pi\right)\equiv Y_t+\left(1-\delta\right)K_t-K_{t+1}-C^W_t .
\] With \(N=D=0\), \(W=R\) and \(S\), \(X\) and \(M^K\) at their initial values, a programme in \(\mathbb S\) defines a path that meets the hypotheses of Lemma Z, so its conclusions (b) and (c) hold on it. A feasible path has \(N=D=0\), \(C^N=C^D=0\), \(W=R\) and these flows, by Lemma Z(a), so its programme is in \(\mathbb S\), with \(C_t=g_t\) the goods constraint, and its value is \[
U\left(\pi\right)\;\equiv\;\sum_{t\ge0}\beta^tu\left(C_t\right)-\sum_{t\ge0}\beta^tv\left(P_t\right).
\]
Every coordinate lies in a compact interval. On \(\mathbb S\), \(R_t\le H_t\le\mu\mathcal W_0\) by Lemma Z(b), and output is zero below the floor, so \(Y_t\le A_0\Gamma^tK_t^{\beta_K}\left(\mu\mathcal W_0\right)^{\gamma}\), as \(K^Y_t\le K_t\), \(R^e_t\le R_t\) and \(e^{-\kappa P_t}\le1\). As \(C_t\ge0\) and \(C^W_t\ge0\), \(K_{t+1}\le\left(1-\delta\right)K_t+Y_t\). Let \(\bar K_0\equiv K_0\), \(\bar Y_t\equiv A_0\Gamma^t\bar K_t^{\beta_K}\left(\mu\mathcal W_0\right)^{\gamma}\) and \(\bar K_{t+1}\equiv\left(1-\delta\right)\bar K_t+\bar Y_t\); the map \(K\mapsto\left(1-\delta\right)K+A_0\Gamma^tK^{\beta_K}\left(\mu\mathcal W_0\right)^{\gamma}\) is nondecreasing, so by induction \(K_t\le\bar K_t\). Hence at every date \(0\le C_t\le g_t\le\bar Y_t+\bar K_t\), \(0\le K_{t+1}\le\bar K_{t+1}\), \(\varpi_t\in\left[0,1\right]\) and \(0\le K^R_t\le\bar K_t\): each coordinate of a programme in \(\mathbb S\) lies in a compact interval that depends on its date alone.
Limits stay in \(\mathbb S\). Every sequence of programmes in \(\mathbb S\) has a subsequence that converges coordinate by coordinate: extract one along which the first coordinate converges, from it one along which the second does, and so on, and take the diagonal. Every flow and state of date \(t\) is a continuous function of finitely many coordinates, by induction on \(t\): \(\mathcal R\) is continuous on \(\left[0,\infty\right)^2\), since \(\mathcal R\left(T,K\right)=\left(1-e^{-\xi K/T}\right)T\) for \(T>0\) and \(0\le\mathcal R\left(T,K\right)\le T\); and \(\theta\), \(c^T\) and \(F\) are continuous. So each inequality that defines \(\mathbb S\) is preserved in the limit, and a coordinatewise limit of programmes in \(\mathbb S\) is in \(\mathbb S\).
The value is upper semicontinuous. Let programmes \(\pi^n\) in \(\mathbb S\) converge coordinate by coordinate to \(\pi\). Each \(P^n_t\to P_t\), and \(\left|\beta^tv\left(P^n_t\right)\right|\le\beta^t\bar v\), so \(\sum_t\beta^tv\left(P^n_t\right)\to\sum_t\beta^tv\left(P_t\right)\), the tails being uniformly small. For every \(m\), \(\sum_{t\le m}\beta^tu\left(C^n_t\right)\to\sum_{t\le m}\beta^tu\left(C_t\right)\) in \(\left[-\infty,0\right)\), as \(u\) is continuous from \(\left[0,\infty\right)\) to \(\left[-\infty,0\right)\), with \(u\left(C\right)\to-\infty\) as \(C\to0\). As \(u<0\), \(\sum_t\beta^tu\left(C^n_t\right)\le\sum_{t\le m}\beta^tu\left(C^n_t\right)\), so \(\limsup_n\sum_t\beta^tu\left(C^n_t\right)\le\sum_{t\le m}\beta^tu\left(C_t\right)\) for every \(m\). Letting \(m\to\infty\), \(\limsup_nU\left(\pi^n\right)\le U\left(\pi\right)\).
A maximiser. Let \(\bar U\equiv\sup_{\pi\in\mathbb S}U\left(\pi\right)\). The feasible path with a finite value gives \(\bar U>-\infty\), and \(\bar U\le-v\left(0\right)/\left(1-\beta\right)\). Take \(\pi^n\) in \(\mathbb S\) with \(U\left(\pi^n\right)\to\bar U\), and a subsequence converging to some \(\pi^*\), which is in \(\mathbb S\). Then \(U\left(\pi^*\right)\ge\limsup_nU\left(\pi^n\right)=\bar U\), so \(U\left(\pi^*\right)=\bar U\). As \(\bar U>-\infty\), \(C^*_t>0\) at every date. And \(C^*_t=g_t\left(\pi^*\right)\) at every date: otherwise, raising \(C^*_t\) to \(g_t\left(\pi^*\right)\) gives a programme in \(\mathbb S\), since \(C_t\) enters no flow and no inequality of \(\mathbb S\) but its own two, with a strictly larger \(U\), \(u\) being increasing.
The maximiser is an optimal path. Complete \(\pi^*\) with \(N_t=D_t=0\), \(I_t\equiv K^*_{t+1}-K^*_t\), \(W_t\equiv R_t\) and \(\Omega_t\equiv R_t/\mathcal D_t\), where \(\mathcal D_t\ge\omega^CC^*_t>0\). The goods constraint is \(C^*_t=g_t\left(\pi^*\right)\) with \(C^N=C^D=0\); the ledger holds with \(M^K=0\); the intensity condition holds with \(\Omega_t\ge0\), as \(\phi^I=0\); the transitions and the domains hold; and \(S\), \(X\) and \(M^K\) stay at their initial values, which meet the mass restrictions. So \(\pi^*\), completed, is a feasible path, with value \(\bar U\). Every feasible path has a value, \(U\) of its programme, which is at most \(\bar U\). So the completed \(\pi^*\) is an optimal path.

title: Shared lemmas: the first-order conditions, the pollution price and the material budget
text:
What the proofs use
This page holds what several proofs of this appendix share: the facts they take from the paper’s model and its long-run section, the first-order conditions of Problem 1 they use, and two lemmas, Lemma P on the sign of the pollution price and Lemma A on what the material budget bounds. The proofs of O.1 to O.6 and O.9 use it. Symbols are the paper’s, as on the notation page; a symbol a proof needs beyond them is defined where it is first used.
From the paper’s model. A feasible path meets every constraint of Problem 1: the goods constraint, the ledger, the intensity condition and the transitions, with the flows defined as in Section 2, the domains \(C,N,D,K^R,W,\Omega\ge0\), \(K_{t+1}\ge0\) and \(\varpi_t\in\left[0,1\right]\), and the mass restrictions \(S_t\ge0\), \(X_t\le\bar X_{\max}\) and \(M^K_t\ge0\). Capital is split between production and recycling, \(K=K^Y+K^R\), so \(K^R_t\le K_t\) and \(K^Y_t=K_t-K^R_t\) is the capital input of \(F\). We impose that the initial stocks are nonnegative. The paper takes \(\theta\) continuously differentiable, so \(\theta'\) is bounded on every bounded interval; only Lemma P uses this. Gross capital formation \(G\) is free in sign, Problem 1 restricting only \(K_{t+1}\ge0\).
Write \(\mathcal M_t\equiv M^K_t+\mathcal W_t\) and \(a_t\equiv a\left(x_t,t\right)\). Since \(R^R_t=a_t\varpi_tH_t\), the collected ledger of Section 2 reads  \[
\mathcal M_{t+1}\;=\;\mathcal M_t+N_t-\left(H_t-R^R_t\right),
\qquad
H_t-R^R_t=\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)H_t .
\tag{L}
\] The displaced mass \(\mathcal N\equiv\Omega^{N,S}N+\Omega^{D,S}D\), with \(\Omega^{N,S},\Omega^{D,S}\ge0\), is in neither stock: Section 2 sends it to the environment in the period it is displaced, and the flow reaching the environment is \(\Xi=\Xi^h+\mathcal N\), with the handled stream’s emission \(\Xi^h\equiv\left[1-\varpi+d^W\varpi\left(1-a\right)\right]H\). The waste-stock transition with \(W_t\ge0\) keeps \(\mathcal W_t\ge0\), so \(\mathcal M_t\ge0\). At a date with no treated flow, \(\varpi_tH_t=0\), nothing is recovered, \(R^R_t=0\), and we set \(a_t\varpi_t\equiv0\). Every cost flow is nonnegative: \(C^N\left(0,S,t\right)=0\) with \(C^N_N>0\), likewise \(C^D\), and \(c^c>0\), \(c^T\ge0\).
From the paper’s long-run section. The material budget is \[
\mathcal B\;\equiv\;\bar N+M^K_0+\mathcal W_0 ,
\qquad
\bar N\;\equiv\;S_0+\bar X_{\max}-X_0 ,
\] with \(\bar N\) the virgin budget, and the loop closes on a path when \(\sum_t\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)<\infty\). A variable \(Z\) grows at rate \(g\) when \(Z_{t+1}/Z_t\to1+g\). The operating set is \(\mathcal O\equiv\left\{t:R_t\ge\bar R\right\}\).
The first-order conditions used. Appendix A of the paper states the first-order conditions of Problem 1 with three provisions. The wedge provision: “Every sign asserted in this appendix holds under the wedge conditions \(1-\zeta\Omega^Y>0\) and \(1+\zeta\Omega^j>0\) for every use \(j\)”, inequalities on endogenous objects “which we maintain wherever a sign depends on them”. The Inada provision: “Consumption is interior by the Inada condition on \(u\)”. The pricing provision: “under the transversality condition \(\lim_{t\to\infty}\beta^t\lambda_tm_tZ_{t+1}=0\) for a stock \(Z\) with costate \(m\) each price is the discounted stream of the dividends the stock pays while it survives, with \(\Lambda_{t,s}\equiv\prod_{j=t+1}^{s}\left(1+r_j\right)^{-1}\)”, where \(1+r_{t+1}\equiv\lambda_t/\left(\beta\lambda_{t+1}\right)\). A candidate is read with the wedge and Inada provisions and with the transversality condition. The proofs use one consequence of the discounted stream, the sign of the pollution price, and Lemma P derives it from the transversality condition. Pollution “survives at the marginal retention factor \(1-\theta-\theta'P\)”, which we write \(\chi_t\equiv1-\theta\left(P_t\right)-\theta'\left(P_t\right)P_t\).
The Lagrangian of Problem 1 adjoins, in period \(t\) and with weight \(\beta^t\), the goods constraint at \(\lambda_t\), the ledger written with \(W\) on the left at \(\lambda_tp^W_t\), the intensity condition written with \(R\) on the left at \(\lambda_t\zeta_t\), and the pollution transition at \(-\lambda_tp^P_t\) (Appendix A.2). Consumption enters the period-\(t\) terms through \(u\left(C_t\right)\), the goods constraint, and \(\mathcal D_t\) with the weight \(\omega^C\), so its interior first-order condition is  \[
u'\left(C_t\right)=\lambda_t\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^C_t\right),
\tag{C}
\] and \(u'>0\) with the wedge condition \(1+\zeta_t\Omega^C_t>0\) gives \(\lambda_t>0\) at every date; hence \(1+r_t>0\) and \(\Lambda_{t,s}>0\). The two recycling controls \(K^R_t\) and \(\varpi_t\) enter the period-\(t\) terms only through \[
\lambda_t\Big\{Y_t-C^W_t-p^W_tR_t+\zeta_t\left[R_t-\Omega_t\left(\mathcal D_t+\phi^IG_t\right)\right]-p^P_t\Xi_t\Big\},
\] with \(Y=F\left(K-K^R,R,P,t\right)\), \(R=N+a\left(x,t\right)\varpi H\) and \(x=K^R/\left(\varpi H\right)\), \(C^W=\left[c^c\varpi+c^T\left(\varpi\right)\right]H\), \(\Xi=\Xi^h+\mathcal N\), of which only \(\Xi^h=\left[1-\varpi+d^W\varpi\left(1-a\right)\right]H\) moves with the two controls, and \(Y\) and \(C^W\) entering \(\mathcal D\) with the weights \(\omega^Y\) and \(\omega^W\). Differentiating, with \(\alpha=a-a'x\), \[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial K^R}=a',\quad
\frac{\partial R}{\partial\varpi}=\alpha H,\quad
\frac{\partial\Xi}{\partial K^R}=-d^Wa',\quad
\frac{\partial\Xi}{\partial\varpi}=-\left[\left(1-d^W\right)+d^W\alpha\right]H,\quad
\frac{\partial C^W}{\partial\varpi}=\left[c^c+c^{T\prime}\left(\varpi\right)\right]H,
\] with \(\partial Y/\partial K^R=F_Ra'-F_K\) and \(\partial Y/\partial\varpi=F_R\alpha H\). Collecting terms with \(\Omega^j\equiv\Omega\omega^j\) and the gains of Appendix A,  \[
\Psi\equiv F_R\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)+\zeta,
\qquad
\mathcal G^K\equiv\Psi-p^W+d^Wp^P,
\qquad
\mathcal G^\varpi\equiv\alpha\left(\Psi-p^W\right)+p^P\left[\left(1-d^W\right)+d^W\alpha\right]=\alpha\,\mathcal G^K+\left(1-d^W\right)p^P ,
\tag{G}
\] the derivative of the braces is \(a'\mathcal G^K-\tilde F_K\) in \(K^R\), with \(\tilde F_K\equiv F_K\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right)\) the material-adjusted marginal product of capital, and \(H\left\{\mathcal G^\varpi-\left[c^c+c^{T\prime}\left(\varpi\right)\right]\left(1+\zeta\Omega^W\right)\right\}\) in \(\varpi\). Dividing by \(\beta^t\lambda_t>0\), a candidate satisfies the recycling-capital and treatment margins  \[
a'\left(x_t,t\right)\mathcal G^K_t=\tilde F_{K,t}
\quad\text{at a date at which }K^R_t\text{ is interior, with }\varpi_tH_t>0,
\tag{KR}
\]  \[
\mathcal G^\varpi_t=\left[c^c\left(t\right)+c^{T\prime}\left(\varpi_t,t\right)\right]\left(1+\zeta_t\Omega^W_t\right)
\quad\text{at a date with }0<\varpi_t<1\text{ and }H_t>0 .
\tag{T}
\] The pollution stock \(P_{t+1}\) enters the Lagrangian through \(-\beta^{t+1}v\left(P_{t+1}\right)\), through \(Y_{t+1}\) in the goods constraint and in \(\mathcal D_{t+1}\) of period \(t+1\), and through the pollution transitions of periods \(t\) and \(t+1\), adjoined at \(-\lambda_tp^P_t\) and \(-\lambda_{t+1}p^P_{t+1}\). Its derivative is \[
-\beta^{t+1}v'\left(P_{t+1}\right)+\beta^{t+1}\lambda_{t+1}F_{P,t+1}\left(1-\zeta_{t+1}\Omega^Y_{t+1}\right)+\beta^t\lambda_tp^P_t-\beta^{t+1}\lambda_{t+1}\chi_{t+1}p^P_{t+1}=0 ,
\] and dividing by \(\beta^{t+1}\lambda_{t+1}>0\) gives the pollution costate recursion  \[
\left(1+r_{t+1}\right)p^P_t=\mathcal V_{t+1}+\chi_{t+1}p^P_{t+1},
\qquad
\mathcal V\equiv\frac{v'\left(P\right)}{\lambda}-F_P\left(1-\zeta\Omega^Y\right).
\tag{PP}
\] Iterated \(n\) times, (PP) reads \[
p^P_t=\sum_{s=t+1}^{t+n}\Lambda_{t,s}\Big[\prod_{t<i<s}\chi_i\Big]\mathcal V_s+\Lambda_{t,t+n}\Big[\prod_{t<i\le t+n}\chi_i\Big]p^P_{t+n},
\] and \(p^P_t\) is the discounted stream of the dividends \(\mathcal V\) the stock pays while it survives at the factors \(\chi\) exactly when the last term tends to zero as \(n\to\infty\).
Lemma P. On a candidate along which pollution is positive at some date, \(p^P_t>0\) at every date; in particular  \[
p^P_t\;\ge\;0 .
\tag{P}
\]
The hypothesis of Lemma P holds on every path with \(P_0>0\) or with a positive handled flow at some date: a handled tonne emits, \(\Xi^h_s>0\) when \(H_s>0\), since \(d^W>0\) and \(a<1\) at every finite intensity, and then \(P_{s+1}>0\).

title: Shared lemmas: the first-order conditions, the pollution price and the material budget
text:
State A (Definition 1): “collapse if \(\mathcal O\) is finite: production ceases after a finite total number of operating periods, output is zero thereafter, and consumption, financed from the capital stock alone, converges to zero”. After the last operating date output is zero, so the goods constraint gives \(K_{t+1}\le\left(1-\delta\right)K_t\) and \(C_t\le\left(1-\delta\right)K_t\), and capital and consumption tend to zero: a path with a finite operating set meets the whole clause.
State C (Definition 1): “if, asymptotically, extraction and discovery die, \(N,D\to0\) with \(\sum_tN_t<\infty\); material input converges to a positive level met entirely by recycling, \(R\to R_\infty>\bar R\) with \(R^R\to R_\infty\); the loop closes, \(a\varpi\to1\) with \(x\to\infty\); the two anthropogenic stocks converge; and the goods block grows at a common rate \(g>0\).” The goods block is output, capital and consumption, as the notation glosses \(g\). Part (a) uses the growth of output only; the construction of part (b) delivers all three.
Available, candidate: “A state is available in a cell when the cell’s primitives and the initial stocks admit a feasible path of Problem 1 in it […]. An available path that also satisfies the first-order conditions is a candidate.” The conditions used are listed in The first-order conditions used.
Assumption 1: “(i) Trending technology. For \(R\ge\bar R\), \(F\left(K^Y,R,P,t\right)=A_t\,\tilde{\mathcal F}\left(K^Y,B_tR^e,P\right)\) with \(A_{t+1}/A_t=1+g_A\), \(B_{t+1}/B_t=1+g_B\), \(g_A,g_B\ge0\) and \(g_A+g_B>0\). Every other primitive converges, uniformly on compact sets, to a stationary limit with the properties of Section 2, and \(\mu\) is constant. (ii) Convergence. Along the paths we classify, every variable converges after detrending: goods-block variables grow at constant asymptotic rates, and material flows and stocks decay at constant rates or converge.” Its part (iii) is not used. Part (i) gives the yield function a limit \(a^\infty\) that is increasing with \(a^\infty\left(x\right)<1\) at every finite \(x\), and since \(a\) is nondecreasing in \(t\), \(a\left(x,t\right)\le a^\infty\left(x\right)\) for all \(x\) and \(t\).





Proof. The terms are positive. \(\Lambda_{t,s}>0\) by (C). \(\mathcal V_s>0\): \(v'>0\) and \(\lambda_s>0\) make its first term positive, and its second is nonnegative because \(F_P\le0\), with \(\mathcal F_P<0\) at an operating date and \(F=0\) below the floor, and \(1-\zeta_s\Omega^Y_s>0\) by the wedge condition. \(\chi_i>0\), because \(\theta<1\), \(\theta'<0\) and \(P_i\ge0\); the pollution stock stays nonnegative from \(P_0\ge0\), since \(\Xi\ge0\) and \(\theta<1\). So the partial sums of the iterated (PP) increase with \(n\).
A nonpositive price forces \(P_{s+1}/\chi_{t,s}\to0\). Suppose \(p^P_t\le0\) at some date \(t\). The last term of the iterated (PP) is \(p^P_t\) less the partial sum, so it is at most \(-\Lambda_{t,t+1}\mathcal V_{t+1}\) for every \(n\ge1\). Write \(\chi_{t,s}\equiv\prod_{t<i\le s}\chi_i\), with \(\chi_{t,t}\equiv1\). Since \(\Lambda_{t,s}=\beta^{s-t}\lambda_s/\lambda_t\) and \(\beta^t\lambda_t\Lambda_{t,t+1}=\beta^{t+1}\lambda_{t+1}\), this reads \[
\beta^s\lambda_s\left(-p^P_s\right)\chi_{t,s}\;\ge\;\beta^{t+1}\lambda_{t+1}\mathcal V_{t+1}\;>\;0
\qquad\left(s>t\right).
\] The costate of pollution is \(-\lambda p^P\), so its transversality condition reads \(\beta^s\lambda_sp^P_sP_{s+1}\to0\). Multiplying the display by \(P_{s+1}/\chi_{t,s}\), it forces \(P_{s+1}/\chi_{t,s}\to0\).
But \(P_{s+1}/\chi_{t,s}\) is bounded away from zero. The stock loses at most its average rate, \(P_{i+1}\ge\left[1-\theta\left(P_i\right)\right]P_i\), while the price survives at the marginal factor \(\chi_i=1-\theta\left(P_i\right)+\left|\theta'\left(P_i\right)\right|P_i\). Take a date \(u>t\) with \(P_u>0\), which the hypothesis provides, since a positive stock stays positive. For every \(s\ge u\), using \(1+y\le e^y\) and \(1-\theta\left(P_i\right)\ge1-\theta\left(0\right)>0\), \(\theta\) being decreasing, \[
\frac{P_{s+1}}{\chi_{t,s}}\;\ge\;\frac{P_u}{\chi_{t,u-1}}\prod_{i=u}^{s}\frac{1-\theta\left(P_i\right)}{\chi_i}\;\ge\;\frac{P_u}{\chi_{t,u-1}}\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{1-\theta\left(0\right)}\sum_{i\ge u}\left|\theta'\left(P_i\right)\right|P_i\Big).
\] The sum is finite. By Lemma A(a) and (b), which use no first-order condition, and \(\Xi^h_i\le\left(1-a_i\varpi_i\right)H_i\), a consequence of \(d^W<1\), cumulated emissions are bounded, \(\sum_i\Xi_i\le\bar\Xi\equiv\mathcal B+\Omega^{N,S}\bar N+\Omega^{D,S}\left(\bar X_{\max}-X_0\right)\). So \(P_i\le P_0+\bar\Xi\), \(\theta\left(P_i\right)\ge\underline\theta\equiv\theta\left(P_0+\bar\Xi\right)>0\) and \(P_{i+1}\le\left(1-\underline\theta\right)P_i+\Xi_i\) at every date, and summing over \(i\le n\) gives \(\underline\theta\sum_{i\le n}P_i\le P_0+\bar\Xi\). Hence \(P_i\to0\) with \(\sum_iP_i<\infty\); as \(\theta'\) is bounded near zero, \(\left|\theta'\left(P_i\right)\right|\) is bounded from some date on, and \(\sum_i\left|\theta'\left(P_i\right)\right|P_i<\infty\). So \(P_{s+1}/\chi_{t,s}\) is bounded away from zero for \(s\ge u\), against the transversality condition, and \(p^P_t>0\).

title: Shared lemmas: the first-order conditions, the pollution price and the material budget
text:
What the material budget bounds
Lemma A. On every feasible path:
(a) \(\sum_{t\ge0}N_t\le S_0+\bar X_{\max}-X_0\) and \(\sum_{t\ge0}D_t\le\bar X_{\max}-X_0\); so \(N_t\to0\).
(b) \(\mathcal M_{n+1}+\sum_{t=0}^{n}\left(H_t-R^R_t\right)\le\mathcal B\) for every \(n\ge0\); so \(\mathcal W_t\le\mathcal M_t\le\mathcal B\) at every date, \(\sum_t\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)H_t\le\mathcal B\), and \(R_t\le N_t+\mu\mathcal B\).
(c) If \(R_t\to R_\infty>0\), then \(H_t\ge R_\infty/2\) from some date \(T_2\) on and \(\sum_{t\ge T_2}\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)\le2\mathcal B/R_\infty\): the loop closes.

Proof. 

Summing \(X_{t+1}=X_t+D_t\) and \(S_{t+1}=S_t+D_t-N_t\) over \(t<n\) gives \(\sum_{t<n}D_t=X_n-X_0\le\bar X_{\max}-X_0\) and \(\sum_{t<n}N_t=S_0-S_n+X_n-X_0\le S_0+\bar X_{\max}-X_0\), by \(S_n\ge0\) and \(X_n\le\bar X_{\max}\). A series of nonnegative terms with bounded partial sums converges, and its terms tend to zero.
Summing (L) over \(t\le n\), \[
\mathcal M_{n+1}+\sum_{t\le n}\left(H_t-R^R_t\right)=\mathcal M_0+\sum_{t\le n}N_t\;\le\;\mathcal M_0+\bar N=\mathcal B
\] by (a). Both terms on the left are nonnegative, since \(\mathcal M_{n+1}\ge0\) and \(R^R_t=a_t\varpi_tH_t\le H_t\). The last claim is \(R_t=N_t+R^R_t\) with the throughput cap of Section 2, \(R^R_t\le\bar a\mu\mathcal W_t\le\mu\mathcal B\).
By (a), \(R^R_t=R_t-N_t\to R_\infty\), so \(H_t\ge R^R_t\ge R_\infty/2\) for all \(t\) from some \(T_2\) on, and by (b) \(\tfrac12R_\infty\sum_{t\ge T_2}\left(1-a_t\varpi_t\right)\le\sum_{t\ge T_2}\left(H_t-R^R_t\right)\le\mathcal B\).

title: The century fit
text:
Section 5 of the paper sets the observed economy of pair B, solved from the stocks of 1900, against the data in its figure of the century. Appendix D.2 gives the calibration: the level of the handling charges is fitted to the data’s 2015 treated share, 0.2407, and on the path drawn the observed economy’s is 0.2389. In 2015 the observed economy’s material input and extraction are on the data, its secondary input is a fifth above and its waste flow a quarter above. It treats and recycles nothing before 1986, while the accounts treat an eighth to a third of the outflow throughout the century, a series the page on the phases draws. Laissez-faire stays within a percent of the observed path in every series but the treated share and secondary input, which differ by about a tenth; the planner corner, at the same charges, treats nearly twice the 2015 share and is the benchmark, not a description of 2015. We give these paths under each preference pair, with the partial property right over the waste stock beside them, year by year.


This figure is drawn in the browser and needs JavaScript. Its data: century.json.


The model’s path of the chosen series under the chosen preference pair and economy, year by year, against the data; it opens on the observed economy under pair B. The partial property right is observed policy, the landfill tax kept, with a partial private property right over the waste stock; the share it covers, named in the selector, is the controlled share of municipal waste. Output \(Y\) and capital \(K\) in trillions of 2011 international dollars; material input \(R\), extraction \(N\), secondary input \(R^R\) and the waste flow \(W\) in gigatonnes a year; the pollution stock \(P\) in gigatonnes; the treated share \(\varpi\) as a share of the handled flow, whose data the figure marks in 2015 alone, the share the handling level is fitted to; the data’s series, which the paper’s figure draws, is on the page on the phases. “As the paper draws it” puts \(Y\), \(K\), \(R\), \(N\), \(W\) and \(P\) on a logarithmic axis and \(R^R\) and \(\varpi\) on a level one. The table view lists the values every tenth year and in the years the paper’s tables print; the download gives every year, and the data page every series at once. Source: century.json. Symbols as on the notation page.

In its opening view the figure shows the observed economy’s output under pair B four fifths above the data in 1950 and at nine tenths of it in 2015.

title: The long-run taxonomy and the floor grid
text:
The long-run state by cell
Section 5 of the paper places the planner corner, the observed economy and laissez-faire of pair B in the taxonomy of Section 3, in its figure of the long-run state by cell. A cell’s state is assigned from its primitives and the closure criterion, not read off a solved path. What the solved paths measure is the survival ratio \(\mathcal M_\infty/(\bar R\mathcal T)\), which must exceed one for the economy to survive (Proposition 3 of the paper). At a floor of 23.8 gigatonnes a year, a quarter of 2015 material input imposed from 1900, the three economies’ ratios are 43.02, 42.74 and 42.71 respectively; at 41.57 gigatonnes, the largest floor that solves on the finer grid of the survival surface, the planner’s is 24.5; so survival is not at stake at any floor we solve. Appendix D.4 adds that a floor cell is a counterfactual economy, its 1900 material input at least the floor, and that the edge, between 41.57 and 41.94 gigatonnes, is where the solver’s route stops, not a property of the model. We give each cell for every economy and preference pair, and the planner’s ratio under pair B on a finer grid of floors.
For the planner corner of pair B the grid assigns state C to every cell of the soft ceiling, the baseline, that solves, and under the hard ceiling of 0.708, the measured one, state B without a floor and state A at each floor that solves, marked n.r. since under pair B a path in state A is worth \(-\infty\).

title: Leakage against welfare
text:
Appendix D.4 of the paper lists this page for the welfare gain of recycling against the leakage it avoids. Each cell of material floor, yield ceiling and tail rate \(\xi\) is set against the same cell without recycling, and gives two numbers: the share of the cumulative emissions of the economy without recycling that recycling avoids, and the consumption-equivalent gain from recycling. We give all eighteen cells under each preference pair. Under pair B recycling avoids 11 to 31 percent of those emissions, and the gain is 0.055 to 0.653 percent of consumption without a floor and 0.106 to 1.098 percent in the three soft-ceiling cells with a floor, where the economy without recycling is in state A and the comparison is decided for the one that recycles. The six hard-ceiling cells with a floor compare two collapsing paths and, under pair B, are not ranked.


This figure is drawn in the browser and needs JavaScript. Its data: leakage.json.


One point per cell of material floor \(\bar R\) (gigatonnes a year), yield ceiling \(\bar a\) and tail rate \(\xi\), each against the same cell without recycling, its yield ceiling set to \(\bar a=0.01\) so that the recycling margin is at its corner, at the same floor and tail rate. Horizontal axis: the cumulative emissions recycling avoids, in percent of the emissions of the economy without recycling, the ratio of the two cumulative sums \(\sum\Xi\) in the table. Vertical axis: the consumption-equivalent gain from recycling, the proportional supplement to consumption, in percent, that would make the economy without recycling as good as the cell. Colour: the long-run state the taxonomy assigns; marker: the floor. A comparison in which one path survives and the other collapses is decided for the survivor (dec., ringed), and the gain drawn is the gap between the two welfare sums to the horizon; one in which both collapse cannot be ranked (n.r.) and is not drawn. The table adds the cumulative emissions with and without recycling and those avoided, in gigatonnes, the retained endowment \(\mathcal M_\infty\) in gigatonnes and the survival ratio \(\mathcal M_\infty/(\bar R\mathcal T)\). Source: leakage.json. Symbols as on the notation page.

In its opening view, pair B, the figure shows the gain from recycling rising, without a floor, with the tail rate at every ceiling and with the ceiling at every tail rate, and each soft-ceiling cell with a floor gaining more than the same cell without one.

title: The sixteen corners
text:
Section 4 of the paper leaves two questions to the calibration: how the owned stockpile, the waste stock owned and no instrument set, ranks against laissez-faire, and in which direction the missing emission tax and the attribution failure move the retained endowment along equilibrium paths. Section 5 states that no setting of the instruments we solve comes near the survival margin, and Appendix D.4 that no corner costs less than the planner corner. We give every corner at no floor and at 23.8 gigatonnes a year, under each preference pair. Every corner is assigned state C, and without an owner of the waste stock the material-content price is inert, so the sixteen corners make twelve allocations. Under pair B the owned stockpile costs more than laissez-faire, 0.0136 against 0.0124 percent of consumption without a floor, as it does in every pair and at both floors. Removing the emission tax from the planner corner raises both the cumulative leakage and the retained endowment, the latter to 48,867 from 46,329 gigatonnes without a floor, and removing the discovery tax raises both too, the endowment to 48,434; removing the material-content price lowers the endowment, to 37,003. At the floor the smallest survival ratio of any corner is 33.75.


This figure is drawn in the browser and needs JavaScript. Its data: corners.json.


Each corner of the policy space, written as four digits: the first is 1 where the waste stock has an owner and 0 where it is open access, and the other three are the instruments, the material-content price, the emission tax and the discovery tax, 1 for the instrument at its Pigouvian level and 0 for the instrument off: \((1,1,1,1)\) is the planner corner, \((1,0,0,0)\) the owned stockpile, \((0,0,0,0)\) laissez-faire. The measures: the consumption-equivalent cost against the planner corner, the proportional supplement to consumption, in percent, that would make the corner as good as the planner corner, zero there by construction; the retained endowment \(\mathcal M_\infty\) in gigatonnes, read at the horizon reached; the cumulative leakage from the waste stock \(\sum(1-a\varpi)H\) in gigatonnes; and the survival ratio \(\mathcal M_\infty/(\bar R\mathcal T)\), infinite without a floor. Each at no floor and at the largest floor that solves on the calibration’s three-floor grid, 23.8 gigatonnes a year, under each preference pair; the order can be the table’s or ranked by the measure. The table adds the long-run state and the first period and year of a negative gate fee, negative throughout where the fee is negative from 1900. Source: corners.json. Symbols as on the notation page.

In its opening view, pair B without a floor, the figure shows every corner costing more than the planner corner, from 0.00197 percent of consumption at \((1,1,1,0)\), which lacks only the discovery tax, to 0.0167 at \((1,1,0,0)\), which lacks both taxes.

title: The gate-fee band
text:
The paper’s Proposition 11 signs the gate fee of an owned waste stock where the emission tax is off: under its hypotheses the fee is never positive, and negative at every date from which treatment lies ahead. With the tax on and treatment ahead, Section 4 leaves the sign to a race between the material value of a tonne and the emissions it will cause, and points here for the sign along the calibrated paths. Under pair B the planner’s fee is positive from 1900, peaks at 0.753 dollars per tonne in 1973 and is negative from 2003, as Appendix D.3 states; the owned stockpile, which faces no emission tax, has a fee negative throughout; and under pairs A and C the planner’s fee turns negative in 2009 and 2007. We give the fee year by year in three views. Each end of the range of \(\xi\) is solved at the calibrated level of the handling charges, not refitted, so across the range the 2015 treated share moves with the tail rate and the range is not a calibrated one; at its low end the observed economy treats nothing in 2015 at any level of the charges, so that end has no calibrated level, and Appendix D.4 points here for it.


This figure is drawn in the browser and needs JavaScript. Its data: gatefee.json.


The gate fee \(\tau^W\), minus the value of a tonne in the waste stock, in dollars per tonne, year by year. Three views: the planner corner under pair B at the calibrated tail rate \(\xi\) and at both ends of its range, each end solved at the calibrated level of the handling charges, with the years between the earliest and the latest change of sign shaded; the planner corner beside the owned stockpile and the partial property right under observed policy; and the planner corner under each preference pair. A marker on the zero line is the first year the fee is negative. The table gives the largest value of the fee and its year, the first period and year it is negative, negative throughout where it is negative from 1900, its value at the horizon and its value in a selection of years, every tenth year to 2100 among them; the download gives every year. Source: gatefee.json. Symbols as on the notation page.

In its opening view the figure shows the planner’s fee under pair B turning negative the earlier, the higher the tail rate: in 2052 at the low end of the range, in 2003 at the calibrated rate and in 1915 at the high end.

title: The phases
text:
The paper’s Proposition 9 gives the condition for entry into treatment, one comparison at every setting of the instruments; Section 4 notes that it orders thresholds at a common point of the price space, not entry dates along paths whose states and prices differ, and points here for the entry dates on the calibrated paths. Section 4 also describes the phases of the gate fee, positive while the waste stock is a pollution liability and negative once it is a reserve of feedstock, and points here for when the calibrated economies pass between them. We give, under pair B, the treated share year by year at the planner corner and at the two unregulated corners, laissez-faire and the owned stockpile, beside the data’s, and the gate fee at the planner corner and the owned stockpile. The planner corner begins to treat in 1980 and both unregulated corners in 1986. From 1980 to 2002 the planner treats with a positive fee, a case in which the theory does not settle the sign, and its fee is negative from 2003; the owned stockpile’s fee is negative from 1900, before it treats, as Proposition 11 requires once later treatment is foreseen.


This figure is drawn in the browser and needs JavaScript. Its data: phases.json.


Under pair B, the treated share \(\varpi\), the share of the handled flow that is treated, year by year, at the planner corner and at the two unregulated corners, laissez-faire and the owned stockpile, with a dotted line at the year each begins to treat; the data’s treated share is the recovery of the non-biomass categories over that recovery plus the disposal outflow. The second measure is the gate fee \(\tau^W\) in dollars per tonne, at the planner corner and the owned stockpile, with the first year it is negative; laissez-faire has no gate fee. The table gives each economy’s long-run state, the period and year it begins to treat and the first period and year its gate fee is negative, negative throughout where the fee is negative from 1900, and the measure in a selection of years, every tenth year to 2100 among them; the download gives every year. Source: phases.json. Symbols as on the notation page.

In its opening view the figure shows each economy’s treated share at zero until it enters, positive in every year after and reaching one, while the data’s share runs between about an eighth and a third throughout the century.

title: The preference pairs
text:
The other figures under pairs A and C
Appendix D.2 of the paper carries three preference pairs \((\rho,\eta)\), because the time preference decides every welfare level and the data do not identify it. Pair B, \((0.010,1.5)\), is the baseline; pair A, \((0.03744,1.409)\), is the intercept and slope of the world’s decade-mean real return to capital regressed on output growth; pair C, \((0.025,1.5)\), shares B’s \(\eta\). The collapse ranking condition fails under B and holds under A and C. The policy gap of Section 5 and its table are pair B’s; Section 5 points here for the smaller gap under the two other pairs, and Appendix D.2 for pairs A and C, each with its level of the handling charges refitted to the 2015 treated share. We give the experiments of that table under each pair, each pair’s calibration and the other figures of this appendix under pairs A and C. The gap is smaller under the other pairs: the planner corner from 2025 gains 0.112 percent of consumption under pair B, 0.0279 under A and 0.0454 under C, with welfare summed to 2300.
The figure shows rows (a) and (f) gaining under every pair, under A and C at between a tenth and about two fifths of their gain under B, and row (e) a loss under every pair.

title: The horizon
text:
The experiments at three horizons
Section 5 of the paper prints each consumption equivalent of its table of the policy gap with welfare summed to 2300, 2200 and 2100, and reads the rows at 2300 with the shorter horizons beside, since the horizon of 2100 leaves 75 years after 2025 and moves rows (b) and (c) by more than their size. Appendix D.4, under The fit and the horizon, states that the fitted level of the handling charges puts the observed economy’s 2015 treated share at 0.243 with the economy solved to 2100, where the level is fitted, and at 0.239 with it solved to 2300, both within the fit’s tolerance of five percent of the data’s 0.2407, and that halving the horizon moves the planner’s output over 1900 to 2000 by \(1.6\times10^{-4}\) and its consumption by \(3.6\times10^{-4}\), inside a tolerance of a thousandth. We give every experiment of pair B at the three horizons, and both checks under each preference pair.
The figure shows rows (a) and (f) gaining and row (e) losing at every horizon, the planner corner from 2025 by 0.112, 0.11 and 0.245 percent with welfare summed to 2300, 2200 and 2100, while the horizon of 2100 moves rows (b) and (c), about zero at the two longer horizons, to 0.124 and 0.169 percent.

title: The observed-policy experiments
text:
The experiments
Section 5 of the paper prices the policy gap in its table of six changes of policy from 2025 on the observed economy of pair B, each measured by its consumption equivalent against the observed economy continued: (a) the planner corner from 2025; (b) to (d) one instrument at its Pigouvian value, the others as observed; (e) an owner of the waste stock, with the landfill tax off; and (f) the planner corner from 2050. The table prints each consumption equivalent with welfare summed to 2300, 2200 and 2100. Appendix D.4 states that every continuation is in state C, so that each comparison is a consumption equivalent, and points here for the experiments in full; Appendix D.3 sets the observed instruments beside their Pigouvian values at seven dates. We add the treated share, the pollution stock, material input, extraction and secondary input, every reading in 2030, 2050 and 2100, the gate fee where the waste stock has an owner, the retained endowment, the same experiments under pairs A and C, and the instruments year by year.
In its opening view, pair B with welfare summed to 2300, the figure shows rows (a) and (f) carrying the gain, 0.112 and 0.0526 percent of consumption, rows (b) to (d) each within a hundredth of a percent of zero, and row (e) a loss of 0.0249 percent.

title: The observed-policy experiments
text:
This figure is drawn in the browser and needs JavaScript. Its data: experiments.json.


Each experiment is an unannounced change of policy, believed permanent, solved from the state the observed path carries into 2025, or into 2050 in row (f), and measured against the observed economy continued from the same state; it opens on pair B. Rows (b) to (d) set one instrument at its Pigouvian value in place of its measured path and leave the others as observed; in row (e) the waste stock has an owner, whose gate fee replaces the landfill tax. The measures: the consumption equivalent, in percent of consumption from 2025 on, the proportional rise in the consumption of the observed economy continued that would make it as good as the experiment, positive where the experiment is better, with welfare summed to 2300, 2200 or 2100 for pair B and to 2300 for pairs A and C; the treated share \(\varpi\) as a share of the handled flow, material input \(R\), extraction \(N\) and secondary input \(R^R\) in gigatonnes a year, and the pollution stock \(P\) in gigatonnes, in 2030, 2050 and 2100, on the path solved to 2300; and the gate fee \(\tau^W\) in dollars per tonne in 2025, 2050 and 2100, where the waste stock has an owner. The table adds each row’s long-run state, its retained endowment \(\mathcal M_\infty\) in gigatonnes, read at 2300, and the first year its gate fee is negative; the download gives every measure in every year. Source: experiments.json. Symbols as on the notation page.

The instruments, observed and Pigouvian

Each instrument the observed economy of pair B faces, in dollars per tonne of its base, year by year from 1900: the emission tax \(\tau^P\) per tonne of \(\Xi\), the discovery tax \(\tau^X\) per tonne of \(D\), a negative value being a subsidy, and the landfill tax \(\tau^L\) per tonne of \(W\), whose path is the upper reading, drawn beside the lower bound and the rate check of 2021, both below it. title: The sensitivities
text:
The damage coefficient and the discovery ceiling
Appendix D.4 of the paper lists this page for the sensitivities, and under The policy gap sets variants of the observed economy of pair B beside the reference of the table in Section 5. With the wedge of fuel excise net of subsidies on material input from 2010, under its revenue and its rate constructions and not refitted, the planner corner’s gain from 2025 is 0.111 and 0.128 percent against the reference’s 0.112, while the 2015 treated share misses the data’s by 6 and 17 percent. Under a sequence of surprises, each change of a measured path from 1990 to 2025 unannounced and believed permanent, the gain stays at 0.112 percent, and the sequence’s consumption equivalent against foresight, from 1900, is \(-0.000106\) percent: expectations about the measured paths move nothing at the precision printed. No variant tests the hold of the measured paths at their last values after the data end. We give the larger damage coefficient under each preference pair and the low discovery ceiling under pair B, and the observed economy beside its variants, series by series.
In its opening view the figure shows the planner corner’s retained endowment at 2300 falling under the larger damage coefficient, 6.69 times the calibrated one, to less than half its calibrated value in every pair, under pair B from 46,329 to 18,073 gigatonnes.

The table gives every quantity, the long-run state and the year the gate fee turns negative. Source: sensitivity.json. Symbols as on the notation page.

title: The series behind the century fit
text:
We give here, as tables and downloads, the data and the model’s paths behind the figure of the century in Section 5 of the paper. The figure draws the observed economy of pair B against the data from 1900 to 2015; the table gives every series of the data, and of each economy under each preference pair, year by year, the data to 2015 and the model’s paths to 2020. The figure’s note says what the data are, the material flow accounts and the national accounts, with the pollution stock the excess carbon dioxide stock converted to material at the composition of 2000 to 2015, and the note to the calibration table of Appendix D names their sources. The waste flow excludes the displaced mass, in the model as in the accounts, so its column net of the displaced mass repeats it; every other series is one panel of the figure, which draws the treated share and secondary input on level axes and the rest on logarithmic ones.

title: The extraction-cost index
text:
Appendix D.1 of the paper holds every cost coefficient constant in time but one, the level of extraction costs \(c_N(t)\), a tabulated path: the cost implied by the century’s real material price index, on a centred forty-year mean, through 2015, and its 2015 value after. It scales the whole extraction cost \(C^N\), which rises with the flow and falls with the reserve. The restriction of Section 2 that extraction costs do not rise in time therefore holds from 2015 on, and over the sample fails wherever the path rises. The calibration table of Appendix D prints the path’s value in 1900 and from 2015; we give it year by year over the sample, as a table and a download.


This figure is drawn in the browser and needs JavaScript. Its data: cn.json.


The level of extraction costs \(c_N(t)\) in the extraction cost \(C^N\), one value a year over the sample, in trillions of dollars per gigatonne raised to the power \(1+\chi_N\), with \(\chi_N\) printed on the axis; the dashed segment is the value at which the model holds it from the last year of the sample on. The table view lists every year and the download gives the same. Source: cn.json. Symbols as on the notation page.

The figure shows the level falling from 0.01446 in 1900 to 0.007397 in 2015, the value held from then on, though not monotonically: it rises over 1954 to 1965 and over 1984 to 1993, with shorter rises elsewhere.
